original_claim: Metcalfe, J., & Finn, B. (2011). Hypercorrection effect persists over a week, but high-confidence errors return. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 18, 1238-1244.
problem: Misattribution. The paper at Psychonomic Bulletin & Review 18, 1238-1244 with that exact title is Butler, Fazio & Marsh (2011), not Metcalfe & Finn. Metcalfe and Finn have their own hypercorrection papers, but not this one at this volume/pages. The brief has fused two research groups into one citation, which means the 'one-week persistence' and 'test-after-feedback blocks error return' findings are being attributed to the wrong lab. Anyone chasing this citation to justify the hypercorrection_requeue feature will not find it where the brief says it is.
corrected_claim: The one-week persistence result plus the finding that a test after corrective feedback blocks the return of high-confidence errors is Butler, A. C., Fazio, L. K., & Marsh, E. J. (2011), Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 18, 1238-1244. Metcalfe (2017, Annual Review of Psychology 68) remains the correct review citation. The substantive claim (hypercorrection is real, moderate evidence) survives; the attribution does not.
sources: Butler, A. C., Fazio, L. K., & Marsh, E. J. (2011). The hypercorrection effect persists over a week, but high-confidence errors return. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 18(6), 1238-1244. [attribution identified from volume/page/title match; NOT verified against source this session - egress blocked]

original_claim: On an error, dim the distractors, keep the item on screen, and require one re-tap of the correct hanzi before advancing - a forced second retrieval, not a passive reveal. Budget ~1.5s for this; it is the cheapest effect size in the whole product.
problem: This is the brief's single most confident UX prescription and it is a design bug that contradicts the brief's own evidence. Re-tapping a correct answer that is visible on screen is a COPY, not a retrieval - there is nothing to retrieve. The brief's own generation-effect finding says the benefit requires producing something not shown; its own prompts-beat-recasts finding is about pushing a learner to re-produce an utterance from memory, which has no analogue in tapping a highlighted option. Worse, the prompts/recasts literature (Lyster & Saito) is entirely about oral, ill-formed learner PRODUCTION in interaction; there is no ill-formed output in a 4-alternative tap, so the prompt/recast asymmetry does not transfer to this interaction at all. The brief has imported an effect size from a different task modality and spent its 'cheapest effect size' budget on a null.
corrected_claim: The mechanism that actually produces the effect the brief wants is feedback-then-RETEST at a delay, not an immediate re-tap. Show the correction, then requeue the item later in the same session (and again across sessions) so the learner must retrieve it with the answer absent. This is the Butler & Roediger (2008) / Metcalfe finding the brief already half-cites under hypercorrection. Ship the requeue; delete the 1.5s re-tap, which costs a tap per error and buys nothing measurable. The corrective-feedback meta-analyses (Li 2010; Lyster & Saito 2010) should be cited as support for 'give feedback', not for 'force an immediate re-tap'.
sources: Butler, A. C., & Roediger, H. L. (2008). Feedback enhances the positive effects and reduces the negative effects of multiple-choice testing. Memory & Cognition, 36(3), 604-616. [memory-sourced; NOT verified this session]
Lyster, R., & Saito, K. (2010). Oral feedback in classroom SLA: A meta-analysis. SSLA, 32(2), 265-302. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ892626

original_claim: Ship a 'first 100 characters' arc that is explicitly framed as 'you can now read ~40% of what's on the wall'.
problem: Two compounding errors, and this one was going to be printed in the UI. (1) Register mismatch: the ~40% top-100 and ~90% top-1000 coverage figures come from GENERAL RUNNING TEXT corpora, whose top ranks are dominated by grammatical particles and function morphemes - 的, 一, 是, 了, 不, 在, 我, 有, 他, 这, 个, 们, 上, 来, 到, 说. Almost none of those appear on signage, menus, or product labels, which are a compressed nominal register (出口, 净含量, 小心地滑, 禁止吸烟). General-corpus coverage therefore does not transfer to this app's target register - and the brief's own strongest content recommendation (build a signage sub-corpus, rank by frequency within it) directly contradicts this claim two findings earlier. (2) Token coverage is not comprehension: 40% token coverage on 2-to-4-character signs means essentially zero complete signs readable, because a short sign is close to all-or-nothing. The brief's own cited Schmitt/Jiang/Grabe linearity result is about proportion of a long text known predicting a comprehension SCORE, not about short-sign readability.
corrected_claim: Do not print any coverage percentage derived from a general-text character frequency list. Compute coverage against a signage/menu/label corpus, and report it as the metric users can verify: number of complete signs in the bank the player can now read end-to-end ('you can read 47 of the 120 signs in the metro set'), not a token percentage. The general Zipfian shape of Chinese character frequency is not in dispute; its applicability to signage is.
sources: Brief's own finding on textbook/authentic-text coverage mismatch (Language, Culture and Curriculum, 2025) https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07908318.2025.2528779
Schmitt, N., Jiang, X., & Grabe, W. (2011). The percentage of words known in a text and reading comprehension. Modern Language Journal, 95(1), 26-43.

original_claim: Build rounds as semantically blocked scenes - one round is entirely 'subway station signage' (出口 入口 换乘 检票) ... Do not shuffle domains within a round.
problem: The brief reaches this from Brunmair & Richter's words g = -0.39 and never encounters the older, directly-on-target L2 literature that cuts the other way: SEMANTIC CLUSTERING interferes with L2 vocabulary learning. Tinkham (1993, 1997), Waring (1997), Erten & Tekin (2008), Nakata & Suzuki (2019) all find that presenting words from the same semantic set together (all colours, all directions, all opposites) IMPAIRS learning relative to unrelated sets, through inter-item interference. Tinkham (1997) is the decisive distinction the brief is missing: THEMATIC clustering (words linked by an event schema - ticket, platform, train, wait) is neutral-to-helpful, while SEMANTIC clustering (co-hyponyms and antonyms) is harmful. The brief's own worked example is a textbook instance of the failure mode: 出口 and 入口 are a semantic antonym pair AND share the character 口 AND would sit as each other's distractors under the brief's 'increase distractor similarity' difficulty rule. That is the maximally interfering configuration on three axes at once.
corrected_claim: Block rounds THEMATICALLY (one event schema: buy ticket -> pass gate -> find platform -> exit), not semantically. Explicitly separate co-hyponym and antonym pairs in time: introduce 出口, consolidate it to stable recognition, and only then introduce 入口 and only then contrast them. Add an `interference_set` field distinct from `confusion_set` (semantic opposites vs visual confusables) and use it as a scheduling EXCLUSION constraint during initial learning, inverting it to a co-presentation rule only at the discrimination stage. Brunmair & Richter's words category is also unconfirmed as to whether it contains L2 vocabulary or L1 word lists - the brief flags this in its gaps but still builds the round architecture on it.
sources: Tinkham, T. (1997). The effects of semantic and thematic clustering on the learning of second language vocabulary. Second Language Research, 13(2), 138-163. [memory-sourced; NOT verified this session]
Erten, I. H., & Tekin, M. (2008). Effects on vocabulary acquisition of presenting new words in semantic sets versus semantically unrelated sets. System, 36(3), 407-422. [memory-sourced; NOT verified]
Nakata, T., & Suzuki, Y. (2019). Effects of massing and spacing on the learning of semantically related and unrelated words. SSLA, 41(2). [memory-sourced; NOT verified]

original_claim: Track rolling accuracy over the last 20 attempts and adjust distractor similarity (visually similar hanzi = harder, unrelated = easier) rather than adjusting item difficulty.
problem: Distractor similarity is the wrong difficulty dial during initial learning, and the brief adopts it without meeting the multiple-choice lure literature. Roediger & Marsh (2005) showed multiple-choice testing produces a positive testing effect AND a negative 'false knowledge' effect, with lure intrusions rising as the number and plausibility of distractors rises - learners later reproduce the lures as answers. Butler & Roediger (2008) showed feedback largely, but not entirely, removes the negative effect. Cranking similarity up exactly when rolling accuracy is low means you are maximising lure exposure precisely when the target trace is weakest. Combined with the semantic-clustering interference above, this dial is actively teaching confusions.
corrected_claim: Use retrieval demand as the difficulty dial - longer lag since last success, direction switch (meaning->hanzi rather than hanzi->meaning), and removing the scene context - while keeping distractors semantically and visually UNRELATED during initial acquisition. Escalate to confusable distractors only for items already at stable recognition, and only inside a declared discrimination drill where the confusion is the explicit learning objective and feedback names the contrast. Keep the 80%-accuracy target; change what moves to hit it.
sources: Roediger, H. L., & Marsh, E. J. (2005). The positive and negative consequences of multiple-choice testing. JEP: Learning, Memory, and Cognition, 31(5), 1155-1159. [memory-sourced; NOT verified this session]
Butler, A. C., & Roediger, H. L. (2008). Memory & Cognition, 36(3), 604-616. [memory-sourced; NOT verified]

original_claim: If the target is 300 characters at >=10 successful retrievals each, that is >=3,000 successful retrieval events ... roughly 4 hours of net play.
problem: Category error in the load-bearing planning number. Webb (2007)'s encounters are INCIDENTAL contextual meetings while reading, with no retrieval attempt and no feedback. The brief silently converts them into 'successful retrievals WITH feedback', which the testing-effect literature it cites elsewhere says are far more potent per event. The brief's own cited intentional-learning meta-analysis (Webb, Yanagisawa & Uchihara 2020: ~58-60% recall on immediate posttests) reaches high learning rates on far fewer than 10 deliberate events per item. The arithmetic is internally clean (3000/0.8 x 4s = 4.2h) but the input is not an evidence-derived constant. Separately, this budget CONTRADICTS the brief's own Cepeda trip-date schedule: a 28-day trip at 3-6 day gaps permits roughly 5-9 exposures per item, which cannot deliver >=10 successful retrievals. Two findings in the same brief prescribe mutually unsatisfiable schedules.
corrected_claim: State the retrieval budget as an engineering assumption to be calibrated from your own attempt log, not as a finding from Webb (2007). Reconcile it with the schedule: either accept ~6 well-spaced retrievals per item for a 28-day horizon (and shrink the v1 character target accordingly), or accept shorter gaps and a smaller retention interval. Instrument retrievals-to-stable-recall per item in the first cohort and replace the assumed 10 with your measured value.
sources: Webb, S. (2007). The effects of repetition on vocabulary knowledge. Applied Linguistics, 28(1), 46-65. https://academic.oup.com/applij/article-abstract/28/1/46/174744
Webb, S., Yanagisawa, A., & Uchihara, T. (2020). Modern Language Journal, 104(4), 715-738.

original_claim: Deliberate vocabulary study is three to four times more efficient than incidental learning from input. (graded: strong)
problem: The multiplier is manufactured by dividing across two meta-analyses that share no design, no time-on-task control, and no common outcome measure. The incidental figure (9-18%) comes from single-exposure reading/listening treatments; the intentional figure (58-60%) from repeated deliberate study activities. Neither meta-analysis equated minutes on task, so this is not an efficiency ratio - it is a ratio of two unrelated denominators. The brief itself notes the intentional range spans 18-77%, which alone destroys the '3-4x' precision. The direction (deliberate beats incidental per unit time for vocabulary) is well supported; the number is not a finding.
corrected_claim: Deliberate vocabulary study is more efficient than incidental learning from input for vocabulary gain per unit time - direction strong, magnitude unquantified. Drop the '3-4x'. Also drop the adjacent framing 'do not build a comprehensible-input mode and expect it to compete': input-based reading has its own meta-analytic support (Nakanishi 2015, TESOL Quarterly; Jeon & Day 2016) at small-to-moderate effects, and it is complementary rather than competing. What is genuinely unsupported is the STRONG input hypothesis - i+1, the affective filter, input as necessary and sufficient - which is a separate and much weaker claim that the brief never actually cites anyone making.
sources: Webb, S., Uchihara, T., & Yanagisawa, A. (2023). Language Teaching, 56(2), 161-180. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1373102
Nakanishi, T. (2015). A meta-analysis of extensive reading research. TESOL Quarterly, 49(1), 6-37. [memory-sourced; NOT verified this session]

original_claim: Gamification ... the effect comes from challenge, meaningful goals and narrative, NOT from reward-and-status mechanics. (graded: moderate, k = 19)
problem: Self-contradiction across two adjacent findings. The brief asserts a moderator conclusion from Sailer & Homner's k = 19 cognitive-outcome set, then in the very next finding correctly warns that with k = 9-19 the field's bias diagnostics are underpowered. Moderator tests are more power-hungry than bias tests, not less. A categorical 'X not Y' moderator claim from 19 studies is exactly the inference the brief tells the reader to distrust. My recollection is also that Sailer & Homner reported most moderators as non-significant and framed the design-quality point in discussion rather than as a significant moderator test - but that needs full-text confirmation I could not obtain.
corrected_claim: Sailer & Homner's headline effects (cognitive g = 0.49, motivational g = 0.36, behavioural g = 0.25) are the defensible part. The 'narrative beats points' moderator claim should be downgraded to a design hypothesis, not an evidence-backed directive. The practical recommendation (build scene fiction rather than a points economy) is still reasonable - it is cheap, it is consistent with the brief's own scene-based content plan, and it costs nothing if the moderator turns out to be null - but it must not be defended in a design review as 'the meta-analysis says so'.
sources: Sailer, M., & Homner, L. (2020). The gamification of learning: A meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review, 32, 77-112. https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10648-019-09498-w

original_claim: Treat any gamification number below g ~ 0.4 as noise.
problem: Invented decision rule with no source, and it is backwards as a bias heuristic. Effect magnitude is not a bias diagnostic - publication bias inflates estimates regardless of where they land, and small-study effects mean LARGE published estimates from small-k literatures are the ones most likely to be inflated. A g = 0.30 from a large preregistered trial is far stronger evidence than a g = 0.50 from k = 9 underpowered studies. The rule would have the team discard the better evidence and keep the worse.
corrected_claim: Replace the magnitude threshold with a provenance rule: weight estimates by study design, preregistration, sample size and k, not by effect size. The brief's own remedy in the same finding (build client-side deterministic bucketing and evaluate every mechanic against 7-day delayed accuracy in your own population) is correct and sufficient - it makes the literature's effect sizes irrelevant to the decision, so no threshold heuristic is needed at all.
sources: No source exists for this heuristic; it appears in the brief without citation.

original_claim: Complex targets (餐, 邊, 藥, 檢) must not be allowed to render thin.
problem: Three of the four exemplars are TRADITIONAL characters and will not appear on mainland Chinese signage. 邊 -> 边, 藥 -> 药, 檢 -> 检 in simplified. Only 餐 is shared across both sets. The brief elsewhere correctly writes 药房 and 检票 in simplified, so this is an internal inconsistency that will propagate into the item bank if anyone lifts the list. Compounding it: the legibility studies the brief cites are Traditional-character studies from Taiwan/HK, and simplified characters have systematically lower mean stroke counts, so 'stroke width dominates for high-complexity characters' over-applies to a simplified corpus where the high-complexity tail is thinner. Separately, porting a print '12pt at 1:10 stroke-width ratio' figure to a 96-120px phone hero element is an extrapolation across viewing distance, medium and rendering stack that the source does not license.
corrected_claim: Use simplified exemplars: 餐, 边, 药, 检 - and for genuinely high-stroke simplified targets that actually occur on signage, 蔬, 醬, no - use 蔬, database-check each. The stroke-weight-over-size principle is a reasonable design heuristic but should be graded weak-to-moderate for simplified characters on phone displays, and validated with an in-house legibility check at your actual render sizes rather than inherited from a Traditional print study. Keep the `stroke_count` metadata field - that part is sound.
sources: Liu, N., et al. (2016). Human Factors and Ergonomics in Manufacturing & Service Industries. https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/hfm.20663

original_claim: Engineer each scene so the player knows every character except at most one, i.e. target 100% minus one unknown per short text, and let the unknown be inferable from context or radical.
problem: Contradicts the two findings it sits between. (1) On a four-character sign, one unknown is 75% coverage - far below the 95% 'minimal comprehension' figure the brief just endorsed, and by the linearity result the brief also endorses, 75% predicts poor comprehension rather than near-complete comprehension. The coverage literature's thresholds were derived on long texts where one unknown word in twenty is a rounding error; on a 4-character sign one unknown is a quarter of the message. (2) 'Inferable from radical' is directly undercut by the brief's own radical finding (Chen & Feng 2020: radical awareness did not help meaning retention for non-transparent compounds), which the brief grades weak. Also, the coverage literature measures WORD families in alphabetic text; the brief slides between character coverage and word coverage without noting that they diverge sharply in Chinese, since many characters are bound morphemes and knowing 检 and 票 does not deliver 检票.
corrected_claim: For short signage texts, target 100% known characters within the scene and place the novelty at the WORD level - a familiar-character compound whose combined meaning is new (检票 from known 检 + known 票). This preserves an inference opportunity without the coverage problem. Reserve genuinely unknown characters for longer texts (menus, label boilerplate) where one unknown in twenty is realistic. Do not cite the 95%/98% thresholds in support of short-sign design at all - they are word-level statistics from long alphabetic texts.
sources: Schmitt, N., Jiang, X., & Grabe, W. (2011). Modern Language Journal, 95(1), 26-43.
Chen, T., & Feng, Y. (2020). SAGE Open. https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/2158244020969669

original_claim: Mekler, E. D., Bruhlmann, F., Tuch, A. N., & Opwis, K. (2017). Computers in Human Behavior, 71, 525-534. URL: sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0360131521001743
problem: URL does not match the citation. PII S0360131521001743 decodes to ISSN 0360-1315 (Computers & Education), publication year 2021 - it is neither Computers in Human Behavior nor 2017. Mekler et al. (2017) is a real and correctly-described paper, but this link points at an unrelated 2021 article. Three further source/URL mismatches in the same brief: Arroyo & Yilmaz (2018, Language Learning 68(4)) is linked to a Cambridge Core *Language Teaching* replication-call article about that study rather than to the study; Gonzalez-Fernandez & Schmitt (2020) is linked to a personal publications index page rather than the article; and the Cepeda 2008 entry is listed twice (journal article plus ERIC record ED505660) which inflates the apparent number of independent sources corroborating the ridgeline finding from one to two.
corrected_claim: Repair the links before this brief is circulated. The Mekler et al. (2017) substantive claim - points, levels and leaderboards did not affect intrinsic motivation and increased only output quantity - is, to my knowledge, accurately described; only the URL is wrong. Treat every 'abstract-only' source in this brief as link-unverified until someone with unrestricted network access re-resolves each DOI.
sources: Mekler, E. D., Bruhlmann, F., Tuch, A. N., & Opwis, K. (2017). Computers in Human Behavior, 71, 525-534.

original_claim: Chen, Chen & Dai (2020) ... meta-analysis of 25 articles (2008-2019), overall effect size 0.386.
problem: The in-text attribution and the source block disagree with each other within the same finding: the detail says 'Chen, Chen & Dai (2020)' while the citation says 'Chen, C.-H., Shih, C.-C., & Law, V. (2020)'. The latter matches the real ETR&D 68, 1855-1873 paper. 'Chen, Chen & Dai' appears to be a hallucinated author list carried into the prose.
corrected_claim: Chen, C.-H., Shih, C.-C., & Law, V. (2020). The effects of competition in digital game-based learning (DGBL): A meta-analysis. Educational Technology Research and Development, 68, 1855-1873. The substantive claim and the design implication (turn-based simultaneous-answer, not first-to-buzz) are unaffected and remain the best-argued UX call in the brief.
sources: https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1266151

original_claim: Foreign language anxiety correlates about r = -0.36 to -0.39 with achievement ... For a co-located multiplayer game this is a direct design risk. (graded: strong)
problem: The correlation is well-replicated; the transfer to this product is not, and the brief grades the package 'strong'. The FLCAS and its correlates are overwhelmingly built on classroom SPEAKING anxiety - oral performance in front of peers and an instructor is the canonical trigger and dominates the scale's items. A silent, private, tap-to-answer reading task among friends at a table is close to the low-anxiety end of that construct's range. The brief's design recommendations (private answers, aggregate-only reveal, no public per-player accuracy) are good and I would keep every one of them - but they are justified by a stronger and more direct argument the brief does not make (see added findings on social contagion), not by extrapolating a speaking-anxiety correlation to a reading tap.
corrected_claim: The FLCA-achievement association is strong as a correlational finding (r ~ -0.36 to -0.39) and causality is unestablished, as the brief correctly notes. Its applicability to a private-answer co-located reading game is an inference and should be graded moderate. Keep the privacy design; re-justify it.
sources: Teimouri, Y., Goetze, J., & Plonsky, L. (2019). SSLA, 41(2), 363-387. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1221543
Botes, E., Dewaele, J.-M., & Greiff, S. (2020). Journal for the Psychology of Language Learning, 2, 26-56.

original_claim: Cepeda et al. (2008) 10-20% rule -> ask the user for a trip date and make it the retention interval that drives scheduling.
problem: Three unstated scope violations. (1) Cepeda et al. (2008) used a SINGLE intervening study session - one gap, one review. The ratio rule is not validated for the multi-session ladder the brief wants to build from it. (2) The ridgeline is deliberately named a ridgeline because it is FLAT near the optimum; Cepeda's own framing is that recall is insensitive to gap across a broad plateau, so precision-tuning gap length buys very little and the brief's 'single most actionable spacing result' framing oversells it. (3) A trip is not a test date. It is a multi-week period of repeated, in-situ, self-reinforcing exposure, so modelling it as a one-shot retention interval at date T is a mismatch with the construct Cepeda measured. Grading this 'strong' imports the internal validity of the experiment into a use case the experiment does not cover.
corrected_claim: Use the trip date as a coarse regime selector (near trip -> shorter gaps; distant trip -> longer gaps), which is defensible and legible to users, and grade it moderate. Do not present per-item gap arithmetic derived from the 10-20% ratio as evidence-based scheduling, and do not spend engineering on precision around a flat optimum. The brief's own conclusion two findings later - that gap SIZE matters and schedule SHAPE does not, so spend nothing on tuning - should be applied to gap precision as well.
sources: Cepeda, N. J., Vul, E., Rohrer, D., Wixted, J. T., & Pashler, H. (2008). Psychological Science, 19(11), 1095-1102. https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1111/j.1467-9280.2008.02209.x

original_claim: one round is entirely 'subway station signage' (出口 入口 换乘 检票) ... real shopfront category words (药房, 便利店, 面馆)
problem: Chinese content accuracy against real mainland signage. All characters, meanings and simplified forms are correct - 出口 chukou exit, 入口 rukou entrance, 换乘 huancheng transfer, 检票 jianpiao ticket inspection, 药房 yaofang pharmacy, 便利店 bianlidian convenience store, 面馆 mianguan noodle shop. But three register problems for a corpus meant to mirror what is actually on the wall: (1) 检票 is a railway-station and scenic-gate word; Beijing/Shanghai metro signage overwhelmingly shows 进站, 出站, 安检, 售票, 自动售票机, 充值, 站台 and 换乘. (2) 药房 is defensible but the standard mainland shopfront form is 药店, or 大药房 in chain branding (老百姓大药房, 益丰大药房); a learner primed on bare 药房 may not parse 大药房. (3) 便利店 is the generic term but real shopfronts show brand names - 全家, 罗森, 美宜佳 - far more often than the category word.
corrected_claim: Swap 检票 for 安检 and 进站/出站 in the metro set; teach 药店 and 大药房 alongside 药房; and add the convenience-store and pharmacy BRAND wordmarks as recognition items, since brand recognition is what actually gets a traveller through the door. Also flag in the item bank that 面 in 面馆 is a simplified-set merger of 面 (face/surface) and 麵 (noodles) - a genuine homograph that a reading app must encode, because the same character on a menu and on a cosmetics label means different things.
sources: Direct knowledge of mainland Chinese signage conventions; no corpus verification possible this session.

original_claim: The one legitimate use of interleaving is at the character level for visually confusable hanzi (末/未, 日/曰, 千/干, 大/太/犬).
problem: The confusion sets are all linguistically correct - 末 mo / 未 wei, 日 ri / 曰 yue, 千 qian / 干 gan-gan, 大 da / 太 tai / 犬 quan - but the set is optimised for a classical-Chinese curriculum rather than for this product. 曰 and 犬 are effectively absent from modern travel signage and are low-value items. Meanwhile the single highest-value confusion pair for THIS app is missing: 人 ren (person) vs 入 ru (enter). 入口 misread as 人口 (population) is a canonical beginner error and it sits at the centre of the brief's own flagship metro scene. Also missing and travel-relevant: 己/已/巳, 天/夭, 木/本/未/末 as one family, and 王/玉.
corrected_claim: Rebuild the confusion sets from the signage corpus rather than from a generic hard-characters list. Priority pairs for a China travel reader: 人/入 (critical - 入口), 大/太, 千/干, 木/本/末/未, 己/已, 天/夭, 田/由/甲, 十/千. Drop 曰 and 犬 from v1. Keep the discrimination-training design; change its contents.
sources: Direct knowledge of Chinese orthography and common L2 confusion errors; no corpus verification possible this session.

original_claim: For 出口 the card carries 'exit - 出 out + 口 mouth/opening' ... radical decomposition on the feedback screen ... `semantic_transparency: high` flag (氵 in 河/海/酒).
problem: The brief conflates two structurally different decompositions under one schema field. 出口 = 出 + 口 is a WORD-level morphemic decomposition (two free characters compose a compound). 河 = 氵 + 可 is a CHARACTER-level semantic-phonetic decomposition (a semantic radical plus a phonetic component within one glyph). These need different UI treatments, different transparency criteria, and different metadata - a single `semantic_transparency` boolean cannot express both. The example set is otherwise correct: 河 he, 海 hai and 酒 jiu all genuinely carry 氵, and 的/是/了 are correctly identified as poor decomposition candidates (了 has no decomposition at all - it is a single-component character).
corrected_claim: Split the schema now, while it is cheap: `word_decomposition` (morphemes, with per-morpheme gloss) and `character_decomposition` (semantic component, phonetic component, transparency of each, independently rated). The phonetic side matters more than the brief realises - 可 ke in 河 he is a partial phonetic cue, and phonetic-component regularity is a real and usable cue in about a third to a half of modern compound characters. The brief models semantic transparency only and drops the phonetic dimension entirely.
sources: Chen, T., & Feng, Y. (2020). SAGE Open. https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/2158244020969669

original_claim: Physical-size conversions throughout the brief: '42 arcmin at 360 mm = 4.4 mm ≈ 17 CSS px'; '32 CSS px (~8.5 mm ≈ 81 arcmin)'; 'prompt hanzi at 48-64 CSS px (~12.7-17 mm ≈ 121-162 arcmin)'; '12pt at 96dpi ≈ 16-17 CSS px'; 'Minimum interactive height 48 CSS px (~12.7 mm) — above Parhi's 9.2 mm floor with margin'; '56 CSS px ... hitting Conradi's 14 mm'.
problem: The brief converts CSS pixels to millimetres at 96 px/inch. That is the CSS *absolute-unit* convention for print and desktop; it is not the physical density of a phone. Android defines dp as 1/160 inch and iOS defines pt as ~1/163 inch, and mobile browsers set the layout viewport to match — a modern phone renders roughly 155-165 CSS px per physical inch (iPhone 15: 393 CSS px across ~64 mm of screen = 156/inch; Pixel 8: ~166/inch). The brief is therefore off by a factor of ~1.67 on every mm and arcmin figure, and the error runs in the unsafe direction in both directions it matters. Its stated legibility floor is far too small, and its touch targets are below the very study it cites as their justification. Verified by arithmetic, not by literature: 48 CSS px is 7.6 mm, which is BELOW Parhi's 9.2 mm floor, not 'above it with margin'; 56 CSS px is 8.9 mm, not Conradi's 14 mm; 32 CSS px subtends 48.5 arcmin at 360 mm, not 81. This single error propagates through findings 3, 7 and 24 — three of the brief's most concrete specs.
corrected_claim: Convert at ~160 CSS px per physical inch (6.3 CSS px/mm) on phones, and never use CSS mm/in/pt units for physical sizing because they are nominal. Repaired numbers at a 360 mm viewing distance: the 42-arcmin preferred-size figure is ~27.7 CSS px, not 17 — so the absolute floor for a hanzi a learner must discriminate is ~28 CSS px, not 24. Running-text hanzi equivalent to the tested 12pt is ~27 CSS px, not 16-17. Answer-option hanzi should be ~40-48 CSS px (60-73 arcmin) and prompt hanzi ~64-80 CSS px (97-121 arcmin). Parhi's 9.2 mm discrete-tap floor is 58 CSS px; the serial 9.6 mm figure is 60 CSS px; Conradi's walking-safe 14 mm is 88 CSS px. So minimum interactive height should be 56-60 CSS px (not 48), answer rows 60-64 CSS px, and a street/walking mode needs ~88 CSS px targets, not 56.
sources: CSS Values and Units Level 4, §6.2: absolute lengths are anchored to 1in = 96px as a fixed ratio, explicitly not to physical device size
Android developer documentation: 1 dp = 1 physical pixel on a 160 dpi baseline screen
Apple iOS Human Interface Guidelines: point (pt) anchored to the original 163 ppi display
Arithmetic recomputation performed in-session (see verdict); contrast/geometry script output

original_claim: 'an 18-stroke character (蔬, 齿, 警)'; and elsewhere 'the easiest items (2-stroke, high-frequency: 出, 入, 男, 女)'.
problem: Every stroke count in both example sets is wrong, and one of them is a traditional/simplified confusion in a brief that explicitly ships Simplified only. 蔬 is 15 strokes (艹 3 + 疏 12). 警 is 19 strokes (敬 12 + 言 7). 齿 is 8 strokes — the 15-stroke form is the *traditional* 齒, so the brief has silently pulled a traditional-character stroke count into a Simplified-only product and used it as its worked example of maximum complexity. In the second set, only 入 is 2 strokes; 出 is 5, 女 is 3, 男 is 7. Since the brief's entire size-compensation formula keys on strokeCount, seeding it with hand-picked exemplars that are all miscounted means the formula was never sanity-checked against a single correct value.
corrected_claim: Correct counts: 蔬 15, 警 19, 齿 8 (traditional 齒 15), 出 5, 入 2, 男 7, 女 3. Do not hand-author stroke counts at all — derive strokeCount programmatically from Unihan's kTotalStrokes field (which carries separate mainland and Taiwan values, kTotalStrokes giving the simplified-context count first) and assert at build time that every character's stored count matches. Genuinely high-stroke Simplified characters suitable as complexity exemplars include 警 19, 攀 19, 囊 22, 罐 23, 蘸 22 — note how rare these are, which itself argues the complexity-compensation formula has a very small blast radius in a signage/menu bank.
sources: Unicode Han Database (Unihan), kTotalStrokes property
Table of General Standard Chinese Characters (通用规范汉字表), 2013, official stroke-count listings

original_claim: 'Distractor generation policy, in priority order: (1) a visual neighbour of the target character sharing ≥1 component (药店 vs 酒店, 大 vs 太 vs 犬)'.
problem: 药店 and 酒店 share no component whatsoever. 药 decomposes as 艹 + 约; 酒 as 氵 + 酉. They are neither visual neighbours nor component-sharing. They are confusable for an entirely different reason — both are two-character shopfront nouns ending in 店, encountered in the same physical environment — which is the brief's own priority-2 category (same semantic/situational field), not priority 1. Because this is the single worked example for the top-priority rule in the distractor policy, an implementer following it will build the wrong generator. (The other examples are fine: 大/太/犬 are genuine visual neighbours, as are 人/入, 日/白, 未/末, 己/已 — though the last should be the triple 己/已/巳 jǐ/yǐ/sì, since 巳 is the third member and the brief drops it.)
corrected_claim: Split the rule properly. Priority 1, *visual* neighbours sharing components or differing by one stroke: 大/太/犬/夫, 人/入/八, 日/白/百/自, 未/末, 己/已/巳, 千/干/于, 我/找, 天/夭. Priority 2, *situational* neighbours sharing a head noun or a place — this is where 药店/酒店/饭店/书店 belongs, along with 入口/出口 and 男/女 on toilet doors. These require different generators: priority 1 from component decomposition, priority 2 from the domain corpus for that scene. Genuine component-sharing pharmacy/hotel confusions would be e.g. 药 vs 约 (shared 约) or 酒 vs 洒 sǎ.
sources: Component decomposition per the Unihan IDS (Ideographic Description Sequence) data / CHISE IDS database
Standard dictionary decompositions: 药 = 艹 + 约; 酒 = 氵 + 酉

original_claim: 'each extra stroke needs roughly +0.25 arcmin of character size to hold legibility constant' → implemented as S_effective = S * (1 + 0.012 * max(0, strokes - 8)), graded moderate.
problem: Three separate failures. (1) The +0.25 arcmin/stroke slope does not appear in any account of Zhang et al. 2007 I can substantiate, and the brief concedes it never read the results section — a precise slope quoted from an abstract-only read is not a moderate-strength finding. (2) The formula does not implement the claim: an additive arcmin slope of 0.25/stroke over a 16-stroke range is +4 arcmin, which against a threshold base of ~20 arcmin is +20%, whereas the multiplicative formula yields +12% at 18 strokes. The formula and the cited slope are mutually inconsistent, so at most one can be right. (3) The deeper error is category: Zhang et al. measured *acuity threshold* — the smallest size at which a character is still identifiable. Threshold-derived compensation does not transfer to suprathreshold display. At 32-64 CSS px the app is running 5-10x above threshold, where the complexity penalty largely collapses; the brief's own finding 10 concedes complexity stopped affecting contrast threshold except below 0.35 deg. Sizing suprathreshold UI from an acuity-chart slope is the same mistake as sizing body copy from an eye-chart line.
corrected_claim: Drop the stroke-count size formula from v1. Set one generous hanzi size that is safe for the most complex character in the bank (≥28 CSS px floor, ≥40 CSS px for answer options per the unit correction above) and stop. The defensible complexity finding is not about size at all but about *how many* characters fit per fixation (Wang, He & Legge) and about recognition latency — so spend the complexity variable on item chunking and on time budgets, not on per-character font-size arithmetic. If a stroke-driven size ramp is wanted later, treat it as an A/B hypothesis with in-app error data as the outcome, exactly as the brief's own gaps section says.
sources: Zhang J-Y, Zhang T, Xue F, Liu L, Yu C (2007). IOVS 48(5):2383-2390 — acuity-threshold paradigm; slope value unverified in this session
Internal arithmetic inconsistency between the stated arcmin slope and the multiplicative formula

original_claim: 'Across Mayer's own multimedia-learning corpus, the biggest single lever is removing extraneous material (g = 1.00)' — used as the #1 ranked design lever ('Coherence first').
problem: The brief correctly flags that the meta-analysis is restricted to Mayer-authored papers, then proceeds to rank its entire design budget by those numbers anyway. Independent meta-analyses of the same seductive-details effect, with unrestricted author sets, find effects roughly a third the size: Rey (2012, Educational Research Review) and Sundararajan & Adesope (2020, Educational Psychology Review) report seductive-details effects in the region of g ≈ -0.30 to -0.35 on retention and transfer, not 1.00. A single-author-corpus estimate that is 3x the independent estimate is the textbook signature of the bias the brief itself named, and it should not have survived to become the top-ranked lever.
corrected_claim: Use g ≈ 0.3 for coherence/seductive-detail removal, not 1.00. Coherence is still worth doing — it is cheap, it has an independent evidence base, and it converges with Hou & Jiang's cognitive-load result — but it is no longer 4x the size of signalling, so the brief's ranking logic ('rank your design budget by these numbers') collapses. The honest position is that these principles are all small-to-moderate and roughly comparable, and the decision between them should be made on implementation cost, not on a spurious effect-size ordering.
sources: Rey GD (2012). A review and meta-analysis of the seductive detail effect. Educational Research Review 7(3):216-237
Sundararajan N, Adesope O (2020). Keep it coherent: A meta-analysis of the seductive details effect. Educational Psychology Review 32:707-734

original_claim: 'Multiple choice ... meta-analytically it produced a *larger* testing effect than short answer (g = 0.70 vs 0.48) ... This overturns the theoretical prediction that recall must beat recognition.' Graded strong.
problem: The g=0.70 vs g=0.48 contrast in Adesope et al. is a between-study moderator, not a randomised within-study comparison. Studies that used MC practice differ from studies that used short-answer practice in materials, populations, retention intervals and — critically — in final-test format. The same meta-analysis separately reports that format match inflates the effect (0.63 vs 0.53), and MC-practice studies disproportionately used MC final tests, so the two moderators are confounded with each other. The direct experimental literature that manipulates format within subjects points the other way: Kang, McDermott & Roediger (2007) found short-answer practice *with corrective feedback* produced better long-term retention than MC practice. 'MC beats recall' is not a supportable reading, and grading it strong is wrong.
corrected_claim: Downgrade to moderate and change the argument. MC is the right core loop here not because it outperforms recall, but because of transfer-appropriate processing: the criterion task (is that shopfront 药店 or 酒店) is itself a recognition task, and the meta-analysis's format-match moderator is the part of it that is not confounded. State it that way. The practical recommendation survives intact; the justification does not. Corollary the brief missed: if you ever add a production goal, the same logic says MC will not serve it, and short-answer-plus-feedback would.
sources: Adesope OO, Trevisan DA, Sundararajan N (2017). Review of Educational Research 87(3):659-701
Kang SHK, McDermott KB, Roediger HL III (2007). Test format and corrective feedback modify the effect of testing on long-term retention. European Journal of Cognitive Psychology 19(4-5):528-558

original_claim: 'Duolingo's own efficacy study gives a more usable anchor: Jiang, Rollinson, Plonsky, Gustafson & Pajak (2021) ... median 112 hours (mean 141) ... Use the Duolingo anchor for honest goal-setting copy and for capacity planning: ~100-140 hours to functional reading.'
problem: Jiang et al. (2021), 'Evaluating the reading and listening outcomes of beginning-level Duolingo courses', evaluated learners of **Spanish and French** by English-speaking US adults. It contains no Mandarin data. Transferring an hours-to-proficiency figure from two shallow-orthography Romance languages — where a Dutch or English L1 learner already knows the script and shares thousands of cognates — to a logographic script with zero orthographic transfer is invalid, and it errs badly toward under-budgeting. This is the brief's only quantitative anchor for item-bank sizing and roadmap copy, so the error is load-bearing.
corrected_claim: Delete the Duolingo hours anchor. The relevant anchor for a Category IV language is the FSI/Defense Language Institute classification placing Mandarin at ~2200 class hours to professional working proficiency versus ~600-750 for Spanish/French — roughly a 3-4x multiplier, though that is a whole-language classroom figure and not a reading-only one. For an app whose scope is genuinely narrow (recognise ~300-600 signage/menu characters, no production, no tone, no listening), do not project a total-hours figure at all; project bank size and review load instead, which you can compute directly from the spacing ladder and are not guessing at.
sources: Jiang X, Rollinson J, Plonsky L, Gustafson E, Pajak B (2021). Foreign Language Annals 54(4) — Spanish and French courses
US Foreign Service Institute / School of Language Studies language difficulty categories (Mandarin: Category IV)

original_claim: Finding 8: 'render a 0.25em gap between word tokens ... Add a native spacing toggle ... switch a learner to native spacing automatically once they clear a level.' Finding 15: 'the character as it appears in the answer options must be pixel-identical in colour and weight to how it would appear on a real sign.'
problem: These two recommendations contradict each other, and the brief never reconciles them. Word spacing is precisely a training-only guidance cue absent from the transfer environment — the exact configuration Skulmowski's guidance-reversal result identifies as producing the *worst* retention and transfer, worse than never having the cue. The brief invokes that mechanism to ban tone colour and radical highlighting, then introduces a spatial cue with the same structure and defends it with a weaker literature. Separately, the recommendation is largely moot for this product: signage and menu targets are 1-4 characters (出口, 火车站, 牛肉面), where word segmentation carries almost no information. The eye-tracking spacing benefit was measured on running prose, which this app does not contain.
corrected_claim: Do not ship word spacing in the answering loop. Apply the brief's own transfer rule consistently: any character the learner must recognise renders exactly as it would on a sign — unspaced, single flat colour, no highlighting. If word spacing is used at all, confine it to a post-answer explanation screen (where the guidance-reversal risk does not apply because nothing is being tested), or to any long-form reading mode added later, and make unspaced the default there too. The brief's own gap note — 'no evidence found on whether word-spacing during training transfers to unspaced real-world reading' — is the correct reason to withhold, not to ship with a toggle.
sources: Skulmowski A (2022). Education and Information Technologies 27:3963-3985 — guidance reversal
Brief-internal contradiction between findings 8 and 15

original_claim: 'Gamification's effect on cognitive learning outcomes is real but small-to-medium (g = 0.49)' — graded strong.
problem: A cognitive effect resting on k=19 and N=1686 is not a strong evidence base, and the gamification literature has exactly the publication-bias and short-duration problems that make point estimates untrustworthy. The dominant unmodelled moderator is study *duration*: most gamification RCTs run days to a few weeks, capturing novelty rather than learning. Hanus & Fox (2015, Computers & Education 80:152-161), one of the few longitudinal designs, ran 16 weeks and found the gamified condition produced *lower* intrinsic motivation, lower satisfaction, less effort and worse exam performance over time. The brief also does not note that Sailer & Homner's own motivational and behavioural effects failed to survive their high-rigour subsplit, which it reports but does not let affect the grade.
corrected_claim: Downgrade to moderate. Treat g≈0.49 as an optimistic short-horizon estimate and expect decay: whatever fiction/competition framing you ship, plan to measure retention at 8+ weeks rather than assuming the effect persists. This actually reinforces the brief's own recommendations — no points economy, no leaderboard — and adds one: do not treat the co-op 'play against the menu' framing as a permanent motivational asset; instrument it and be willing to find it stops working after the third session.
sources: Sailer M, Homner L (2020). Educational Psychology Review 32:77-112
Hanus MD, Fox J (2015). Assessing the effects of gamification in the classroom: a longitudinal study. Computers & Education 80:152-161

original_claim: 'Positive polarity ... is measurably more legible ... Ship light mode as the default.' Graded strong.
problem: The polarity literature is largely bright-office-illumination LCD proofreading work, and the mechanism the brief itself names — a bright background contracting the pupil — is inherently ambient-light-dependent. In dim environments the positive-polarity advantage shrinks or reverses, and a bright white full-screen ground becomes a glare and discomfort source. That matters unusually much here because the product's stated criterion environments are a restaurant at dinner and a metro platform at night. The brief grades this strong and hard-codes light-as-default without a single word about ambient illumination, which is the moderator most likely to flip the recommendation in actual use.
corrected_claim: Downgrade to moderate. Ship light as the default but honour prefers-color-scheme rather than forcing light, and treat dark mode as a first-class path rather than a grudging swap — the brief's own dark-mode compensations (larger size, heavier weight) are the right instinct. Note also that the brief's dark palette introduces an unflagged problem: HSB 0/50/12 is a red-tinted ground (#1F0F0F), which will sit poorly against red incorrect-answer feedback. Use a neutral or blue-shifted dark grey instead. The 6.1:1 contrast figure for #949494 on #1F0F0F is arithmetically correct — I verified it — and it does clear AA but not AAA, and ~6:1 is thin for stroke-level discrimination by a learner. Raise the dark-mode foreground toward #B8B8B8 (≈9:1) for the target character specifically while keeping the dimmer grey for chrome.
sources: Piepenbrock C, Mayr S, Buchner A (2014). Human Factors 56(5)
WCAG 2.1 SC 1.4.3 (4.5:1 AA) and 1.4.6 (7:1 AAA); contrast computed in-session

original_claim: 'Do not colour-code tones' derived from Godfroid et al. 2017, graded strong; and the brief's separate claim that Godfroid used n=303.
problem: The brief's own summary of the study says colour training *worked* — ~11% item-learning and ~12% system-learning gains — and was only slightly behind numbers and contours, with no dual-cue benefit. 'Slightly worse than the best alternative' is not 'do not do it'; that is an over-read of a near-null difference into a prohibition. Two further problems: the study trained tone *perception* (auditory discrimination) via colour, which is a different manipulation from tinting a glyph in a reading interface, so the transfer is not direct; and tone is close to irrelevant to this product's stated criterion task, which is silent visual recognition of signage. The n=303 figure is also unverified and larger than I can substantiate. Meanwhile the genuinely decisive argument against linguistic colour coding is absent from the brief entirely.
corrected_claim: Keep the recommendation, replace the justification, downgrade the grade to moderate. The robust reasons not to encode linguistic information in colour are (a) colour vision deficiency affects roughly 8% of males and 0.5% of females of Northern European ancestry — directly relevant to a Dutch user base — making any colour-only cue an accessibility failure and a WCAG 1.4.1 (Use of Colour) violation; and (b) the guidance-reversal/transfer argument the brief already makes in finding 15, which is mechanism-appropriate. Godfroid is supporting evidence that colour is not *necessary*, not evidence that it is harmful. Also: for a reading-only product, the prior question is whether to surface tone at all, and the answer is probably 'only in the audio, never as a visual system to be learned'.
sources: Godfroid A, Lin C-H, Ryu C (2017). Language Learning 67(4):819-857
WCAG 2.1 SC 1.4.1 Use of Color (Level A)
Epidemiology of congenital red-green colour vision deficiency: ~8% of males, ~0.5% of females of Northern European descent

original_claim: 'Note the 44px folklore has no comparable published experiment behind it — Parhi does.' And: 'Minimum interactive height 48 CSS px.'
problem: Half right, misleading as stated, and it causes the brief to cite no accessibility standard anywhere in a document specifying touch targets. It is true that Apple's 44pt has no published origin experiment. But 44×44 CSS px is *normative* — it is WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 2.5.5 Target Size (Enhanced), Level AAA — and 24×24 CSS px is normative at Level AA under SC 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum), published October 2023. Dismissing 44px as folklore invites an implementer to treat the number as ignorable when it is in fact a conformance target that procurement, public-sector customers and app-store accessibility review may hold the product to. Combined with the unit error above, the brief's 48px recommendation is simultaneously below Parhi's empirical floor (7.6 mm vs 9.2 mm) and framed as exceeding it.
corrected_claim: Cite both the empirical and the normative basis. Normative floor: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.8, 24×24 CSS px (AA), with the spacing exception; aspirational: SC 2.5.5, 44×44 CSS px (AAA). Empirical floor, converted correctly: Parhi 9.2 mm ≈ 58 CSS px, Conradi 14 mm ≈ 88 CSS px for walking use. Specify answer rows at 60-64 CSS px height, which clears AAA and Parhi simultaneously, and a street mode at ~88 CSS px. Also add SC 1.4.4 Resize Text (content must remain functional at 200% zoom) as a layout constraint — the brief's 'single Larger text toggle rather than a continuous slider' is a reasonable product choice but does not discharge the requirement to survive OS-level text scaling.
sources: W3C WCAG 2.2 (October 2023), SC 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum), SC 2.5.5 Target Size (Enhanced), SC 1.4.4 Resize Text
Parhi P, Karlson AK, Bederson BB (2006). MobileHCI '06

original_claim: 'Ship Simplified only (target is mainland China).'
problem: This is wrong for the specific criterion task the brief chose. Mainland law (国家通用语言文字法, 2001) mandates simplified characters for public signage, but it carves out calligraphy, seal carving, handwritten inscriptions and historical/heritage contexts — and commercial shopfront and restaurant signage exploits those exceptions constantly for stylistic effect. Traditional forms, seal script, and heavily calligraphic 行书/隶书 renderings are pervasive on exactly the shopfronts, tea houses, noodle shops and old-town streets the product is aimed at. A Simplified-only bank rendered in a single Hei face trains recognition of a form the learner will frequently not encounter in the wild. Transit signage is the one place the brief's assumption holds cleanly, because metro and road signage is standardised Hei.
corrected_claim: Ship Simplified as the learning target, but store the traditional counterpart for every character (Unihan kTraditionalVariant / kSimplifiedVariant) and surface it on the post-answer reveal for characters whose forms diverge visibly (门/門, 车/車, 面/麵, 药/藥, 饭/飯, 银/銀) — these are precisely the high-frequency signage characters where divergence is large. Segment the bank by environment: transit items can assume standardised Hei; food and shopfront items must not.
sources: 中华人民共和国国家通用语言文字法 (2001), Articles 13-17, including the exceptions for calligraphy, seals and heritage inscriptions
Unicode Han Database (Unihan), kTraditionalVariant / kSimplifiedVariant

original_claim: Mitigations for the negative suggestion effect: '(a) never reuse a wrong option as a correct answer for a different item in the same session; (b) after a wrong answer, immediately re-present the same item with the chosen lure removed.'
problem: Rule (a) is unworkable for this bank and would degrade it. In a menu domain the confusable set *is* the syllabus: 牛肉 is the correct answer for one item and the ideal distractor for 羊肉 and 猪肉. Forbidding reuse within a session either forces weak filler distractors — which the brief's own Rodriguez finding says destroys the 3-option result — or fragments the confusable set across sessions, which is the opposite of what discrimination learning needs. Rule (b) is worse: immediate re-presentation of the same item with the lure removed is massed repetition of a now-trivial two-option item. It produces a correct response with almost no retrieval difficulty and therefore almost no durable benefit, and the literature the brief is drawing on (Butler & Roediger) attributes the repair to *corrective feedback*, not to immediate re-testing.
corrected_claim: Drop rule (a) entirely; deliberate reuse of set members as each other's distractors is the correct design (see the interleaving finding below). Replace rule (b) with: show full corrective feedback (correct hanzi + meaning + audio), then re-queue the item at a spaced interval within the same session (5+ intervening items) at full option count, and again the next day. Keep rule (c) — logging {itemId, lureId, timestamp} — it is the good one. Note also that the brief flattens Butler & Roediger 2008: the two feedback timings were equal at reducing lure intrusions, but delayed feedback showed an advantage for retention of correct answers, which strengthens rather than merely permits the brief's end-of-round batch reveal for multiplayer.
sources: Butler AC, Roediger HL III (2008). Memory & Cognition 36(3):604-616
Roediger HL III, Marsh EJ (2005). JEP:LMC 31(5):1155-1159
Rodriguez MC (2005). Educational Measurement: Issues and Practice 24(2):3-13 — the 3-option result requires retained options to be effective

original_claim: 'Converging: a MALL RCT (n=150, 9 weeks) found the push-notification group hit 82% daily adherence vs 67% self-scheduled and 49% control' — cited to journals.kmanpub.com.
problem: KMAN Publications journals are not indexed in the major bibliographic databases and carry the hallmarks of a predatory or near-predatory outlet: rapid publication, minimal editorial footprint, no discoverable peer-review record. The brief uses this source to supply three precise adherence percentages that are doing real work ('converging' evidence supporting the reminder-dependency conclusion). Precise numbers from an unvetted outlet are worse than no numbers, because they lend false specificity to a claim the peer-reviewed source (Nobbe et al.) states much more tentatively.
corrected_claim: Strike the KMAN source and its three percentages. The Nobbe et al. (2024, npj Science of Learning) finding stands on its own and is appropriately hedged — but note its own limits, which the brief partly acknowledges: n=85 children aged 10-12 over 36 days, generalising to adult Dutch learners by inference. The design recommendations (one self-scheduled reminder per day, an explicit wean, separate tracking of selfInitiatedOpens vs notificationOpens) are sensible and cheap, and survive without the fabricated-precision support. Add a general rule for the brief: no non-indexed outlet supplies a number that enters a spec.
sources: Nobbe L, Breitwieser J, Biedermann D, Brod G (2024). npj Science of Learning
Source-quality assessment of journals.kmanpub.com (not indexed in Scopus/Web of Science/PubMed)

original_claim: 'Characters with fewer strokes were recognised roughly 100 ms (~9%) faster than high-stroke characters.'
problem: Internally inconsistent: 100 ms as 9% implies a baseline reaction time of ~1111 ms, which is well above typical single-character lexical-decision latencies for native readers (commonly ~550-750 ms), where 100 ms would be 13-18%. Either the millisecond figure or the percentage is wrong, or the baseline is from a different task than implied. The brief also attributes the 'simplified characters are more visually confusable with one another' claim jointly to a lexicon-project megastudy and to Liu et al. (2016, Cognitive Science) — but the latter is about *transfer of perceptual expertise between scripts in readers*, not about relative confusability of the simplified inventory. That is a source that does not support the claim made from it.
corrected_claim: Drop both the 100 ms/9% figure and the confusability attribution until verified. The stroke-count-to-latency relationship is real in direction but the magnitude quoted is not self-consistent. For the design decision that actually depends on it — building a visual-neighbour distractor list — you do not need the latency figure at all: derive neighbours from component decomposition and stroke-edit distance, then let live confusion logs rank them, which is what the brief already recommends and is the right approach.
sources: Internal arithmetic inconsistency (100 ms ÷ 0.09 = 1111 ms baseline)
Liu T et al. (2016). Cognitive Science — cross-script expertise transfer, not confusability

original_claim: 'ruby text at 0.45em of the hanzi size' with pinyin rendered as HTML ruby.
problem: Not wrong, but it has an unflagged failure mode that ships as broken content. At a 48 px hanzi, 0.45em gives ~22 px pinyin — and the information-bearing part of pinyin at that size is the tone diacritic, a 2-3 px mark. The pairs most at risk are exactly the discriminations that matter (ǎ vs à vs á, and ǚ/ǘ/ǔ where the umlaut and the tone mark stack). Compounding this, many system CJK fallback faces render Latin-with-diacritics from a different, poorly-hinted fallback, and ü specifically is frequently substituted or mis-stacked. The brief specifies a hanzi font stack carefully and specifies nothing for the pinyin, which is the more fragile of the two.
corrected_claim: Specify a separate, explicitly diacritic-complete Latin face for pinyin (Noto Sans, Source Sans, or Inter, all of which cover ǖǘǚǜ), set ruby text no smaller than 0.5em with a minimum absolute floor of ~20 CSS px, and add a build-time render test asserting that ā á ǎ à / ē é ě è / ī í ǐ ì / ō ó ǒ ò / ū ú ǔ ù / ǖ ǘ ǚ ǜ all render from the intended face rather than a fallback. Also verify ruby positioning in Safari, where ruby-position support has historically diverged.
sources: Lee CH, Kalyuga S (2011). Language Learning 61(4):1099-1118 — the split-attention finding, which the ruby implementation is an interpretation of, not a direct replication
Unicode coverage of pinyin tone-marked vowels including U+01D6-U+01DC (ǖǘǚǜ)

original_claim: META — six findings are graded evidence_strength: "strong" (cognate facilitation, T2/T3, HVPT, glossing, spaced practice, game-based learning).
problem: The brief's own gaps section states that WebFetch was blocked for every domain and that not one full text was read; every source is graded access: abstract-only. An evidence grade is a claim about evidence you inspected. Grading "strong" off a search-result snippet grades the abstract's rhetoric, not the evidence. Worse: not one of the six meta-analyses is reported with any publication-bias diagnostic — no funnel plot, Egger's test, trim-and-fill, p-curve, or PET-PEESE — yet the brief converts their point estimates directly into product decisions (retrieval counts, sprint length, gloss format). A meta-analysis without a bias diagnostic is not "strong" evidence; it is an unweighted average of what got published. I must disclose the same limitation in the opposite direction: this session's egress proxy refuses scholar.google.com, api.semanticscholar.org, aclanthology.org, arxiv.org, dl.acm.org, www.isca-archive.org, doi.org, api.crossref.org, api.openalex.org, PMC, Frontiers and MDPI, and the WebSearch budget was exhausted at 200/200 by the brief's own run. I could not open a single source either. So none of these grades can be repaired here — they can only be marked unearned.
corrected_claim: Downgrade all six "strong" grades to "unverified — abstract-only, no bias diagnostic". Before any of these effect sizes appears in a public deck, investor memo, or App Store copy, one person must open the six PDFs and record: k, N, the comparison condition (active control vs. business-as-usual), whether outcome measures were researcher-made, and the bias diagnostic. That is roughly two hours of work and it is the cheapest risk reduction available.
