original_claim: Finding 3 + its implication: top 100 characters cover ~42%, top 500 ~75%, top 1,000 ~89–90%. "Ship the first 100 domain characters as tier 1 (target: player reads ~40% of a real menu after tier 1)."
problem: This is the single most load-bearing arithmetic error in the brief, and it needs no source to refute. Character coverage is a *token* statistic; menu and sign reading is an *item* task. Under even a generous independence approximation, knowing 40% of characters gives P(reading a whole 4-character dish name) = 0.40^4 ≈ 2.6%, not 40%. At 75% coverage (top 500) it is 0.75^4 ≈ 32%. At 89% coverage (top 1,000) a 6-character sign has 1 − 0.89^6 ≈ 50% chance of containing at least one unknown character. The brief's tier-1 promise is off by more than an order of magnitude, and its stated corollary — "the marginal value of character 1,001 is roughly two orders of magnitude below character 10" — inverts the actual economics: moving 1,000→3,000 characters takes coverage 89%→99%, which removes ~90% of the *remaining* unknowns. In a Zipfian tail the last decile of coverage is where whole-item readability is won, which is exactly why the brief's 600–900 character target may be under-scoped rather than over-scoped. Separately, the sourcing is not triangulated: HandWiki, the Wenlin guide and HanziCraft are three secondary compilations of substantially the same underlying list (Jun Da), and no Taiwan or Hong Kong corpus is cited despite the claim of consistency "across mainland, Taiwan and Hong Kong corpora."
corrected_claim: Coverage ≠ comprehension. Set tier targets by simulating whole-item read rate over your own domain corpus, not by character coverage. State the honest tier-1 promise: "you will recognise some characters in most signs," never "read 40% of a menu." Expect the character budget needed for ~50% whole-sign readability to exceed 900, and treat that as the finding that reshapes scope. Cite one actual corpus (Jun Da's Modern Chinese Character Frequency List, ~258M characters) rather than three downstream wikis, and drop the unsupported Taiwan/HK consistency claim.
sources: Analytic — arithmetic over the brief's own coverage figures; no external source required
Frequency figures as-quoted trace to a single upstream list (Jun Da), not to three independent corpora

original_claim: Finding 18: mobile games g = 0.962 overall, vocabulary g = 1.251, "~83% of game-using learners outperformed non-users"; app vocabulary g = 1.28 at ≥10 weeks. Implication: design a 10–12 week arc "the duration at which effects reach g ≈ 1.28."
problem: Three separate defects. (1) The magnitudes are not credible as causal estimates. In education RCTs the median effect is ~0.10 SD and 0.30 SD is large (Kraft 2020, Educational Researcher, "Interpreting Effect Sizes of Education Interventions"). Effects near 1.0 SD in CALL/gamification meta-analyses are the signature of researcher-made outcome measures aligned to the treatment, small quasi-experimental samples, no active control (so the contrast confounds time-on-task and novelty), and publication bias — a literature the reviewer prompt correctly flags as bias-ridden. (2) The "~83% of game-using learners outperformed non-users" figure is not an observed proportion. It is Cohen's U3, mechanically derived from g = 0.962 under normality and equal variance (Φ(0.962) ≈ 0.83). Reporting a distributional conversion as a headcount of learners is a misreading of the meta-analytic output, and it is the kind of number that ends up in a pitch deck as a factual claim about people. (3) The "10 weeks" moderator is being read as a design constant. Longer treatments are confounded with greater total exposure; the moderator is dose, not calendar shape. Nothing in that literature says effects "reach" g = 1.28 at week 10.
corrected_claim: Treat the game-format benefit for L2 vocabulary as probably real but small-to-moderate (~0.2–0.4 SD) against an active control, and treat 0.96/1.25/1.28 as upper bounds contaminated by publication bias and construct-aligned outcome measures. Delete the U3 sentence entirely. Keep the 10–12 week arc if you want it, but justify it as a retention/behavioural design choice, not as reading an effect size off a moderator curve.
sources: Kraft, M. A. (2020). Interpreting Effect Sizes of Education Interventions. Educational Researcher, 49(4) — benchmark distribution for education RCTs (cited from knowledge; doi.org blocked in session)
Cohen's U3 identity: Φ(0.962) ≈ 0.83 — arithmetic, verifiable without a source

original_claim: Finding 7: "identification training beats discrimination training by a wide margin" (g = 0.95 vs 0.57), therefore "never same-or-different"; and "ship at least 4–6 distinct recorded voices per item."
problem: Two problems. (1) The identification-vs-discrimination gap is a between-study moderator, not an experimental manipulation — different studies, targets, learners and outcome measures. The brief's own quoted numbers contain the tell: identification *testing* g = 1.08 vs discrimination *testing* g = 0.77. Training format and test format are confounded, so much of the apparent superiority is construct alignment (identification-trained learners are measured with identification tests). The design directive may still be right, but the meta-analysis as quoted cannot establish it. (2) The "4–6 talkers" number is invented precision — no talker-count dose-response is quoted, and the high-variability premise itself is contested: controlled comparisons have found high-variability training does not reliably beat low-variability training for non-native contrasts (Brekelmans et al., on HV vs LV phonetic training), with variability sometimes helping only higher-aptitude learners. The brief grades this "strong" and then derives an audio asset table keyed (item_id, talker_id) plus multi-talker pre-caching for offline play — a real storage and pipeline cost built on an unquantified parameter.
corrected_claim: Identification-format training is a defensible default, but present it as a design preference supported by a confounded moderator, not as a 0.4 g experimental fact. Drop "4–6 talkers" to "≥2, treat talker count as an untested parameter" and note that HVPT's variability component is itself contested. Then ask the prior question in Correction 12: whether this reading-only product should carry an audio channel at all.
sources: Brekelmans, G. et al. — controlled comparison finding no reliable advantage of high-variability over low-variability phonetic training (cited from knowledge; unverifiable this session)
Internal: the brief's own testing-format figures (id-test 1.08 vs disc-test 0.77) evidence the training×testing confound

original_claim: Finding 6 implication: "render the tone as a separate coloured diacritic badge next to the syllable."
problem: This is an unevidenced design claim smuggled in as an implication of a perception study — exactly the tone-colour-coding folklore the review brief was told to attack. No source in the brief supports colour-coding tone; the controlled evidence for tone colour schemes (Dummitt-style palettes, Pleco/MDBG colouring) is essentially absent. It also fails three internal tests. (a) It contradicts the brief's own finding 14, which bans added colour information on the glyph on the grounds that it slowed reaction times and lowered accuracy — the brief prohibits colour in one finding and prescribes it in another, eight findings apart. (b) It builds a crutch with no transfer target: real signage carries no colour-coded tone, so the cue is guaranteed to be absent at test. (c) The common four-tone palettes are red/green/blue/purple, and red-green is the failing pair for the ~8% of males with colour vision deficiency — colour must never be the sole carrier of a distinction (WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.1, Use of Color).
corrected_claim: Drop the coloured tone badge. If tone is displayed at all, carry it redundantly in shape or number as well as colour, and never as the only channel. The separable segments/tone data model (the actually useful half of this implication) does not require colour and should be kept independently of it.
sources: W3C WCAG 2.2, SC 1.4.1 Use of Color (Level A)
Internal contradiction with the brief's own finding 14 (Hou & Jiang)

original_claim: Finding 6: "Advanced learners showed strongest sensitivity to T1 and weakest to T4."
problem: This runs against essentially the whole Mandarin tone-perception literature. T4 (high-falling) has the steepest, most salient F0 excursion and is consistently among the *best*-identified tones by non-tonal-L1 learners — including in Hao (2012), which the brief cites approvingly two findings earlier. A claim that advanced learners are *weakest* on T4 is the shape of error a search-snippet misreading produces. There is a second problem: if the paradigm was contrast-based (T1–T2, T2–T3, T3–T4), "sensitivity to T1" is not a well-formed unit of that design at all, which suggests the sentence was assembled from an abstract rather than from results.
corrected_claim: Mark as probably reversed or mis-transcribed and quarantine it. Do not ship any design decision keyed to "T4 is hardest for advanced Dutch learners" until someone reads the Frontiers paper's results section. The safe, literature-consistent prior is T4 among the easiest and T2/T3 the hardest, which is what the brief's own finding 5 says.

original_claim: Finding 10 implication: add per-syllable boolean `elided_vowel`, "true for -iu, -ui, -un, -ün rimes," affecting "~40 rime/syllable combinations," rendering e.g. duì ⟨du-ei⟩.
problem: A content bug that would ship wrong pronunciation. (a) "-ün" is not a pinyin rime spelling. The umlaut is dropped after j/q/x/y, so the spelling is always -un (jun, qun, xun, yun) — and that rime is /yn/, which has *no* elided vowel. Expanding it the way the brief prescribes would render jūn as ⟨ju-en⟩ and teach a pronunciation that does not exist. (b) The consequence is that `elided_vowel` cannot be computed from the spelling: the string "-un" is /wən/ after d/t/l/g/k/h/zh/ch/sh/r/z/c/s (elided e, expand it) but /yn/ after j/q/x/y (do not expand). The flag must be computed from initial+rime, not from a substring match — precisely the naive implementation the brief's wording invites. (c) The real elided set is exactly three rimes: -iu = /jou̯/, -ui = /wei̯/, -un = /wən/. (d) The "~40" count is unsourced and roughly right only if you count syllable types (~30–32 across the three rimes) and wrongly include the j/q/x/y-un set.
corrected_claim: `elided_vowel` = true only for -iu, -ui, and -un-after-a-non-palatal-initial. Explicitly false for jun/qun/xun/yun. And note the brief picked the smallest pinyin trap: larger ones for an alphabetic-L1 reader are that ⟨i⟩ spells three different vowels (zi/ci/si, zhi/chi/shi/ri, and elsewhere /i/), ⟨-ian⟩ is /jɛn/ not /jan/, ⟨-ong⟩ is /ʊŋ/, and ⟨o⟩ in bo/po/mo/fo is really /wo/.
sources: Standard Hanyu Pinyin orthography (GB/T 16159); ü-dropping after j/q/x/y is a spelling rule, not a phonological one

original_claim: Finding 15 implication: "Prioritise the ~15 radicals that carry the domain: 饣/食, 月 (meat), 鱼, 肉, 辶, 门, 车, 钅, 氵, 酉, 米, 艹, 女/男, 口, 页."
problem: Three content errors. (1) 男 is not a radical. It is a compound of 田 (field) + 力 (strength) and is indexed under one of those; it cannot head a radical grouping. (2) 页 as a radical (from 頁) means head, and its derivative set — 顶 顺 须 顾 颈 项 领 颜 额 题 — has essentially zero menu/signage payoff. It does not belong in a fifteen-slot domain list. (3) Teaching "月 = meat" will misfire on 期, 朗, 服, 有, 望, where 月 is the moon component or a graphic merger, not the 肉 radical — this is exactly the semi-opaque false-friend case the brief's own finding 14 warns produces worse outcomes than whole-unit memorisation. Meanwhile the list omits the radicals that actually carry the food domain: 火/灬 is the cooking-method radical (炒 stir-fry, 炸 deep-fry, 烤 roast, 煮 boil, 蒸 steam, 焖 braise) and is arguably the single highest-value radical for menu reading; 刂 (cut: 切, 剁, 割), 阝(place: 部, 都, 邮), 宀 (building), 亻 and 纟 are also absent. Also, 饣 is the simplified form of 飠/食 — a traditional-tagged bank needs 飠.
corrected_claim: Drop 男 and 页. Add 火/灬 as a priority-one radical and 刂 and 阝as priority-two. Tag 月 items explicitly as meat-radical vs. non-meat-radical so the grouping mode never teaches the false rule, or exclude 月 from the taught set. Keep 女 (radical 38) without 男.
sources: Kangxi radical index: 男 is not among the 214 radicals; 页/頁 is radical 181 (head)

original_claim: Throughout: 牛肉面 used as the canonical item, with a plan to store a traditional variant alongside simplified.
problem: 面 is the single worst simplified→traditional trap in the food domain, and the brief centres its example on it. Traditional Chinese distinguishes 麵 (noodles) from 面 (face/surface); both simplify to 面. So 牛肉面 is 牛肉麵 in Taiwan and Hong Kong, not 牛肉面. Any `traditional` field generated by naive 1:1 character mapping ships wrong characters on exactly the vocabulary the product is built around. The same one-to-many split hits other domain-critical items: 干 → 乾 (dry, as in 干货/乾貨) vs 幹 vs 干; 发 → 發 (develop) vs 髮 (hair, 头发/頭髮); 后 → 後 (behind) vs 后 (empress); 里 → 裡 (inside) vs 里; 松 → 鬆 (fluffy, 肉松/肉鬆 pork floss) vs 松 (pine); 只 → 隻 (classifier) vs 只; 面 as above.
corrected_claim: Simplified→traditional is one-to-many and must be a per-item authored field with human disambiguation, never a runtime character map. Add a `trad` string per item and a lint rule that flags any item containing 面/干/发/后/里/松/只/几/表/系/术 for manual traditional review before publish. Fix the running example to 牛肉面 (simp) / 牛肉麵 (trad).
sources: Standard simplified–traditional correspondence: 麵/麪 → 面 is a documented many-to-one merger, as are 發/髮 → 发, 乾/幹/干 → 干, 後/后 → 后, 裡/里 → 里, 鬆/松 → 松

original_claim: Finding 22 implication: "encode as a lint rule over the item bank (reject items whose segmentation lacks an overt subject when a verb is present)."
problem: This rule would empty the item bank. Chinese public signage is overwhelmingly subjectless and imperative or nominal: 禁止吸烟, 请勿触摸, 小心地滑, 严禁烟火, 营业中, 暂停服务, 卖完了, 推, 拉, 出口, 请扫码点单. Nearly every string in the product's stated domain has a verb and no overt subject. The lint rule as written is directly incompatible with finding 1's product definition, and it would have been caught by running it mentally against the brief's own example items. The underlying pedagogical point (English-L1 learners misparse topic-comment structures) is about *sentence* parsing in connected prose and does not transfer to fixed nominal/imperative signage, which is learned as whole units — as the brief itself argues in finding 23 (`atomic = true`).
corrected_claim: Delete the lint rule. Signage strings are memorised as atomic whole units, so topic-prominence transfer is not a live risk for tiers 1–2. If a lint rule is wanted, make it the opposite: flag any item that is a full sentence with an overt subject as out-of-domain for a signage deck.
sources: Internal contradiction: the rule rejects 禁止吸烟, 小心地滑, 请勿触摸, 卖完了 — the brief's own tier-1 exemplars

original_claim: Finding 16 implication: "Model pronunciation as an independent learnable attribute per character with its own scheduling state — three fields (form→meaning, form→sound, sound→form)."
problem: Pronunciation is not a property of a character. Mandarin has pervasive 多音字 (heteronyms), and they saturate this exact domain: 行 is háng in 银行 (bank) but xíng in 人行道 (footpath) and xíng in 行李 (luggage, as in 行李寄存 at every station); 便 is biàn in 方便 but pián in 便宜 (cheap — a shop-sign word); 地 is dì in 小心地滑 (slippery floor) but de as an adverbial marker, and a naive per-character pinyin generator gets that exact famous sign wrong; 了 is le in 卖完了 but liǎo in 了解; also 长 cháng/zhǎng, 重 zhòng/chóng, 少 shǎo/shào, 还 hái/huán, 干 gān/gàn, 得 dé/de/děi, 好 hǎo/hào, 中 zhōng/zhòng. A per-character `form→sound` scheduling field will teach the wrong reading roughly whenever the character is one of these, and the errors land on high-frequency signage.
corrected_claim: Key pronunciation to (character, word-context), not to the character. Store readings at the token level with a per-item `pinyin` string authored or verified against a segmenter-plus-dictionary, and keep a `heteronym = true` flag so the generator never asks for a character's pronunciation in isolation. The three-attribute scheduling idea survives; the unit of the sound attribute does not.
sources: Descriptive fact of Mandarin: 行 háng/xíng, 便 biàn/pián, 地 dì/de, 了 le/liǎo, 长 cháng/zhǎng are standard heteronyms

original_claim: Structural: findings 5–10 (T2/T3, Dutch tone perception, HVPT, musicians, sibilants, pinyin orthography) — six of twenty-six findings, all phonology — each generating schema fields and UI in a product finding 1 defines as "a deliberately narrow reading-recognition goal" for real-world signage.
problem: The brief never reconciles its own scope decision with its research emphasis. Real Chinese signage and menus contain no pinyin and no audio; if the product is recognition-only with no production, then the sibilant three-way contrast, the HVPT talker rotation, the pitch-contour pre-test and the coloured tone badge are all training a channel that is absent at the transfer target. The cost is not rhetorical: the phonology findings collectively mandate an audio table keyed (item_id, talker_id) with 4–6 talkers pre-cached per item for offline play. At ~900 items × 5 talkers × ~30 KB Opus that is roughly 135 MB of audio, on top of ~900 in-situ photographs at two resolutions — into a phone's PWA cache, offline, in China. Neither budget appears anywhere in the brief, and finding 12 simultaneously declares offline photo play "a core use case."
corrected_claim: Make the scope call explicitly and once. Either (a) reading-only: cut findings 7, 8, 9 and the tone badge entirely, keep one reference audio per item as an optional non-scored affordance, and reclaim the storage budget for photos; or (b) reading-plus-listening: keep the audio channel and re-derive the item bank size downward to fit the cache budget. The current brief buys both and budgets neither.
sources: Analytic — storage arithmetic over the brief's own stated asset requirements (findings 7 and 12)

original_claim: Finding 26: "Handwriting practice measurably improves L2 character recognition and orthographic knowledge," supported principally by fMRI activation differences between handwriting and pinyin typing.
problem: The neuroimaging citations cannot support the behavioural claim. "Handwriting produced stronger bilateral superior parietal and right postcentral activation than pinyin typing" is a statement about neural activation, not about learning outcomes — writing with your hand should activate sensorimotor cortex more than typing regardless of whether anything is learned better. Using activation differences as evidence of superior recognition is reverse inference. The behavioural literature is genuinely mixed once time-on-task is equated, and the brief's own caveat ("L2 learners need a large amount of writing practice for the effect to appear") is a dose confound that undercuts the causal reading. This is the "handwriting is essential for hanzi" folklore the review brief flagged, and the brief half-swallowed it.
corrected_claim: Downgrade the claim to contested: handwriting practice may help L2 character recognition, but the evidence quoted here does not establish it, and the neuro evidence establishes nothing about learning. The brief's *recommendation* — keep handwriting off the critical path — survives intact and should be stated as a product-scope decision rather than as following from the evidence.

original_claim: Finding 11: "multiple-choice glosses were the most effective gloss type, in-text glosses and glossaries the least," used to justify the core game mechanic (4-option forced choice on meaning).
problem: The moderator is being asked to carry a claim it cannot. (a) Gloss type is a between-study moderator confounded with an added retrieval/inferencing demand — a multiple-choice gloss is a gloss *plus a test*, so the effect is better attributed to the testing effect (which the brief already has, correctly, in finding 17) than to gloss format. (b) More seriously, in that literature a gloss is encountered *while reading a text*, where the reader has sentence context to constrain the choice. This product has no text; it is context-free isolated cards. The moderator does not transfer to that task, and the brief never notices the mismatch. (c) The L1-over-L2 advantage is g = 0.33, a small effect, yet the finding is graded "strong" and two product decisions are said to "fall straight out" of it. (d) The Kim/Lee/Lee citation is dated 2024 but the DOI given (10.1177/1362168820981394) is a 2020-series Language Teaching Research identifier — a brief that opened no paper should not assert a year.
corrected_claim: Keep the 4-option meaning choice, but justify it from retrieval practice (finding 17, better evidenced), not from the gloss-type moderator. Keep L1-default glossing as a reasonable prior while noting the effect is small (g ≈ 0.33) and that no gloss study exists for a context-free logographic recognition task. Fix or drop the 2024 date.

original_claim: Finding 2: "DLI runs Category IV Chinese at 64 weeks full-time with a minimum aptitude screen (DLAB ≥ 111)."
problem: The published DLI aptitude floors are 95/100/105/110 for Categories I–IV. 110, not 111, is the Category IV minimum; 111 looks like a transcription slip. Separately, "roughly 64% DLPT success" is quoted with no denominator — success at which threshold (2/2/1+? 2+/2+/2?), over which cohort, and counting retests how? Without that, the number cannot be compared to anything and should not be cited.
corrected_claim: DLAB ≥ 110 for Category IV. Either supply the DLPT threshold and cohort for the 64% figure or drop it — the architectural implication (design for churn, persist state, offer a 60-second re-entry review) is sound and does not depend on either number.

original_claim: Finding 1: ILR 3/3 is "roughly upper-B2/low-C1."
problem: Standard ILR↔CEFR crosswalks place ILR 2+ at B2 and ILR 3 at C1. Calling ILR 3 "upper-B2/low-C1" understates the target, which in turn makes the 2,200 hours look like worse value than it is and slightly inflates the rhetorical force of the "do not scope this as learn Mandarin" argument. The argument is right; the number supporting it is shaded. Minor, but it is the kind of shading that shows up in a pitch deck.
corrected_claim: ILR 3 ≈ CEFR C1 (General Professional Proficiency). The scoping conclusion is unaffected.

original_claim: Finding 25: HSK 3.0 "revised standards published Nov 2025 and full implementation July 2026"; "5,207 words changed level in the 2026 update."
problem: The only sources are two commercial blogs (hskstory.com, literatelanguages.com). A specific four-digit figure (5,207) and two specific dates, sourced to SEO content and used to justify a schema decision, is the weakest sourcing in the brief. The stable, checkable parts of the claim — 9 levels in 3 bands, 11,092 words, 3,000 characters, released 2021 — are fine.
corrected_claim: Keep the versioned-field advice (`hsk_version`, `hsk_band`), which is good practice regardless. Mark the Nov-2025/July-2026/5,207 specifics as unverified commercial-blog sourcing and do not repeat them externally until confirmed against a Chinese Ministry of Education / CLEC primary document.

original_claim: Finding 24: Chinese has been a VWO exam subject "since 2015–16," schoolexamen only, 400 characters actively mastered.
problem: The brief concedes slo.nl was unreachable, so all three specifics rest on secondary sources. The date in particular is contestable: the Chinese VWO programme ran as a pilot from around 2010 and there are competing accounts of when definitive introduction took effect (2015–16 vs. per 1 August 2017 with first exams 2018–19). I cannot resolve it in this session either.
corrected_claim: Mark the start year as unresolved (2015–16 or 2017–18) and the CEFR per-skill targets as unverified, as the brief already does. Note that the '400 characters' figure and schoolexamen-only structure are the load-bearing parts for the product wedge and are the two worth confirming — one email to SLO settles all of it.

original_claim: The large majority of Chinese characters are semantic-phonetic compounds (~80-85%), so component structure is the dominant statistical regularity. Graded 'strong'. Implication: 'Do NOT build a pictograph-story pipeline as the primary path — it covers under 10% of the script.'
problem: Unit-of-analysis error with direct product consequences. The 80-85% figure is a whole-script/large-dictionary statistic. Phonetic-compound share is strongly and monotonically inversely related to frequency, and this product's entire bank is the head of the frequency distribution. I computed etymology type over makemeahanzi (n=9,574) crossed with a character-frequency ranking derived from jieba's corpus lexicon (1e8 weighted char tokens). Result by band: rank 1-100 = 28.8% pictophonetic; 101-300 = 37.7%; 301-600 = 53.0%; 601-1000 = 66.3%; 2001-3500 = 79.6%; 3501-6000 = 84.9%; whole dictionary = 77.1%. For the brief's own stated core bank (top 1000) it is 53.1% pictophonetic, 37.8% ideographic, 9.1% pictographic. In the literal first 50 characters by frequency only 12/50 (24%) are pictophonetic — 一是人了不大中国 are not decomposable into meaning+sound. So pictographs+ideographs are ~47% of the core bank, not 'under 10%', and pictographs alone are 3.6x enriched in the top 1000 (9.1%) relative to the whole script (2.5%). The methodological point that protects this result: because the same etymology labelling is applied to both bands, labelling bias largely cancels in the within-dataset comparison, even though the absolute percentages are soft (makemeahanzi's etymology is compiled from secondary sources, not a peer-reviewed corpus analysis, and its 'ideographic' bucket probably absorbs compounds with opaque phonetics). Separately, the 'strong' grade is unjustifiable on the brief's own account: it states it read only abstracts and that 'the exact denominators differ between sources'.
corrected_claim: Across the full script ~77-85% of characters are semantic-phonetic compounds, but that statistic does not describe this product's item bank. In the top 1,000 characters — the brief's own scope — only ~53% are phonetic compounds and ~47% are pictographs or ideographs; in the first 100 it is ~29% vs ~71%. Component decomposition should still be a first-class stored field, but it cannot be the primary pedagogical path for the early game, and a non-phonetic-compound explanation path (pictographic/ideographic origin, or an explicit 'no useful decomposition, learn as a whole' state) is required for roughly half of the core bank rather than being a <10% edge case.

original_claim: Compound characters are overwhelmingly left-right structured (~72%) and the semantic component is on the left ~90% of the time. Measured over all 3,500 Tier-1 characters, top-level ⿰ (left-right) is 58.1%. Over the top 1,000 it is 44.8%, over the top 600 it is 40.0%, and over the top 100 it is 30.0%. (2) The error COMPOUNDS with the first correction: a card whose left box is a 'meaning slot' and right box a 'sound slot' is only semantically honest for characters that are BOTH left-right AND phonetic compounds. That intersection is 13.0% of the top 100, 24.2% of the top 600, 30.7% of the top 1,000, and 46.1% of Tier-1. So the proposed default layout is a false description of the character for roughly 70-87% of the earliest items — it would actively teach a wrong analysis of 一是人了不中国大 and every ideograph. However, only ~31% of the top-1,000 bank (and ~13% of the first 100) is both left-right and phonetic, so a two-slot meaning/sound card must be a conditional layout selected off a stored structure+etymology enum, never the default card. original_claim: Phonetic components are unreliable; 'Budget for ~1 in 3 phonetic hints being wrong.'
problem: Roughly 2x too optimistic for the frequency band the product plans to ship, and the brief's own gap section correctly said to compute this on the item bank — so I did. Using makemeahanzi's explicit 'phonetic' field and Unihan-derived pinyin (mozillazg/pinyin-data), comparing each character's primary reading to its phonetic component's primary reading: TOP 1000 (n=438 scored) — exact match including tone 16.9%, segmental match only 21.7%, rime-only 26.0%, NO CUE AT ALL 35.4%. TOP 2500 (n=1,383) — exact 23.0%, segmental 18.1%, rime 24.6%, no cue 34.3%. WHOLE DICTIONARY (n=6,788) — exact 34.3%, segmental 16.5%, rime 20.3%, no cue 29.0%. So in the core bank the phonetic hint is fully right about 1 time in 6, and gives no usable cue about 1 time in 3. The frequency gradient bites here too: reliability roughly doubles between the top 1,000 and the full dictionary, again because the head of the distribution is where the phonetics have eroded most. (Caveat: primary-reading-only comparison; polyphony and phonetic-component identification introduce noise, so treat these as bank-specific estimates, not literature-grade constants.) Also: the brief's Zhou (1978) citation URL is the Wikipedia biography page of Zhou Youguang, which cannot support the 26%/39% figures attributed to it.
corrected_claim: Over the top 1,000 characters, a phonetic component predicts the full reading (segments + tone) only ~17% of the time, predicts the syllable ignoring tone ~39% of the time, and gives no cue at all ~35% of the time. A phonetic-hint feature should therefore be gated on a computed per-character reliability field and suppressed entirely for the ~35% no-cue set; the copy must never imply a rule. Reliability improves markedly in later bands (~34% exact dictionary-wide), so the feature is worth more at intermediate level than at beginner level — the opposite of where the brief would surface it.

original_claim: HSK 3.0 has 'roughly 300 new characters per band'; and 'HSK band order is not frequency order and a travel-reading player needs 出口 and 元 before HSK's sequencing would give them.' Implication: 'do not let [HSK] drive ordering'; ship strict frequency bands of 50 instead. Graded 'strong'.

HSK gives the player 出口 and 元 immediately; the example chosen to justify overriding HSK ordering is refuted by the HSK list itself. (2) Per-band new-character counts are markedly non-uniform, not ~300: HSK 1 = 246, HSK 2 = 125, HSK 3 = 284, HSK 4 = 441, HSK 5 = 431, HSK 6 = 413, HSK 7-9 = 1,148 (community OCR of the official syllabus; totals ~3,088 vs the official 3,000, so ~3% noise, but the shape is unambiguous — HSK 2 adds half what HSK 4 adds). (3) The core assertion that HSK order is not frequency order is overstated: median frequency rank per band rises cleanly and monotonically — 291, 479, 674, 872, 1302, 1702, 2637 — with the share of each band inside the top 1,000 falling monotonically 88%→79%→69%→57%→34%→13%→2%. (4) Worse for the brief's recommendation, HSK BEATS raw frequency on exactly the travel vocabulary the product cares about: 厕 is frequency rank 3107 (a pure frequency-band scheme would place it around band 63 and never teach it) but sits in HSK 4; 禁 (947) and 止 (735) likewise appear in HSK 4. corrected_claim: HSK 3.0 band size is uneven (~125-441 new characters per band, with 7-9 adding ~1,150), and HSK band order IS strongly frequency-aligned (monotonic median rank 291→2,637 across bands). HSK should not be demoted to a display label: it is a frequency-correlated ordering that additionally corrects for concreteness and practical utility in ways raw corpus frequency does not. Use a blended ordering (frequency × HSK band × task relevance) rather than strict frequency bands of 50, and verify per-band counts against the official 汉语水平等级标准 GF 0025-2021 before printing any band label.

original_claim: 'Ship simplified only... Do store the traditional variant as a nullable field per character so a later Taiwan/HK mode is a data change, not a schema migration.'
problem: The schema is wrong because simplified→traditional is one-to-many, and the ambiguity is concentrated in exactly the highest-frequency characters. From OpenCC's STCharacters table (4,013 entries): 277 simplified characters (6.9%) map to two or more traditional forms. The ambiguous set is heavily front-loaded: 面→面/麪(/麵), 发→發/髮, 干→幹/乾/干/榦, 后→後/后, 里→裏/里/哩, 台→臺/檯/颱/台, 只→只/隻/祇, 几→幾/几, 出→出/齣, 了→了/瞭, 复→復/複/覆, 系→系/係/繫, 谷→谷/穀, 历→歷/曆, 钟→鍾/鐘. A single nullable column silently picks one and will render wrong text (e.g. 头发 → 頭發 instead of 頭髮). Correct conversion is word-level and context-dependent, not character-level. Minor related note: the brief's own signboard example 麵 is the Taiwan/HK standard form; OpenCC's default variant for 面 is 麪 — so even the example needs a variant policy.
corrected_claim: Ship simplified only (the legal-mandate reasoning is sound). But traditional forms cannot be a nullable per-character field: ~6.9% of simplified characters map to multiple traditional forms, disproportionately among the most frequent characters. If a Taiwan/HK mode is ever wanted, it requires word-level conversion (an OpenCC-style phrase table), so the right cheap hedge today is to store the traditional mapping as a nullable LIST plus a word-level override table — or to store nothing and defer entirely, rather than store a single value that encodes a silent error.

original_claim: 'a mandatory ~30-radical onboarding module (口 木 氵 女 人 心 门 车 食 etc.)'
problem: 食 is the wrong form for a simplified-only product and would ship as incorrect content. In simplified Chinese the productive left-hand food radical is 饣, not 食. Measured in makemeahanzi: 43 characters take 饣 as their radical (饭 饿 馆 饼 饺 饮 馒 饥 饰 饱 饲 ...), all of them common food/eating vocabulary that a travel-reading app needs; only 12 take 食, and those are mostly traditional or rare forms (食 飧 飨 餍 餐 餮 饔 饕 饗 饜). Learners taught 食 as 'the food radical' will not recognise it in 饭馆 or 饺子 — precisely the words the product targets. 餐 (as in 餐厅/早餐) does contain 食, but as a bottom component, not a left radical, so it does not rescue the choice.
corrected_claim: The simplified food radical to teach is 饣 (43 characters in the common set, incl. 饭 饿 馆 饺 饼 饮), with 食 taught separately as a standalone character and as the bottom component of 餐. More generally, the onboarding radical list must be validated against simplified component forms rather than dictionary/traditional head forms — the same trap applies to 讠/言, 钅/金, 纟/糸, 饣/食, 见/見. The rest of the brief's list (口 木 氵 女 人 心 门 车) is correct simplified form.

original_claim: On the largest independent spaced-repetition benchmark, FSRS's advantage over trivial baselines is small, and a zero-parameter moving average beats every FSRS version on calibration.
problem: The brief read only one of the two result tables in the benchmark README. In the 'Without same-day reviews' table it is right (MOVING-AVG 0.3369 LL / 0.05915 RMSE beats FSRS-7 recency 0.3414 / 0.0627). But the README also publishes a 'With same-day reviews' table — 10,000 collections, 519,296,315 reviews — where the ordering flips: FSRS-7 recency 0.3236±0.0041 LL and 0.06339±0.00088 RMSE(bins) versus MOVING-AVG 0.3301±0.0044 and 0.0789±0.0010. FSRS-7, FSRS-7 preset and FSRS-7 sched. penalties all beat MOVING-AVG there on both calibration metrics. For a co-located party game, where the same card can legitimately recur inside one evening, the same-day table is the more relevant one, not the less. (The brief's separate phrase 'beats ... on calibration' is at least metric-correct: the benchmark states explicitly that both Log Loss and RMSE(bins) measure calibration, and AUC measures discrimination.)
corrected_claim: On the no-same-day-review split a zero-parameter moving average edges out every FSRS version; on the same-day split — 519M reviews, the split that includes the within-session repeats this product will generate — FSRS-7 beats the moving average on both calibration metrics. The honest summary is 'FSRS and a moving average are within ~0.007 log loss of each other, in whichever direction the split is chosen', not 'a moving average wins'.

This matters because the brief's whole 'the prize is only 0.019 log loss' argument silently uses MOVING-AVG as the alternative, when the realistic alternative for a team told not to use a library is a hand-rolled SM-2/Leitner interval-doubling scheme.

So FSRS is ~0.38 log loss better than the scheduler a team would otherwise write by hand, roughly twenty times the 0.019 that per-user optimisation buys. 'FSRS's advantage over trivial baselines is small' is true only if 'trivial baseline' means a moving average of the user's own recent outcomes, which is not a scheduler and cannot produce intervals.

original_claim: Forgetting curve: R(t,S) = (1 + FACTOR · t/S)^DECAY, defined so R = 0.9 when t = S; FSRS-4.5 used DECAY = −0.5, FACTOR = 19/81; FSRS-6 makes decay a fitted parameter with default 0.1542. Inverse: I(r,S) = (S/FACTOR)·(r^(1/DECAY) − 1).
problem: The brief mixes two sign conventions across two different findings and pairs an FSRS-4.5 constant with an FSRS-6 parameter. Read from source: ts-fsrs computes `decay = -w[20]` and `factor = exp(ln(0.9)/decay) - 1`, then `R = (1 + factor*t/S)^decay`; fsrs-rs computes `factor = 0.9^(1/-decay) - 1` with `FSRS6_DEFAULT_DECAY = 0.1542`. So the exponent is −0.1542, not +0.1542, and FACTOR for FSRS-6 is 0.980346, not 19/81 = 0.234568 (19/81 is correct only for decay 0.5, i.e. FSRS-4.5/5). An implementer copying the brief's finding-11 form literally gets R(10S) = 1.443 — a probability above 1 — and copying 19/81 alongside decay 0.1542 gets a curve that is wrong at every t. The brief's finding-2 form, ^(−DECAY) with 0.1542, is the correct one; the two findings contradict each other and neither flags it. Separate trap: ts-fsrs's own docstring writes R(t,S) = (1 + FACTOR × t/(9·S))^DECAY while the code uses t/S — do not copy the docstring.
corrected_claim: For FSRS-6: decay_param w[20] = 0.1542; exponent = −w[20]; FACTOR = 0.9^(1/−w[20]) − 1 = 0.980346; R(t,S) = (1 + 0.980346·t/S)^(−0.1542), which gives R = 0.9 at t = S. Inverse: I(r,S) = S·(r^(1/−0.1542) − 1)/0.980346. Verified numerically against both reference implementations.

problem: The character-level results check out — I verified every one of the 33 'street characters' (乘 促 储 冻 刷 勿 厅 厢 售 巾 扶 招 料 炒 烧 禁 素 腐 荐 藏 袋 询 账 质 购 辣 递 酸 铺 销 闸 馒 鲜) is inside HSK 3,000 (levels 4–7) and outside the HSK 1–3 900-character set, and that 荤 is indeed outside the 3,000. But the word-level 'absent' counts are inflated by parse artefacts. 面条 is not absent: the standard lists it at level 1, entry 244, as 面条儿. 服务员 is not absent: it appears in the level-3 list as the entry 员（服务员）, i.e. inside the parentheses the brief's parser stripped. 牛肉/猪肉/羊肉/鸡肉 are transparent N+N compounds whose every character is in HSK (牛 L1, 肉 L1, 鸡 L1, 猪 L3, 羊 L3) — counting them as 'absent vocabulary' conflates a wordlist convention with a learner-facing gap.
corrected_claim: The character-level finding is solid and is the one to build on: survival signage characters are 99.5% inside HSK 3,000 and ~74% inside HSK 1–3. The word-level '40% absent' figure is not usable as stated — it counts 儿-suffixed forms, parenthesised sub-entries and semantically transparent compounds as absences. Re-run the audit with (a) 儿-suffix normalisation, (b) parenthesised forms expanded, (c) transparent compounds scored as decodable-if-characters-known, before quoting any percentage.

original_claim: The top-end requirement roughly doubled between HSK 2.0 and HSK 3.0 — 11,092 words vs roughly 5,000 at HSK 2.0 level 6 — which is itself evidence that the earlier level claims were not stable.
problem: Apples to oranges, and the brief had the data to see it. HSK 3.0's cumulative word count through level 6 is 5,456 (500+772+973+1000+1071+1140), which is within ~9% of HSK 2.0's ~5,000 at level 6. The apparent doubling is entirely the newly created 7–9 band (5,636 words) sitting above the old ceiling. Adding three new levels above an existing top level is not evidence that the old level descriptors were inflated.
corrected_claim: HSK 3.0 left the six-level word load essentially unchanged (5,456 cumulative at L6 vs HSK 2.0's ~5,000) and added a new advanced band of 5,636 words above it. Whatever the merits of the CEFR-alignment criticism — which neither the brief nor I could source — this particular arithmetic does not support it. The brief's actual recommendation (put no CEFR letter in the UI) stands on its own and needs no such argument.

original_claim: Do not model mastery as a binary latent state and do not ship a BKT — BKT's latent state is binary with a monotone learn transition and NO forget transition in its standard form.
problem: The 'no forget transition' premise is contradicted by the very repository the brief read in full. pyBKT exposes `forgets` as a first-class model option (`model.fit(..., forgets=True)`, cross-validated in the README's own examples) and documents the parameter as 'the probability of transitioning to the "not knowing" state given "known"'; the transition matrix `As` is documented as containing both learns and forgets. The claim is true of Corbett & Anderson's 1995 canonical formulation, not of the maintained implementation being cited.
corrected_claim: BKT with forgetting is a standard, implemented variant. The reason not to ship BKT here is not that it cannot forget — it is that its latent state is still binary while retrievability in a reading task is continuous and time-dependent, and that the brief's own preferred learner model (logistic regression over counts, per Gervet et al.) is cheaper and at least as accurate. Keep the recommendation; drop the stated reason. Also keep the UI consequence (no permanent 'mastered' badge) — that one is independent of the model class.
sources: pyBKT README — model variants incl. `forgets`, parameter documentation, and the Badrinath et al. (EDM 2021, 468–474) / Bulut et al. (Psych 5(3), 770–786) citations, all verified 2026-08-22 — https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CAHLR/pyBKT/master/README.md

original_claim: There is no experimental evidence behind the industry's most-cited efficiency number; never justify a design decision on the grounds that a smarter scheduler drives learning, and do not instrument the PWA to optimise for it.
problem: The narrow claim is verified — the FSRS 'ABC of FSRS' wiki does say 20–30% fewer reviews than SM-2 with the parenthetical '(2026-02-12 update: the figure is based on simulation results)', and I confirmed no experiment repository in the org. But the brief generalised from 'FSRS has run no experiment' to 'no experimental evidence exists', and the FSRS project's own Research-resources page — one click from the two wiki pages the brief did read — lists two randomised learning-outcome studies: Upadhyay, Lancashire, Moser & Gomez-Rodriguez (2021), npj Science of Learning 6:26, 'Large-scale randomized experiment reveals machine learning helps people learn and remember more effectively', whose code and trial data are public; and Nioche, Murena, de la Torre-Ortiz & Oulasvirta (2021), IUI '21, 445–453, 'Improving Artificial Teachers by Considering How People Learn and Forget'. Tabibian et al. (2019, PNAS 116(10):3988–3993) sits behind the first.
corrected_claim: FSRS's own 20–30% figure is simulation-only and should never appear in product copy — that part stands. But randomised field experiments on algorithmic scheduling and item selection do exist and are published; a claim that 'no experimental evidence exists' is false and would be embarrassing in a design document. Read Upadhyay et al. 2021 before writing the measurement plan: it is a randomised trial of exactly the layer the brief calls novel (which items to serve in this session), not of when a single item returns.

original_claim: Session accuracy is targeted at ~85% and is controlled by response format (2-choice / 4-choice / free entry), each player's tier chosen from their own predicted R; map 2-choice correct → Hard, 4-choice correct → Good, free correct → Good/Easy.
problem: The controller conflates observed accuracy with retrievability, and the conflation runs the wrong way. For a k-alternative forced choice with guessing, P(correct) = R + (1−R)/k. Solving at the brief's 85% target: 2AFC → true R = 0.700; 4AFC → 0.800; free recall → 0.850. So holding observed accuracy at 85% across tiers puts the *weakest* players — the ones on 2AFC — at the *lowest* true retrievability, the opposite of the stated intent to make the task easier for them. The grade discount does not fix this: it changes what the scheduler records after the fact, it does not change what the controller is targeting. A second consequence: roughly half of all 2AFC 'correct' responses at that operating point are guesses, so the outcomes fed to FSRS from tier 1 are ~50% noise regardless of which grade you assign.
corrected_claim: Set the target in retrievability, not in observed accuracy, and invert the guessing correction per tier: to hit a common true R of 0.85, target observed accuracy of 0.925 in 2AFC, 0.8875 in 4AFC and 0.85 in free entry. Better still, do not feed 2AFC outcomes into stability updates at all — use tier 1 as a scaffolding/participation format whose review rows are logged with `role: exposure`, and let scheduling state advance only on 4AFC and free entry. Store `format_tier` and `n_alternatives` on every row so the correction can be re-derived.
sources: Standard k-AFC guessing correction P(correct) = R + (1−R)/k; solved numerically for the brief's own 0.85 target, 2026-08-22

original_claim: Wilson et al. (2019) derives an optimal training error rate of ≈15.87% (accuracy ≈84.13%, the normal-distribution point at one standard deviation).
problem: I could not verify this either — nature.com, doi.org and every publisher host returned 403 from the same egress policy that blocked the brief's session, and the replication repository the brief cited (github.com/d-r-b-o-b/EightyFivePercentRule) does not resolve for me. original_claim: 'There is, to my knowledge, no published character-frequency corpus of Chinese urban signage.' The brief calls this 'the single most consequential' finding in the report and builds the peer-to-peer photo-capture architecture (finding 2) on top of the absence.
problem: False. The brief searched the linguistic-landscape literature — the wrong field. A character-level frequency corpus of Chinese text in the urban wild has existed since 2018 and lives in computer vision, not sociolinguistics. I verified it first-party from the project's own homepage source and repository this session: CTW (Chinese Text in the Wild), Tsinghua University / Tencent Joint Laboratory — 32,285 high-resolution street-view images, 1,018,402 individually character-labelled instances, 3,850 distinct character categories, annotations CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, baseline code MIT. Every instance carries the underlying character plus a polygon and six attributes (occluded, bgcomplex, distorted, raised, wordart, handwritten). The shipped baseline even has a STAT_FREQUENCY = 'products/stat_frequency.json' step, i.e. the frequency distribution the brief says nobody has published is a build target in the reference implementation. RCTW-17 (12,263 Chinese scene-text images) corroborates.
corrected_claim: A published, downloadable, character-level frequency corpus of Chinese text in the urban wild exists: CTW, ~1M labelled character instances over 32,285 street-view images. Compute the signage frequency distribution from it in an afternoon and seed the item bank corpus-derived rather than practitioner-derived. Two honest caveats: (a) CTW is Tencent street-view imagery, so it over-represents shopfront fascias and street signage and under-represents menus, shelf-edge labels and indoor plates — the brief's three highest-payoff domains, so the capture feature still has a job, just a much smaller one; (b) the 'wordart' attribute is itself a finding the brief's typography section needed — decorative display lettering is common enough in real signage to warrant its own annotated class, which argues for MORE typeface variation in the card templates, not the five-template cap of finding 6.
sources: Yuan, T.-L., Zhu, Z., Xu, K., Li, C.-J., Mu, T.-J., & Hu, S.-M. (2019). A Large Chinese Text Dataset in the Wild. Journal of Computer Science and Technology, 34(3), 509-521. Verified this session against the project's own homepage source and BibTeX entry.
https://ctwdataset.github.io/ (source retrieved via https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ctwdataset/ctwdataset.github.io/master/index.html)
https://github.com/yuantailing/ctw-baseline (tutorial/1-basics.ipynb: character-level annotation format; judge/settings.py: STAT_FREQUENCY)

original_claim: Finding 21's four recorded predictions: survival set absent from HSK 2.0 L1-3 ≈ 75-82%; survival CHARACTERS present in HSK 3.0's first 900 ≈ 75-85%; survival COMPOUNDS present in HSK 3.0 L1-3 ≈ 35-45%; 'if the character/compound gap is smaller than ~30 points, finding 21's headline is wrong.'
problem: The brief graded these 'weak' and recorded them so they could be scored. I scored them against the real lists this session — the official HSK 3.0 (GF 0025-2021) character and word lists and the official HSK 2.0 (2012) word lists, both cloned and parsed. All three point estimates are wrong, and the brief erred in the SAME direction each time: it was too generous to HSK. Transcribing the brief's own lexis into a machine-readable set (214 characters, 266 compounds, 480 items) and intersecting: absent from HSK 2.0 L1-3 = 87.9% (predicted 75-82%); survival characters inside HSK 3.0's first 900 = 63.6% (predicted 75-85%); survival compounds inside HSK 3.0 L1-3 = 15.4% (predicted 35-45%). The compound figure is off by a factor of ~2.5.
corrected_claim: Measured, not estimated: 88% of the survival set is absent from HSK 2.0 levels 1-3; only 64% of survival characters appear in HSK 3.0's first 900; only 15% of survival compounds appear in HSK 3.0 levels 1-3 (39% appear anywhere in all 11,092 words; 162 of 266 appear at no level at all, including 换乘 安全出口 净含量 冷藏 时价 单程票 二等座 无障碍 扶梯 干煸 会员价 买一送一 去结算 提交订单 售罄 托运 改签 失物招领). The 'bricks not buildings' headline SURVIVES and clears the brief's own falsification threshold — the char/compound gap is 48 points, not under 30 — but the correct story is harsher and more useful: HSK 3.0 withholds a third of the bricks too, and the missing third is not random. It is exactly the high-payoff zones: every cooking method (炒炸煮蒸烤焖炖涮拌卤烧煎爆), every organ term (肠肚肝肺肾腰舌筋), and 禁 折 质 藏 冻 辣 咸 酸 鲜 素 荤. Restate finding 21 as 'HSK gives you two thirds of the bricks and almost none of the buildings' and re-grade it strong.
sources: 国际中文教育中文水平等级标准 GF 0025-2021, official character and word lists, via https://github.com/elkmovie/hsk30 (Pleco Inc., MIT). Cumulative counts independently confirmed this session: L1 500/300, L1-2 1272/600, L1-3 2245/900, L1-4 3245/1200, L1-6 5456/1800, L1-9 11092/3000 — the brief's cited figures are all correct.

original_claim: Finding 1: 'the first 50 characters by frequency give you perhaps 15-20 that change your behaviour on a sign; 50 characters chosen functionally give you ~50. That is a ~2.5-3x efficiency gap over the first 100 characters, converging with frequency ordering somewhere around 1,200-1,500 characters.'
problem: The brief's central strategic argument is badly UNDER-stated, and its convergence point is wrong by a factor of two. I ran the brief's own verification recipe against the real SUBTLEX-CH character-frequency table. Of the top 50 characters by frequency, exactly 4 are in the survival set (到 上 生 时) — and of those, arguably only 上 changes what you do at a sign. Of the top 100, 15. Not 15-20 out of 50; 4 out of 50. On convergence: at 1,000 frequency-ordered characters a learner holds 66% of the survival set, at 2,000 they hold 86%, and they need ~3,000 to reach 97%. 斤 sits at frequency rank 2,551, 荤 at 4,012, 辣 at 1,420, 禁 at 1,140.
corrected_claim: The gap is roughly 10x at rank 50 and ~6x at rank 100, not 2.5-3x, and the orderings do not converge until ~2,500-3,000 characters, not 1,200-1,500. Say this louder: it is the strongest argument in the brief and the one that most justifies not seeding from a frequency list. Separately, drop the specific coverage percentages the brief attributes to Jun Da (1,000≈89%, 2,000≈97%, 3,000≈99%) unless someone opens that list — I could not reach lingua.mtsu.edu either, and the equivalent curve I measured on SUBTLEX-CH is materially different (top 1,000 = 93.97%, top 2,000 = 98.86%, top 3,000 = 99.81%), which shows the number is register-dependent by ~5 points at rank 1,000. Neither corpus is a signage corpus, so quote neither in product copy; quote CTW instead.
sources: SUBTLEX-CH character frequency table (Cai & Brysbaert 2010), full data file read this session. Header confirms 'Total character count: 46,841,097', 'Total word count: 33,546,516', 'Context number: 6,243' — the brief's '~47M characters of film/TV subtitles' is CORRECT.
Computation performed this session over the survival set transcribed from the brief (200 characters with SUBTLEX ranks; median rank 702).

original_claim: Finding 16's implication: 'teach the 月 flesh radical as a single card BEFORE any of 肠肚肝肺肾脑 ... Render 月 in the accent colour inside each of the six.' Finding 8 likewise lists '月 = flesh/body-part' among the semantic-component hints. Finding 16 also states the organ set 'all share the 月 flesh radical except 血 and 皮 and 筋'.
problem: Three errors, one of which ships as a silent bug. (a) The component in 肠肚肝肺肾腰脑胗 is ⺼ (U+2EBC, the meat/flesh radical, Kangxi 130 肉), NOT 月 (U+6708, moon, Kangxi 74). They are homoglyphs in almost every font and different codepoints. Any implementation that string-matches or regex-matches on 月 to apply the accent colour will highlight ZERO of the six target characters, and will instead fire on 期 (in 保质期, a Tier-1 item) and 朋 — i.e. it fails silently and teaches the wrong thing. I verified radical assignment and decomposition for all thirteen characters against the makemeahanzi database this session. (b) 筋 is listed as an exception but it decomposes as ⿱⺮肋 and 肋 contains the flesh component — so it is not an exception in the way stated (its Kangxi radical is ⺮, which is the real point and is not what the brief says). (c) 舌 IS in the brief's taught set, does NOT contain the component (radical 舌, decomposition ⿱千口), and was omitted from the exception list entirely.
corrected_claim: The taught component is ⺼ / U+2EBC (flesh, Kangxi 130), and the app must key highlighting off a per-item stored component field or a decomposition database, never off a substring match on the moon character. Correct exception list for the brief's own organ set: 血, 皮 and 舌 do not carry it; 筋 carries it inside 肋 but takes ⺮ (bamboo) as its Kangxi radical. The pedagogical idea is excellent and worth keeping — it is the best card in the curriculum — but as written it would not work. The brief's other nine radical glosses all check out exactly (辶 walk, 疒 sickness, 氵 water, 钅 metal, 忄 heart, 灬 fire, 饣 food, 讠 speech, 车 vehicle).
sources: makemeahanzi character database (radical, decomposition, stroke data), https://github.com/skishore/makemeahanzi — 9,574 entries, queried directly this session.
Unicode: U+2EBC KANGXI RADICAL MEAT vs U+6708 CJK UNIFIED IDEOGRAPH-6708.

original_claim: Finding 13: 'the survival set is stroke-dense. 警 (19), 藏 (17), 檢/检, 續, 禁 (13), 蒸 (13), 醬/酱 (18), 麻 (11), 辣 (14), 鹹/咸, 餃/饺, 質/质, 藥/药 (18 traditional, 9 simplified), 攤, 邊/边 ... Simplified characters help but 警, 蒸, 酱, 辣, 藏, 檢 are all simplified-set and still dense.'
problem: The stroke counts I could check are mostly right (警 19, 藏 17, 禁 13, 蒸 13, 麻 11, 辣 14, 药 9 — all confirmed) but the argument's two clinching examples are wrong. 檢 is a TRADITIONAL form; the simplified set uses 检, which is 11 strokes, not 17. Listing 檢 among characters that 'are all simplified-set' is a category error in a product that ships simplified. And 酱 is 13 strokes, not 18 — 18 is 醬, the traditional form. Once you use the actual simplified forms the brief's own example list collapses: 检 11 (not 17), 质 8 (not 15), 边 5 (not 18), 咸 9 (not 20), 饺 9 (not 14), 摊 13 (not 22), 药 9 (not 19). The finding argues for larger type by citing densities its own target script does not have.
corrected_claim: The direction (Chinese needs a larger visual angle than Latin for equivalent legibility) is almost certainly right, but the brief's evidence for it is self-undermining and its two source citations are 17-25 years old and predate high-DPI displays, which the brief itself concedes. The genuinely dense simplified survival characters are a much shorter list — 警 19, 藏 17, 燥 17, 蒸 13, 酱 13, 辣 14, 醋 15, 糖 16 — so gate the +25% render bump on a real per-item strokeCount rather than on a hand-picked list, and drop 檢 續 醬 鹹 餃 質 藥 攤 邊 from the product entirely unless you intend to support Hong Kong and Taiwan. The 96px/48px/40px pixel specs remain engineering judgement with no study behind them, exactly as the brief admits; treat them as a starting point for an in-house legibility test, not a spec.
sources: Stroke counts verified this session against makemeahanzi graphics.txt (stroke arrays), https://github.com/skishore/makemeahanzi
Simplified/traditional pairs verified with OpenCC s2t/t2s (https://github.com/BYVoid/OpenCC)

original_claim: Finding 21 lists specific HSK 2.0 memberships: '禁止 请勿 严禁 危险 注意 当心 免费 收费 营业 休息 (all of prohibition and status, though 小心 is at HSK 3)' are absent from HSK 1-3; and '医院 银行 超市 洗手间 arrive at HSK 3'.

The rest of the brief's specific claims check out exactly and are worth recording as confirmed: 出口 L5, 入口 L4, 禁止 L4, 危险 L4, 免费 L4, 辣 L4, 折 L6, 小心 L3, 甜 L3, 银行 L3, 超市 L3, 洗手间 L3, 商店 L1, 饭店 L1, 学校 L1, 块 L1, 米饭 L1, 面条 L2 — and 烤 and 斤 are absent from HSK 2.0 entirely, as claimed.
corrected_claim: Remove 注意, 休息 and 医院 from the 'absent from HSK 1-3' list. This does not change the argument — the corrected absence rate is 88%, higher than the brief claimed — but three wrong memberships in a list presented as the evidence base would be the first thing a reviewer checks, and 医院 at HSK 1 is the kind of error that costs credibility cheaply.
