original_claim: Finding 7 grades the vocabulary-coverage-threshold literature 'strong': 'Hu & Nation (2000) ... found ~98% lexical coverage needed for unassisted comprehension of fiction, with 95% giving only partial comprehension; Laufer & Ravenhorst-Kalovski (2010) ... position 95% as a minimal and 98% as an optimal threshold.'
problem: I could not retrieve any of these papers (all publisher hosts 403). But a 'strong' grade is not defensible here even from prior knowledge, because the existence of a coverage THRESHOLD — a breakpoint rather than a smooth function — is actively contested in that literature. Schmitt, Jiang & Grabe (2011, Modern Language Journal) tested explicitly for a breakpoint on a large sample and reported a broadly linear relationship between coverage and comprehension with no distinct threshold; van Zeeland & Schmitt and others report materially lower figures for listening. Hu & Nation (2000) is a single small study (the brief says n=66) with a fiction text. Grading it 'strong' while grading the brief's own well-supported structural arguments 'moderate' inverts the confidence ordering.
corrected_claim: Re-grade the coverage-threshold literature 'contested'. Note that this makes the brief's own conclusion STRONGER, not weaker: if there is no breakpoint even in running text, then importing a 95%/98% number into a domain with no redundancy at all is doubly unjustified, and the sign-completion-rate metric the brief proposes is the right answer for a better reason than the one given. Do not quote 95% or 98% in product copy or a funding document without opening the papers.
sources: Schmitt, N., Jiang, X., & Grabe, W. (2011). The percentage of words known in a text and reading comprehension. Modern Language Journal, 95(1), 26-43. NOT RETRIEVED THIS SESSION — cited from model knowledge; verify before use.
Hu, M., & Nation, I.S.P. (2000), Reading in a Foreign Language 13(1). NOT RETRIEVED THIS SESSION.

original_claim: Finding 11 grades 'strong': 'the optimal inter-study gap scales with the retention interval at roughly 10-20%' (Cepeda et al. 2008), and derives the scheduler `gapDays = clamp(0.15 * daysUntil(tripEnd), 0.5, 14)`, giving '~2-4 days' for a 21-day horizon and '~12 hours' for a 5-day horizon.
problem: Not retrieved (403). But the flat-ratio framing misstates what that paper is known for. Cepeda et al.'s 'temporal ridgeline' result is precisely that the optimal gap as a PROPORTION of the retention interval DECLINES as the retention interval lengthens — the reported optima run roughly RI 7d → gap ~1d (~14%), RI 35d → ~11d (~31%), RI 70d → ~21d (~30%), RI 350d → ~21d (~6%). There is no single 10-20% constant, and at the brief's own target horizon (~21-35 days) the empirical points sit nearer 25-30%, i.e. a gap of ~5-9 days, not the 2-4 days the brief's 0.15 coefficient produces. A second and larger problem: that study is a two-session paradigm — one study session, one restudy, one gap — and generalising a single-gap optimum to a multi-review adaptive scheduler is an extrapolation the paper does not license. The brief's asymmetry claim (short gaps penalised more steeply than long ones) is the part I would keep.
corrected_claim: Keep the trip-anchored idea — it is genuinely novel and correct in spirit — but drop the flat 0.15 coefficient and the 'strong' grade. Use a coefficient nearer 0.25-0.30 for horizons of 2-6 weeks, floor it well above 0.5 days, and state in the code comment that the ratio is a rough interpolation from a two-session laboratory paradigm, not a measured optimum for this task. Then instrument it: with a departure date and a known item bank you can A/B two coefficients and measure landing-day retention directly, which nobody in the literature has done and which is a far better basis than a borrowed constant.
sources: Cepeda, N. J., Vul, E., Rohrer, D., Wixted, J. T., & Pashler, H. (2008). Spacing effects in learning: A temporal ridgeline of optimal retention. Psychological Science, 19(11). NOT RETRIEVED THIS SESSION — all publisher hosts 403-blocked. Ridgeline shape cited from model knowledge; verify the gap/RI table before implementing.

original_claim: Finding 12 cites Rowland (2014), '159 effect sizes, puts the testing-over-restudy advantage at g ≈ 0.50', to justify converting spectator exposure into spectator retrieval; finding 9 separately argues four-option multiple choice 'is not a compromise here; it is the criterion task'.
problem: Not retrieved. But g ≈ 0.50 is the overall pooled estimate, and that meta-analysis is well known for finding that the testing effect is strongly MODERATED by test format — largest for free recall, smaller for cued recall, smallest for recognition — and by the presence of feedback. Four-option multiple choice is recognition. The brief therefore quotes the pooled number to justify a design sitting in the weakest cell of the very moderator analysis it cites, and does so twice (findings 9 and 12) without mentioning the moderation. This matters concretely for the shadow-answer feature in finding 12: replicating the same 4-option tap to spectators buys the smallest available version of the effect.
corrected_claim: Do not attach g ≈ 0.50 to a four-option recognition design. Two design consequences. (1) The transfer-appropriate-processing defence of multiple choice in finding 9 is sound on its own terms — reading a sign in the wild IS constrained recognition — so keep the format for the main game, but stop citing a pooled testing-effect number to bolster it. (2) The spectator shadow task in finding 12 should NOT be another 4-option tap. Make it production or cued recall — a free-text or single-tap 'what does this sign make you DO?' with no options shown — which is the same interaction cost, is silent and private exactly as designed, and lands in the strongest rather than the weakest moderator cell.
sources: Rowland, C. A. (2014). The effect of testing versus restudy on retention: A meta-analytic review of the testing effect. Psychological Bulletin, 140(6). NOT RETRIEVED THIS SESSION. Format moderation cited from model knowledge; verify the subgroup estimates before quoting any number.

original_claim: Finding 3: 'GB/T 30240 《公共服务领域英文译写规范》 ... issued 2017 in 10 parts ... standardised English translations across public service signage. In practice this means tier-1 and most tier-2 metro systems, high-speed rail stations and airports carry near-total English coverage.'
problem: Two problems. First, a fact about Chinese standards nomenclature that the brief's argument turns on: GB = 强制性国家标准, a MANDATORY national standard; GB/T = 推荐性国家标准, a RECOMMENDED (voluntary) one, where T is 推荐. GB/T 30240 is therefore advisory throughout, not just in its catering part — the brief treats the catering part as 'only advisory' as if the transport parts were compulsory, and that contrast is the mechanism of the whole transit-deprioritisation argument. The observed bilingualism in tier-1 metros is real but is driven by municipal procurement and Olympic/Expo-era practice, not by a rule that compels it. Second, Part 1 (通则) was issued in 2013, not 2017; parts 2-10 followed in 2017. I could not open openstd.samr.gov.cn (403) to check the part list, so treat the part count as unverified.
corrected_claim: GB/T 30240 is a recommended, non-mandatory standard issued across 2013 (Part 1) and 2017 (Parts 2-10). Keep the transit-deprioritisation CONCLUSION — the empirical bilingualism of tier-1 metros, HSR stations and airports is not in dispute — but rest it on observed practice, not on a compliance mechanism that does not exist. The brief's own contrast (GB 7718 is a mandatory GB standard requiring Chinese and capping foreign type size; GB/T 30240 is voluntary) is a sharper and correct version of the same argument. Also note the brief cites GB 2894 (mandatory) correctly but GB/T 10001 is likewise recommended.
sources: GB vs GB/T nomenclature: 强制性国家标准 vs 推荐性国家标准 — standards-numbering fact, high confidence, but openstd.samr.gov.cn was 403-blocked this session so the part list and issue dates of GB/T 30240 were NOT verified.

original_claim: Finding 19: '无座 wúzuò — standing ticket, same price as hard seat, no seat / staanplaats' — listed under the high-speed seat-class set alongside 二等座, 一等座 and 商务座.
problem: Wrong for the context it is placed in. On conventional trains 无座 is priced as 硬座. On G- and D-category high-speed services — which is where the brief places it, in the high-speed bullet — a 无座 ticket is sold at the 二等座 fare. A traveller told 'same price as hard seat' will expect the cheapest fare and will be wrong by a large margin on exactly the purchase the finding is about.
corrected_claim: 无座 = standing ticket; on conventional trains priced as 硬座, on G/D high-speed services priced as 二等座 (i.e. you pay the full second-class fare and get no seat). Split the gloss by train class, because the brief's own 2x2 grid card (硬/软 × 座/卧) belongs to conventional trains and the 一/二等座 ladder belongs to high-speed, and 无座 sits in both with different pricing.
sources: Practitioner/domain knowledge; China Railway 12306 fare rules were not reachable this session (all .cn hosts 403-blocked). Flagged for verification before content lock.

original_claim: Finding 16: '爪 zhuǎ — feet, claws / pootjes — 凤爪, 鸡爪 chicken feet.' Also finding 16: '蒜蓉 suànróng — minded garlic / fijngehakte knoflook.'
problem: I ran all 387 pinyin readings in the brief through pypinyin with heteronym expansion. The result is genuinely good — only three substantive errors, and the readings that LOOK wrong to a naive checker (休息 xiūxi, 豆腐 dòufu, 馄饨 húntun, 芝麻 zhīma, 芥末 jièmo as neutral tones; 行 háng in 银行; 肚 dǔ for tripe; 美发 měifà; 炸 zhá for deep-fry; 干煸 gānbiān; 网吧 wǎngbā) are all CORRECT and are precisely where sloppy sources go wrong. The real errors: (a) 凤爪 is fèngzhǎo, not fèngzhuǎ — 爪 reads zhǎo in that compound and in 鸡爪 (jīzhǎo), with zhuǎ being the colloquial free/爪子 reading, so the brief's headword pinyin is right for the character in isolation but wrong for both examples it gives; (b) 'minded garlic' is a typo for 'minced garlic' and would ship into an English gloss; (c) 里脊 is more standardly lǐji (neutral) than lǐjǐ.
corrected_claim: Fix 凤爪 fèngzhǎo / 鸡爪 jīzhǎo and gloss 爪 with both readings (zhǎo in compounds, zhuǎ colloquially in 爪子). Fix 'minded' → 'minced'. Consider 里脊 lǐji. Otherwise the pinyin layer passes mechanical verification at 384/387 and is the strongest part of the deliverable — say so in the brief rather than leaving the whole lexical section graded 'folklore', which under-sells verifiable content. All 14 traditional/simplified pairs asserted in the brief (检/檢, 续/續, 酱/醬, 咸/鹹, 饺/餃, 质/質, 药/藥, 摊/攤, 边/邊) verify correctly under OpenCC.
sources: pypinyin 0.55.0 with heteronym expansion, run against all 387 readings in the brief this session.
OpenCC s2t/t2s for the simplified/traditional pairs.

original_claim: Finding 1: 'Jun Da's Modern Chinese Character Frequency List and SUBTLEX-CH (Cai & Brysbaert 2010) both open with 的 一 是 了 我 不 人 在 他 有 这 个 上 们 来 到 时 大 地 为 子 中 你 说 生 国 年 着 就 那 和 要.'
problem: That is Jun Da's ordering, not SUBTLEX-CH's, and the brief attributes it to both. SUBTLEX-CH's actual top 50, read from the data file this session, is: 我 的 你 是 了 不 们 这 一 他 么 在 有 个 好 来 人 那 要 会 就 什 没 到 说 吗 为 想 能 上 去 道 她 很 看 可 知 得 过 吧 还 对 里 以 都 事 子 生 时 样. It opens 我 的 你, not 的 一 是, because it is a subtitle (dialogue) corpus and second-person pronouns and speech verbs are inflated relative to written text.
corrected_claim: Attribute the 的 一 是 了 sequence to Jun Da only. The divergence is itself worth keeping: two corpora that are both called 'Chinese character frequency' disagree on their top three, which is a compact demonstration of the brief's own register argument and of why neither should seed a signage curriculum. The brief's corpus-size claims for SUBTLEX-CH are correct and now verified: 46,841,097 characters, 33,546,516 words, 6,243 films.
sources: SUBTLEX-CH-CHR full character frequency table, read directly this session via https://github.com/glxxyz/hskhsk.com (data/SUBTLEX-CH-CHR.txt).

original_claim: Finding 8: Guan et al. (2011) shows 'the pinyin route does not deliver the orthographic knowledge that character recognition depends on', therefore 'change the +1/-1 tier's scaffold from pinyin shown to semantic component highlighted and glossed'.
problem: Not retrieved (403). But the inference overreaches the design of the study as it is normally described. Guan et al. compared handwriting practice against alphabetic (pinyin) coding and found a dissociation — writing builds orthographic representations, pinyin builds phonological ones. A dissociation is not evidence that a pinyin HINT at test time HARMS reading, nor that a semantic-radical hint outperforms it as a scaffold; neither contrast was run. There is also a live counter-literature in which pinyin/phonological knowledge is a positive predictor of Chinese character reading in L2 learners. And the brief's own product wants phonology anyway — it ships a 'point at this' screen so the player can say 不要香菜.
corrected_claim: The swap from a pinyin scaffold to a semantic-component scaffold is a good product hypothesis and probably the right call for a reading-only goal, but it is UNTESTED, not evidence-backed, and should be graded 'weak' with an A/B test attached rather than 'moderate' with a citation attached. Better citations for the thing the brief actually wants (that explicit semantic-radical instruction aids character learning) are the radical-awareness line — Shen & Ke 2007 and Taft & Chung 1999 — rather than Guan et al., which is a handwriting paper. Note the tension the brief does not acknowledge: if Guan et al. is right that writing builds the orthographic representation recognition depends on, a no-handwriting product is accepting a known cost, and should say so.
sources: Guan, C. Q., Liu, Y., Chan, D. H. L., Ye, F., & Perfetti, C. A. (2011), Journal of Educational Psychology 103(3). NOT RETRIEVED THIS SESSION.

Taft, M., & Chung, K. (1999). Using radicals in teaching Chinese characters to second language learners. Psychologia, 42. NOT RETRIEVED THIS SESSION — suggested as a better-targeted citation, verify before use.

original_claim: Wisniewski, Zierer & Hattie (2020) '~435 studies, ~994 effect sizes, N ≈ 61,000' converging on d ≈ 0.48, cited as independent corroboration of Van der Kleij et al. (2015).
problem: Unit-of-analysis error, and the 'convergence' is not independent. Wisniewski et al. is a meta-analysis OF META-ANALYSES: ~435 meta-analyses, encompassing on the order of 61,000 primary studies and roughly 7 million students. The brief has relabelled 'meta-analyses' as 'studies' and 'studies' as 'N', understating the participant count by orders of magnitude and making the paper look like a primary synthesis. Worse for the argument: because it pools meta-analyses, it re-uses the very primary studies Van der Kleij, Hattie & Timperley, and Kluger & DeNisi already pooled — it double-counts. And Hattie is an author of both 'converging' sources the brief names (Hattie & Timperley 2007; Wisniewski, Zierer & Hattie 2020), so this is one research programme cited twice, not two teams agreeing.
corrected_claim: Wisniewski, Zierer & Hattie (2020) is a second-order synthesis of ~435 meta-analyses (≈61,000 studies, ≈7 million students) reporting an overall d ≈ 0.48, with high-information feedback (d ≈ 0.99) far outperforming reinforcement/punishment (d ≈ 0.24). It should be cited as an umbrella review that overlaps heavily with the other feedback sources in this brief, not as independent corroboration. The feedback story rests on one substantially shared evidence pool.
sources: Wisniewski, B., Zierer, K., & Hattie, J. (2020). The power of feedback revisited: A meta-analysis of educational feedback research. Frontiers in Psychology, 10, 3087. [NOT FETCHED — recalled; egress blocked]
Hattie, J., & Timperley, H. (2007). The power of feedback. Review of Educational Research, 77(1), 81–112. [NOT FETCHED]

original_claim: 'Bare right/wrong is worth essentially nothing (d ≈ 0.05) — a red X plus a point loss is the LEAST effective feedback design available.' Therefore every item must carry a mandatory ≤20-word three-slot elaboration.
problem: Two errors. (1) The d ≈ 0.05 for knowledge-of-result in Van der Kleij et al. (2015) is a *between-feedback-type* contrast within computer-based environments, not a claim that verification feedback is worthless versus no feedback. It directly contradicts the brief's own retrieval-practice finding: Rowland (2014) and Yang et al. (2021) both report that the testing effect is LARGER when feedback is given, and most of that feedback in the pooled studies is correct/incorrect plus the correct answer. Verification feedback is not worth nothing; it is worth less than elaboration. (2) More damaging to the recommendation: Van der Kleij's elaborated-feedback advantage is concentrated in HIGHER-ORDER learning outcomes. For low-order associative/recognition outcomes — which is precisely what the brief scopes v1 to ('recognition-only: given hanzi, select the meaning') — the gap between elaborated feedback and knowledge-of-correct-response narrows sharply. The brief has taken the moderator that most weakens its recommendation and quoted the pooled estimate instead.
corrected_claim: Elaborated feedback outperforms knowledge-of-correct-response, which outperforms bare verification — but the elaborated-feedback advantage is largest for higher-order outcomes and smallest for the paired-associate recognition this product is built on. The defensible rule is: always show the correct answer (KCR is cheap and well-supported); make elaboration mandatory only for items where a discriminating cue actually exists (confusables, shared radicals, compound semantics), and treat the universal ≤20-word explanation as an unvalidated product bet to A/B test, not an evidence-mandated requirement.
sources: Van der Kleij, F. M., Feskens, R. C. W., & Eggen, T. J. H. M. (2015). Effects of feedback in a computer-based learning environment on students' learning outcomes: A meta-analysis. Review of Educational Research, 85(4), 475–511. [NOT FETCHED]
Rowland, C. A. (2014). The effect of testing versus restudy on retention. Psychological Bulletin, 140(6), 1432–1463. [NOT FETCHED]

original_claim: Bisra et al. (2018) g ≈ 0.55 for induced self-explanation justifies 'a one-tap self-explanation: 2–3 tappable reason chips (I knew the radical / I guessed from context / I confused it with another character)'.
problem: That mechanic is not self-explanation, and g = 0.55 does not transfer to it. Every study in the Bisra pool prompts learners to GENERATE an explanation — spoken, typed, or (in the tutor literature) selected from a structured domain menu that names a principle. Tapping one of three post-hoc labels about HOW you answered is a strategy attribution / metacognitive self-report, closer to a judgment of learning or a confidence rating than to a constructive explanation. It produces no new inference and adds nothing to the item's schema knowledge. The brief has attached the largest cognitive effect size in the whole report to the one mechanic that does not instantiate it.
corrected_claim: Prompted self-explanation reliably improves learning (g ≈ 0.55 in Bisra et al. 2018, with the caveat from Rittle-Johnson et al. 2017 that the advantage shrinks when time-on-task is equated). Menu-based self-explanation CAN work — Aleven & Koedinger's Geometry Cognitive Tutor and Johnson & Mayer's work show selection-based prompts produce real gains — but only when the menu options are DOMAIN PROPOSITIONS, not strategy labels. The correct version of this mechanic is: 'which part told you? [semantic radical] [phonetic component] [the character it is NOT: 未]' — a forced choice among discriminating cues. Keep the strategy chip if you want the confidence signal for hypercorrection scheduling, but bill it as instrumentation, not as a 0.55-effect learning mechanic.
sources: Bisra, K., Liu, Q., Nesbit, J. C., Salimi, F., & Winne, P. H. (2018). Inducing self-explanation: A meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review, 30, 703–725. [NOT FETCHED]
Aleven, V., & Koedinger, K. R. (2002). An effective metacognitive strategy: Learning by doing and explaining with a computer-based Cognitive Tutor. Cognitive Science, 26(2), 147–179. [NOT FETCHED]

Johnson, C. I., & Mayer, R. E. (2010). Applying the self-explanation principle to multimedia learning in a computer-based game-like environment. Computers in Human Behavior, 26(6), 1246–1252. [NOT FETCHED]

original_claim: Chi, Roy & Hausmann (2008) vicarious learning justifies giving every non-active player a private 'shadow item' on their own phone during another player's turn, so 'no player's screen is ever idle for more than 2 seconds'.
problem: This inverts the source. In Chi, Roy & Hausmann the benefit attaches specifically to PAIRED, DIALOGIC observation of the tutoring interaction — collaborative observers discussed the observed dialogue with a partner and learned comparably to tutees; SOLO observers did substantially worse. The brief's design gives each observer a private item on their own device, answered alone, silently, in parallel. That is the solo condition — and worse, it removes the observation entirely, because a player answering their own item is not attending to the target player's reasoning. The recommendation implements the arm of the study that failed while citing the arm that succeeded.
corrected_claim: Collaborative, dialogic observation of another learner's problem-solving produces learning comparable to being the tutee; solo passive observation does not. To use this result, downtime must be filled with PAIRED talk ABOUT THE ACTIVE PLAYER'S ITEM — e.g. the two non-active players confer aloud on a shared prediction of the answer and one discriminating cue — not with parallel private items. If the product wants parallel private retrievals during downtime, that is defensible on retrieval-practice grounds (more attempts per minute) but must be justified by Rowland/Yang, not by Chi et al., and it forecloses the vicarious-learning benefit rather than capturing it.
sources: Chi, M. T. H., Roy, M., & Hausmann, R. G. M. (2008). Observing tutorial dialogues collaboratively: Insights about human tutoring effectiveness from vicarious learning. Cognitive Science, 32(2), 301–341. [NOT FETCHED]

Craig, S. D., Chi, M. T. H., & VanLehn, K. (2009). Improving classroom learning by collaboratively observing human tutoring videos while problem solving. Journal of Educational Psychology, 101(4), 779–789. [NOT FETCHED]

original_claim: Gamification cognitive g ≈ 0.49 (Sailer & Homner 2020), ≈ 0.46 (Huang et al. 2020), ≈ 0.50 (Bai, Hew & Huang 2020) — 'three independent teams converging near 0.5 is the strongest convergence in this whole literature.' Graded STRONG.
problem: The three teams are not independent in the way that matters: they searched the same databases over overlapping windows for the same construct and pool a substantially shared set of primary studies. Agreement between meta-analyses drawing on the same primary pool is arithmetic, not replication — it tells you the pool has a mean near 0.5, including whatever bias the pool carries. Three specific problems the brief does not raise: (a) gamification studies are dominated by short interventions in the window where NOVELTY effects operate, and effects attenuate with duration; (b) the outcome measures are frequently researcher-made post-tests aligned to the gamified content, inflating estimates; (c) the brief asserts Sailer & Homner's bias diagnostics 'did not indicate severe publication bias' while simultaneously admitting it cannot name the test or its value — that is exactly the kind of reassurance that should not be recorded as evidence. This is the single most over-graded item in the brief and sits squarely in the literature flagged as bias-prone.
corrected_claim: Meta-analytic estimates for gamification cluster around g ≈ 0.45–0.50 on cognitive outcomes, but the estimates derive from a heavily overlapping and bias-prone primary pool characterised by short durations, novelty confounds, and researcher-made outcome measures. Treat ~0.5 as an upper bound on a poorly-controlled literature, not as a replicated parameter. Grade: contested. Bai/Hew/Huang and Bai/Hew/Sailer/Jia also share authors with each other, so the brief's 'independent teams' framing overstates independence twice over.
sources: Sailer, M., & Homner, L. (2020). The gamification of learning: A meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review, 32, 77–112. [NOT FETCHED]
Hamari, J., Koivisto, J., & Sarsa, H. (2014). Does gamification work? A literature review of empirical studies on gamification. HICSS-47. [NOT FETCHED]
Koivisto, J., & Hamari, J. (2014). Demographic differences in perceived benefits from gamification. Computers in Human Behavior, 35, 179–188. [NOT FETCHED]

original_claim: Murayama & Elliot (2012): competition's direct effect on performance is ~zero because approach and avoidance paths cancel — therefore 'competition is a null you can tip either way' and 'approach-framing is the entire ballgame.' Graded STRONG.
problem: The null total effect is well-supported; the design inference is not. The opposing-processes model was tested by meta-analytic structural equation modelling over largely CORRELATIONAL, cross-sectional studies in which achievement-goal endorsement was measured, not manipulated. Nothing in that paper demonstrates that a UI copy change ('+3 for your team' vs 'don't lose 3') shifts goal adoption, still less that shifting goal adoption shifts performance causally. The brief has upgraded a meta-analytic mediation model into a design lever and staked its central product licence on it. The mediation is also vulnerable to the standard MASEM objection that the paths come from different study sets. Separately, the near-zero pooled r masks very high heterogeneity — 'approximately zero on average' is compatible with substantial harm in identifiable subgroups, which is in fact the brief's own concern three findings later.
corrected_claim: Competition has approximately no average direct association with performance (r near zero) across a large meta-analytic base, and an opposing-processes account (approach helps, avoidance hurts) fits the correlational structure. That licenses the claim 'competition is not automatically harmful.' It does NOT license 'we can reliably tip the sign with framing' — that step is an untested design hypothesis and should be labelled as one, and made the first thing the product A/B tests rather than the assumption the product is built on.
sources: Murayama, K., & Elliot, A. J. (2012). The competition–performance relation: A meta-analytic review and test of the opposing processes model of competition and performance. Psychological Bulletin, 138(6), 1035–1070. [NOT FETCHED]

original_claim: 'Horwitz, Horwitz & Cope (1986) defined foreign language classroom anxiety as COMPRISING communication apprehension, test anxiety, and fear of negative evaluation' — and fear of negative evaluation is therefore 'one of the three constitutive factors.'
problem: This is the standard textbook misreading. Horwitz et al. drew an ANALOGY to those three performance anxieties to motivate the construct, and were explicit that foreign language anxiety is a distinct, situation-specific construct not reducible to their sum. Empirically the FLCAS does not factor into those three components — factor-analytic replications over three decades recover anywhere from two to five factors, most commonly collapsing communication apprehension and fear of negative evaluation, and Horwitz herself has publicly objected to the three-component reading and to the practice of scoring FLCAS subscales. The brief's inferential chain ('the mechanic is close to a laboratory operationalisation of one of the three constitutive factors') therefore rests on a component that is not a validated subscale.
corrected_claim: Horwitz, Horwitz & Cope (1986) introduced foreign language classroom anxiety as a situation-specific construct related to — but not composed of — communication apprehension, test anxiety, and fear of negative evaluation, and produced the 33-item FLCAS as a unidimensional-intent scale. Fear of negative evaluation remains a well-motivated theoretical concern for a publicly-observed answering mechanic, but it should be cited as a related construct with its own instrument (Leary's Brief FNE scale) rather than as a scored FLCAS subscale. If the brief's 3-item post-match check-in is meant to measure it, it must draw items from a validated FNE instrument, not from a nonexistent FLCAS subscale.
sources: Horwitz, E. K., Horwitz, M. B., & Cope, J. (1986). Foreign language classroom anxiety. The Modern Language Journal, 70(2), 125–132. [NOT FETCHED]
Horwitz, E. K. (2010). Foreign and second language anxiety. Language Teaching, 43(2), 154–167. [NOT FETCHED]
Leary, M. R. (1983). A brief version of the Fear of Negative Evaluation Scale. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 9(3), 371–375. [NOT FETCHED]

original_claim: Deci, Koestner & Ryan (1999), k ≈ 128, free-choice d ≈ −0.34 for tangible expected rewards, cited without qualification as the backdrop for 'never make the reward contingent on winning.'
problem: Presented as settled; it is one of the most contested meta-analytic disputes in psychology. Cameron & Pierce (1994) and Eisenberger & Cameron (1996) meta-analysed overlapping evidence and concluded the undermining effect is limited and largely an artefact of specific reward contingencies; the exchange ran through Psychological Bulletin and American Psychologist without resolution. The free-choice behavioural measure that carries the d ≈ −0.34 has itself been criticised as conflating boredom, demand characteristics, and task completion. Cerasoli, Nicklin & Ford (2014, Psychological Bulletin) later found intrinsic motivation and incentives operate more as complements than substitutes, with incentive salience as the moderator. The brief flags allegiance bias for Johnson & Johnson but not for SDT, where the same problem is at least as severe.
corrected_claim: The reward-undermining effect (tangible, expected, performance-contingent rewards reducing free-choice persistence, d ≈ −0.34) is real in the SDT meta-analysis but contested by independent re-analyses reaching materially weaker conclusions, and later work finds intrinsic and extrinsic motivation more complementary than opposed. The design recommendation — award credit for retrievals attempted rather than for winning — is still sensible, but it should be justified by the competence-feedback studies (Vansteenkiste & Deci 2003; Reeve & Deci 1996) and by simple fairness under mixed proficiency, not by treating undermining as established fact.
sources: Deci, E. L., Koestner, R., & Ryan, R. M. (1999). A meta-analytic review of experiments examining the effects of extrinsic rewards on intrinsic motivation. Psychological Bulletin, 125(6), 627–668. [NOT FETCHED]
Cameron, J., & Pierce, W. D. (1994). Reinforcement, reward, and intrinsic motivation: A meta-analysis. Review of Educational Research, 64(3), 363–423. [NOT FETCHED]

Cerasoli, C. P., Nicklin, J. M., & Ford, M. T. (2014). Intrinsic motivation and extrinsic incentives jointly predict performance: A 40-year meta-analysis. Psychological Bulletin, 140(4), 980–1008. [NOT FETCHED]

original_claim: Bond & Titus (1983) shows audience presence explains only 0.3–3% of variance, therefore 'the mere-observation part of the mechanic is not, by itself, a big harm — do not over-engineer against it.'
problem: The mechanic is not mere presence, so the reassuring number does not apply to it. Bond & Titus pooled studies of the presence of a passive audience or co-actors. This product's mechanic is an OPPONENT who selects your item, has a competitive stake in your failure, and observes the outcome — that is evaluation apprehension plus outcome interdependence, the conditions under which the Cottrell evaluation-apprehension account and the test-anxiety literature predict substantially larger impairment on non-dominant (i.e. not-yet-learned) responses. The brief has used the weakest operationalisation of observation to license the strongest one. This correction cuts against the brief's own conclusion, which is why it matters.
corrected_claim: Mere audience presence is a small effect (roughly 0.3–3% of variance, direction depending on task dominance and on trait moderators per Uziel 2007). But an evaluative, stake-holding observer is a different manipulation with a plausibly larger effect, and hanzi recognition for a beginner is by definition a non-dominant response — the impairment side of Zajonc's account. The brief's private-input mitigation is therefore MORE important than it concludes, not less, and should be treated as a v1 requirement rather than an optional nicety.
sources: Bond, C. F., & Titus, L. J. (1983). Social facilitation: A meta-analysis of 241 studies. Psychological Bulletin, 94(2), 265–292. [NOT FETCHED]
Cottrell, N. B. (1972). Social facilitation. In C. G. McClintock (Ed.), Experimental Social Psychology. [NOT FETCHED]
Uziel, L. (2007). Individual differences in the social facilitation effect: A review and meta-analysis. Journal of Research in Personality, 41(3), 579–601. [NOT FETCHED]

original_claim: 'Errors followed by corrective feedback produce BETTER retention than error-free study... so a public wrong answer is a learning asset provided the correction arrives immediately.' Therefore ship a confusable-pairs category to induce confident errors.
problem: The errorful-generation benefit is conditional in a way that excludes most of this product's error cases. The benefit reliably appears when the learner has a basis for generating — when cue and target are semantically or associatively related, or when the learner holds related prior knowledge (which is also the precondition for hypercorrection: high-confidence errors hypercorrect because the learner has adjacent knowledge to recruit). For genuinely unknown, arbitrary cue–target pairs, the evidence is mixed and errorful generation can be neutral or harmful relative to study. A beginner shown an unseen hanzi has no generative basis at all; their wrong answer is a blind guess, not a productive error. The brief's own eligibility rule (≥5 prior exposures) partially rescues this, but the rescue is stated as an anxiety mitigation, not as the cognitive precondition it actually is.
corrected_claim: Generating an error then receiving corrective feedback outperforms errorless study WHEN the learner has related knowledge to recruit, and errors made with high confidence are the most likely to be corrected. Both conditions require prior exposure. The confusable-pairs item type is therefore well-founded — confusables are precisely the case where the learner has competing prior knowledge — but it must be gated behind demonstrated familiarity with BOTH members of the pair. Presenting a confusable pair before either character is known converts a hypercorrection opportunity into a coin flip.
sources: Metcalfe, J. (2017). Learning from errors. Annual Review of Psychology, 68, 465–489. [NOT FETCHED]
Butterfield, B., & Metcalfe, J. (2001). Errors committed with high confidence are hypercorrected. JEP: LMC, 27(6), 1491–1494. [NOT FETCHED]
Grimaldi, P. J., & Karpicke, J. D. (2012). When and why do retrieval attempts enhance subsequent encoding? Memory & Cognition, 40(4), 505–513. [NOT FETCHED]
Potts, R., & Shanks, D. R. (2014). The benefit of generating errors during learning. JEP: General, 143(2), 644–667. [NOT FETCHED]

original_claim: Rowe (1986) / Tobin (1987) wait-time research justifies 'minimum 5 seconds before any timeout pressure, soft window ~10 seconds.' Graded MODERATE.
problem: Over-graded and transferred across an unbridged gap. The wait-time corpus is 1970s–80s classroom-observation research on TEACHER pause duration after an oral question in whole-class discourse, with small samples, no randomisation, unblinded observers, and outcome measures that are largely properties of student talk (response length, number of speculative responses) rather than learning. Its transfer to a self-paced, silent, single-item recognition tap on a phone is essentially unsupported — there is no oral discourse, no teacher, and no turn-taking norm to violate. The brief's specific 5s and 10s numbers have no source at all.
corrected_claim: Extending teacher wait time to ~3 seconds is associated with longer and more elaborated oral student responses in classroom observation studies, including from lower-achieving students, but this is dated, methodologically weak, and about oral classroom discourse. Grade: weak, and non-transferable to digital item pacing. The relevant literature for setting a response window is instead retrieval-practice work on retrieval latency and on how long learners should attempt retrieval before feedback — and the honest position is that the product should set a generous default and measure the latency distribution of its own correct responses, then set the window at roughly the 90th percentile.
sources: Rowe, M. B. (1986). Wait time: Slowing down may be a way of speeding up. Journal of Teacher Education, 37(1), 43–50. [NOT FETCHED]
Tobin, K. (1987). The role of wait time in higher cognitive level learning. Review of Educational Research, 57(1), 69–95. [NOT FETCHED]

original_claim: Tsai & Tsai (2018) g ≈ 0.87 for digital game-based L2 vocabulary; Chiu, Kao & Reynolds (2012) d ≈ 0.5 for DGBL in EFL, cited as a meta-analytic anchor.
problem: Two separate problems. (a) A pooled g near 0.87 for a vocabulary intervention is a magnitude that should be disbelieved on sight: it exceeds nearly every well-controlled educational effect in this brief, including retrieval practice, and in a literature with k ≈ 26, short interventions, and predominantly passive controls it is far better explained by small-study effects plus control-group weakness than by the intervention. The brief flags low confidence in the number but still lets it stand as the headline of a 'moderate'-graded finding. (b) Chiu, Kao & Reynolds (2012) is paginated E104–E107 in BJET — a four-page Colloquium note, not a full meta-analytic paper. A four-page note is not a suitable anchor for a design decision and should not sit alongside Review-of-Educational-Research-grade syntheses without that flag.
corrected_claim: Digital game-based L2 vocabulary meta-analyses report large pooled effects, but the largest of them is best read as an upper bound contaminated by weak comparison conditions — which is the explicit contribution of Tsai & Tsai's own moderator analysis ('conditions of research designs'). Plan against the active-control subgroup estimate, not the pooled one, and if that subgroup estimate cannot be recovered from the paper, plan against the general game-vs-nongame figure (g ≈ 0.33) instead. Treat Chiu et al. (2012) as a short colloquium note, cited for orientation only.
sources: Tsai, Y.-L., & Tsai, C.-C. (2018). Digital game-based second-language vocabulary learning and conditions of research designs: A meta-analysis study. Computers & Education, 125, 345–357. [NOT FETCHED]
Chiu, Y.-H., Kao, C.-W., & Reynolds, B. L. (2012). BJET, 43(4), E104–E107 (Colloquium). [NOT FETCHED]

original_claim: Sitzmann (2011): 'the advantage held when the comparison group was PASSIVE and shrank toward zero when comparison trainees were actively engaged with the same content.'
problem: I believe this conflates two different moderators. Sitzmann's reported moderators centre on properties of the GAME and its deployment — whether the simulation conveyed course material actively rather than passively, whether trainees had unlimited access to the game, and whether the game supplemented rather than replaced other instruction. A moderator defined by the activity level of the COMPARISON group is a different variable, and 'shrank toward zero' is a stronger statement than a moderator analysis with k ≈ 65 across heterogeneous designs can usually support. The brief then builds its entire framing ('the game is a compliance and scheduling technology, not a learning technology') on this one sentence. The underlying methodological point is sound and is better carried by Mayer's media-comparison-versus-value-added critique, which the brief already cites and which does not depend on a possibly-misremembered moderator.
corrected_claim: Simulation games outperform comparison conditions on declarative knowledge, procedural knowledge, retention and self-efficacy (roughly +9% to +20%), with effects moderated by how actively the game conveys material, by unlimited access, and by whether the game supplements rather than replaces instruction. The claim that the advantage specifically vanishes against active comparison groups should be verified before it is quoted; the general point that game-versus-nongame media comparisons cannot isolate the game's contribution is safely carried by Mayer (2019) alone.
sources: Sitzmann, T. (2011). A meta-analytic examination of the instructional effectiveness of computer-based simulation games. Personnel Psychology, 64(2), 489–528. [NOT FETCHED]
Mayer, R. E. (2019). Computer games in education. Annual Review of Psychology, 70, 531–549. [NOT FETCHED]

original_claim: Numerous hard product specifications presented as flowing from the evidence: ≥60/≤40 content-vs-game-feel budget split; ≥40 scored retrievals per 10-minute session; opponents may deal only from categories with ≥5 prior exposures; ≤20-word explanations; ≤14px uncoloured score delta and ≥17px explanation text; correction within 300ms; no screen idle >2s; matches capped at 8–12 minutes; re-queue at 5 and 15 intervening items; 1-match-in-5 anxiety sampling; 3-row leaderboard.
problem: None of these numbers appears in, or is derivable from, any cited source. Every one is an invented product decision wearing a citation. This is the brief's most pervasive and most dangerous pattern, because downstream readers will treat '≥5 prior exposures, per Horwitz et al.' as evidence-backed and will not re-derive it. Only the 20-word cap is honestly labelled as an arithmetic heuristic, and even that combines a native-English silent-reading rate with an invented on-screen degradation factor and an invented window length.
corrected_claim: Separate the document into two registers and label every line as one or the other: (1) findings, with a source and an effect size; (2) product decisions, which are defaults chosen by the team, consistent with the findings but not implied by them. All the numbers above belong in register 2. Each should carry an owner, a rationale, and — for the ones that are cheap to test — a planned in-product experiment. A design doc that cannot distinguish 'the literature says' from 'we decided' will not survive its first disagreement.
sources: Internal consistency check of the brief under review; no external source is claimed or exists for these figures.

original_claim: Confusable-pair item category exemplified by 未/末, 己/已/巳, 土/士, 干/千, 白/百, 人/入, 天/夭.
problem: The character forms, and the visual confusions among them, are all correct — no errors of fact. But roughly half of this set is out of scope for a product whose stated domain is menus, subway signage, supermarket labels and shopfronts. 夭 (yāo, 'die young') and 巳 (sì, sixth earthly branch) essentially never appear on consumer signage; 己 (jǐ) appears almost exclusively bound in 自己 zìjǐ; 士 (shì) appears mainly in 博士/护士/巴士. Building a category around the classic pedagogical confusables imports a rare-character tail into an app whose whole premise is high-frequency real-world reading, and it does so at the exact moment the brief argues for spending the budget on item quality and coverage.
corrected_claim: Keep the confusable-pair mechanic, but source the pairs from the product's own domain rather than from the traditional teaching list. Retain the pairs that earn their place in signage — 未/末 is justified because 末 appears in 末班车 mòbānchē 'last train' and 周末 zhōumò 'weekend'; 干/千 because 干 appears in 干炒 gānchǎo and 饼干 bǐnggān; 白/百 because both appear in prices and product names; 人/入 because 入口 rùkǒu 'entrance' is core subway vocabulary and 人 is ubiquitous. Drop 夭 and 巳 outright. Then add the confusions that actually cause failure on real signage and are absent from the brief: 入口 rùkǒu 'entrance' vs 出口 chūkǒu 'exit'; 推 tuī 'push' vs 拉 lā 'pull'; 男 nán vs 女 nǚ; 大 dà vs 太 tài; 己/已 only in the compounds where they occur.
sources: Direct inspection of the character set in the brief; standard readings verified against my own knowledge of modern standard Mandarin. [No dictionary or corpus fetched — egress blocked]

original_claim: Foreign-language anxiety correlates r ≈ −0.34 to −0.39 with achievement across three independent meta-analyses; 'direction of causation is bidirectional and contested — but the magnitude is not in serious doubt.'
problem: The magnitude is credible but the brief omits the specific counter-account that would most change the product decision. Sparks and colleagues' Linguistic Coding Differences Hypothesis argues that the anxiety–achievement correlation is substantially a CONSEQUENCE of underlying language-learning aptitude and L1 literacy differences — anxious learners are anxious largely because they are struggling — and that treating anxiety as the causal input inverts the arrow. This has run as an explicit, decades-long exchange with MacIntyre in the Modern Language Journal. It matters here because the brief's mitigation logic assumes reducing anxiety will improve outcomes; under the LCDH reading, the same correlation predicts that improving decoding skill reduces anxiety, and that anxiety-reduction alone buys little. Also unmentioned: these are overwhelmingly cross-sectional self-report studies with course grades as the outcome, so common-method variance inflates the pooled r.
corrected_claim: Foreign-language anxiety correlates around r ≈ −0.36 with L2 achievement across large meta-analyses, but the causal direction is genuinely disputed, with a substantial body of work (Sparks & Ganschow's LCDH and the Sparks–MacIntyre exchange) arguing the arrow runs predominantly from low proficiency to anxiety. The design consequence: keep the anxiety instrumentation, but do not promise that anxiety mitigation will improve learning. The stronger and less contested rationale for the mitigations is retention and attendance — anxious players quit — which the product can measure directly.
sources: Teimouri, Y., Goetze, J., & Plonsky, L. (2019). Second language anxiety and achievement: A meta-analysis. SSLA, 41(2), 363–387. [NOT FETCHED]
Sparks, R. L., & Ganschow, L. (2007). Is the Foreign Language Classroom Anxiety Scale measuring anxiety or language skills? Foreign Language Annals, 40(2), 260–287. [NOT FETCHED]
MacIntyre, P. D. (1995). How does anxiety affect second language learning? A reply to Sparks and Ganschow. Modern Language Journal, 79(1), 90–99. [NOT FETCHED]

original_claim: Two internal inconsistencies: (a) v1 item bank is 'recognition-only: given hanzi... select/say the meaning' while the same brief argues private input is free because 'reading, not speaking, is the target skill'; (b) the gamification claim headline reads 'g ≈ 0.36–0.50 on cognitive outcomes' while its own detail assigns 0.36 to motivational and 0.49 to cognitive.
problem: (a) 'Select/say' quietly admits a spoken production modality into a spec that elsewhere forbids it and that depends on forbidding it — the whole private-input mitigation collapses if any item type requires speaking aloud at a table. (b) The headline range conflates two different outcome families, producing a 'cognitive' range whose lower bound is actually the motivational estimate. Small, but it is the number a skim-reader will carry away.
corrected_claim: (a) State the v1 modality as recognition-and-selection only: given a hanzi or short sign-like string, SELECT the meaning from options on the player's own device. No spoken response of any kind in v1. (b) Report gamification as cognitive g ≈ 0.49, motivational g ≈ 0.36, behavioural g ≈ 0.25, as separate outcome families, with the contested grade above.
sources: Internal consistency check of the brief under review.

original_claim: Fontsource ships Noto Sans SC with only five named subsets — latin, latin-ext, cyrillic, vietnamese, chinese-simplified — i.e. the entire Simplified Chinese repertoire is ONE woff2 per weight. So `npm i @fontsource/noto-sans-sc` naively pulls a multi-megabyte blob per weight into your bundle. Treat 'full single weight ≈ 4–5 MB woff2 / ~10 MB OTF over ~44k glyphs' as an order-of-magnitude figure.
problem: Both halves are factually wrong, and I measured them. I downloaded @fontsource/noto-sans-sc@5.3.0 (73 MB tarball) and inspected it with fonttools. (1) The package ships 97 NUMBERED unicode-range chunk files per weight IN ADDITION to the five named subsets — i.e. exactly the Google-Fonts-style split the brief says Fontsource does not do. The DEFAULT entry point `index.css` uses the numbered chunks, not the named blob: the first @font-face is `noto-sans-sc-4-400-normal.woff2` with `unicode-range: U+1f1e9-1f1f5,...`. So the naive `npm i` does NOT pull one multi-megabyte blob. (2) The named `chinese-simplified` woff2 at weight 400 is 1,142,552 bytes = 1.09 MB, and its cmap contains 7,946 codepoints / 7,333 CJK ideographs / 8,248 glyphs — not 4–5 MB and not ~44k glyphs. The brief is ~4x high on size and ~5x high on glyph count. The 97 numbered chunks at weight 400 total 2.27 MB (mean 24 KB each).
corrected_claim: Measured, this session, with fonttools/pyftsubset. @fontsource/noto-sans-sc@5.3.0 ships BOTH ~97 numbered unicode-range chunks per weight (used by the default index.css) and five named subsets. The named `chinese-simplified` woff2 @400 = 1.09 MB / 7,946 codepoints / 7,333 hanzi. Subsetting that file with pyftsubset (woff2, --layout-features= stripped, --no-hinting, plus 121 Latin/punctuation codepoints) measures: 300 hanzi → 44.7 KB; 600 → 84.9 KB; 900 → 123.5 KB; 1,200 → 164.0 KB; 2,000 → 277.4 KB; 3,000 → 418.6 KB. The brief's '250–450 KB for a 3,000-glyph one-weight subset' is CONFIRMED (418.6 KB) and its near-linearity claim is CONFIRMED (109 → 137 bytes/glyph). But the baseline was wrong, so the SAVING from subsetting is 1.09 MB → 0.42 MB (2.6x), not 4–5 MB → 0.42 MB (10x). ARCHITECTURE CONSEQUENCE, and it reverses the brief's recommendation: for a ~1,200-character bank the subset saves ~925 KB, but shipping the whole 1.09 MB `chinese-simplified` file deletes the entire 'walk the item bank, emit codepoints, fail the build if any is missing' risk class the brief spent a finding on. On an offline-first PWA where a missing glyph is unrecoverable at a restaurant table, 670 KB is cheap insurance. Subset only if the 3 MB install budget is genuinely tight, and if you do, keep the build gate.
sources: Measured this session: npm pack @fontsource/noto-sans-sc@5.3.0; file sizes via stat; cmap/glyph counts via fontTools.ttLib.TTFont.getBestCmap(); subsets produced with pyftsubset 4.63.0
https://www.npmjs.com/package/@fontsource/noto-sans-sc
https://github.com/fontsource/font-files/tree/main/fonts/google/noto-sans-sc

original_claim: FAIL THE BUILD if any item-bank codepoint is missing from the produced subset. Step (3) is the important one — a menu game will reach for 焗 煲 涮 菌 藕 韭, characters that a naive 'subset from HSK' would drop, and the failure mode is tofu boxes on a customer's phone at a restaurant table with no network to recover.
problem: I tested the brief's own six scare-examples against the actual font cmap. All six — 焗 煲 涮 菌 藕 韭 — are present in the Fontsource `chinese-simplified` subset. So is every one of the 3,000 HSK 3.0 characters (0 missing). The tofu failure mode the brief warns about is not a property of Noto Sans SC or of Fontsource; it is a hazard created solely by the brief's own recommended subsetting step. Stated as written, it argues for the subsetting build gate using evidence that actually argues against needing to subset at all.
corrected_claim: Verified: the Fontsource `chinese-simplified` Noto Sans SC subset covers all 3,000 HSK 3.0 characters and all of 焗 煲 涮 菌 藕 韭 (and 笋 蒜 姜 葱 炝 烩 氽 煨 熘 腌 蕈 蚝 蛏 鲈 鳕 鳝). Tofu risk is zero if you ship that file. The build gate remains correct advice ONLY in the branch where you subset — and it is then genuinely load-bearing, because the risk comes from your codepoint-extraction step, not from the typeface.
sources: Measured this session: fontTools cmap of noto-sans-sc-chinese-simplified-400-normal.woff2 intersected with the 3,000-character HSK 3.0 list and the brief's own signage exemplars

original_claim: HSK is the wrong content spine for this product regardless of licensing. HSK 1-3 does not contain the characters on a Chinese menu, a subway sign or a supermarket label — the exact four tasks the user named. […] 出口 入口 闸机 换乘 末班 首班 站台 (transit), 保质期 净含量 配料 生产日期 冷藏 (labels), 折 满减 特价 现磨 (shopfronts). Several of these are outside HSK entirely and outside the common-3500 list.
problem: I parsed elkmovie/hsk30 and computed this per character. The claim holds for MENUS and fails for the other three registers, which is two thirds of the argument. Transit (出口 入口 闸机 换乘 末班 首班 站台): 12/12 characters are in HSK 3.0 and 10/12 are in HSK 1–3 (only 闸 at 7–9 and 乘 at level 5 fall outside 1–3). Labels (保质期 净含量 配料 生产日期 冷藏): 13/13 in HSK 3.0, 9/13 in HSK 1–3. Shopfronts (折 满减 特价 现磨): 7/7 in HSK 3.0, 4/7 in HSK 1–3. Zero characters in those three groups are outside HSK 3.0. Separately, the 'outside the common-3500 list' rider is refuted: against 通用规范汉字表 (8,105 chars), 笋 藕 韭 菌 are all tier-1 (within the common 3,500); only 焗 炝 烩 煲 fall outside 3,500, all in tier 2.
corrected_claim: Measured. The MENU register genuinely is outside HSK: of the brief's ten cooking verbs, 0/10 are in HSK 1–3 and 焗 炝 烩 are outside HSK 3.0 entirely; of its seven ingredients, 0/7 are in HSK 1–3 and 笋 藕 韭 are outside HSK 3.0. But transit, product-label and shopfront signage is built almost entirely from HSK 1–3 characters. The correct and more useful claim: for menus the barrier is unknown CHARACTERS; for transit/labels/shopfronts the barrier is WORD and compound parsing over characters the learner already nominally knows — 换乘, 末班, 净含量, 保质期 are all made of high-frequency characters whose combined meaning is opaque. That is a different pedagogical problem and a different item format. CONTENT CONSEQUENCE: split the v1 bank into two item types — character-acquisition items for the menu register, and compound-parsing/cloze items for the transit-label-shopfront register — instead of treating all four tasks as one 'signage register' the way the brief does.
sources: Parsed this session: https://github.com/elkmovie/hsk30 charlist.txt (3,000 chars: 300 × levels 1–6 + 1,200 at 七—九级; 0 duplicates; handwriting sub-lists 初等 300 / 中等 400 / 高等 500) and wordlist.txt (11,092 words; level 1 = 500) — all counts in the brief CONFIRMED exactly, and 中等手写字表 = 400, which the brief left blank
https://github.com/jaywcjlove/table-of-general-standard-chinese-characters (通用规范汉字表, 8,105 characters in tiers 3,500 / 3,000 / 1,605, MIT)

original_claim: FSRS (Ye et al. / open-spaced-repetition) is now Anki's default scheduler and is evaluated on a large public benchmark of real review logs against SM-2 and other algorithms. […] ARCHITECTURE: implement FSRS, not SM-2, and therefore store a full per-item review log. Anki with mainstream Chinese decks is the strongest scheduler in the landscape (FSRS is a real, benchmarked improvement over SM-2).
problem: I read the current srs-benchmark README in full. Three problems. (1) SM-2 IS NOT IN THE PUBLISHED RESULTS TABLES AT ALL. It survives only as a runnable `--algo` CLI option in the usage section. The specific FSRS-beats-SM-2 comparison the brief invokes cannot be read off this source. (2) FSRS-7 is mid-table, not the leader. Over 9,999 collections and 349,923,850 evaluated reviews, Log Loss: RWKV-P 0.2773, RWKV 0.3193, LSTM 0.3332, GRU 0.3333, MOVING-AVG 0.3369, Logistic Regression 0.3393, FSRS-7 recency 0.3414, FSRS-7 0.3437. A ZERO-PARAMETER moving average of recent outcomes beats FSRS-7 on Log Loss and on RMSE(bins) (0.0592 vs 0.0655); FSRS-7 leads it only on AUC (0.7069 vs 0.7001). (3) The benchmark is authored and maintained by FSRS's own developer, and its headline metric RMSE(bins) was designed by the same project — the README itself lists 'RMSE-BINS-EXPLOIT', a 0-parameter algorithm that games that metric to a best-in-table 0.0135 while scoring a catastrophic 4.608 Log Loss. Finally, everything here measures predictive calibration on Anki review logs; no learning-outcome RCT is cited anywhere.
corrected_claim: Honest version: FSRS beats every other SCHEDULABLE, interpretable model in the benchmark (DASH, DASH[MCM], DASH[ACT-R], ACT-R, HLR, Ebisu v2, and all earlier FSRS versions) — MOVING-AVG and RWKV-P outscore it on calibration but MOVING-AVG cannot produce an interval and the README says it 'has no practical applications'. SM-2 is not benchmarked in the current tables. And the benchmark measures prediction, not learning. PRODUCT CONSEQUENCE, which is the part that matters here: a co-located party game played at a restaurant table generates almost no longitudinal per-item review history. FSRS-7 with DEFAULT parameters (no per-user optimisation, which is the only regime this usage pattern will ever reach) scores Log Loss 0.3629 — WORSE than the zero-parameter MOVING-AVG's 0.3369 and worse than every optimised FSRS variant. Implementing FSRS and storing a full timestamped review log is real architectural complexity buying a benefit that cannot materialise at fortnightly play frequency. Recommend instead: store per-item (n_seen, n_correct, last_seen, last_outcome) and select items with a simple recency-weighted difficulty estimate. Revisit FSRS only if telemetry shows a cohort playing several times a week.
sources: https://github.com/open-spaced-repetition/srs-benchmark — README read in full this session; results tables for 9,999 collections / 349,923,850 reviews (without same-day) and 10,000 collections / 519,296,315 reviews (with same-day)

original_claim: VERIFIED: read the comment header of the distributed cedict_ts.u8 […] CC-CEDICT is Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International — NOT 3.0. The 3.0 figure is the single most commonly misreported licence fact in the Chinese-learning tooling world.
problem: The licence fact is right and I independently re-confirmed it on two copies with different build stamps (2023-09-03T08:57:17Z, entries=121617; and 2024-12-06T15:50:49Z, entries=122898) — both state 'Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International License' with the by-sa/4.0 URL, MDBG as publisher, and the Denisowski 1997/1998 ancestor. Two sub-claims are wrong. (a) Sourcing: the brief says it read 'the distributed cedict_ts.u8'. Both files it cites are TEST FIXTURES — huwd/learn_hanzi's is 53 lines and danslocombe/ceot_maau's is 31 lines, against a real distribution of ~123,000 entries. The header is authentic; the description of what was read is not, and that matters because the brief uses 'I read the real file' as its grounds for grading Part 2 'strong'. (b) 'The 3.0 figure is the most commonly misreported licence fact': CC-CEDICT genuinely WAS CC BY-SA 3.0 for many years before the switch. Sources saying 3.0 are stale, not wrong-about-the-present-having-always-been-4.0 — and anyone relying on an old vendored copy may legitimately be under 3.0 terms.
corrected_claim: CC BY-SA 4.0 confirmed on two independent copies (2023 and 2024 builds). But cite it as a header quotation from small fixture files, not as a read of the distribution, and drop the 'most commonly misreported' framing — 3.0 is a stale figure, not a myth, and if you vendored a pre-switch copy you are on 3.0 terms for that copy. MISSED OBLIGATION, and it bears on architecture: CC BY-SA 4.0 §2(a)(5)(B) forbids applying effective technological measures to the Licensed Material. A pure PWA served over the open web is fine. The moment the same bundle is wrapped for the iOS App Store behind FairPlay DRM, the gloss file's ShareAlike terms are in tension with the distribution channel — the classic CC/App Store problem. Note the same clause exists in the Arphic Public License §5 ('You may not impose any further restrictions on the recipients' exercise of the rights granted herein'), so it applies to stroke data too. Practical rule: stay a PWA, or serve the gloss/stroke assets as separately-fetched, non-DRM'd files.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/danslocombe/ceot_maau/master/test/cedict_ts.u8 (31 lines, build 2023-09-03T08:57:17Z, entries=121617)

original_claim: CONTENT + ARCHITECTURE: make Unihan the *spine* of the item bank […] Derive radical, stroke count and pinyin from Unihan rather than from CC-CEDICT where both have the field, so those columns carry no ShareAlike obligation. Useful Unihan fields: kTotalStrokes, kRSUnicode, kMandarin, kDefinition, kGradeLevel, kFrequency, kSimplifiedVariant/kTraditionalVariant.
problem: This is the most damaging recommendation in the brief because it trades content CORRECTNESS for an attribution line, and it will ship wrong pinyin. Unihan kMandarin gives ONE reading per character. I measured the heteronym (多音字) rate against the 597-entry 多音字 table in the MIT-licensed 通用规范汉字表 dataset: 387 of HSK 3.0's 3,000 characters are heteronyms — 12.9%. Of the common-3,500, 430 are — 12.3%. So a single-reading-per-character pinyin column is wrong for roughly one character in eight. And the brief's OWN signage examples are heteronyms: 现磨 needs mó, not mò; 净含量 needs liàng, not liáng; 打折 needs zhé (折 = shé / zhē / zhé); 银行 is háng but 人行道 is xíng (行 = háng / héng / xíng). The sharpest case is the brief's own menu example: 菌 is jūn / jùn, and on a menu (菌菇, 野生菌) it is jùn 'mushroom' while the default single reading is jūn 'bacterium'. A licence-motivated column choice would ship 'jūn' as the pinyin for a mushroom dish. Separately, kFrequency and kGradeLevel are legacy fields derived from small 1990s sources and are on the deprecated track — I could not confirm their current status because unicode.org is egress-blocked this session, but do not build item ordering on them without checking.
corrected_claim: Keep Unihan for kTotalStrokes and kRSUnicode (character-intrinsic, single-valued, permissive — the brief is right there). Do NOT take pinyin from kMandarin. Pinyin is a property of the STRING, not of the character: take it per-word from CC-CEDICT (whose readings are per-entry and therefore contextually right) or author it by hand for a 600–900-string bank, and discharge the BY-SA obligation once at build time exactly as the brief already proposes for the gloss table. Do not use kFrequency or kGradeLevel for ordering without verifying they are still live. SCHEMA CONSEQUENCE: the brief's per-item schema {string, gloss, semantic_component[], phonetic_component[], confusable_with[], tier, signage_frequency} has NO reading field at all. Add reading as a per-character array on the string — reading: [{char, pinyin}] — plus a has_variant_reading flag, so the confusable-distractor generator can never pair 磨 mó against 磨 mò as though they were the same item.

original_claim: Chinese-language content in the brief: 'the ability to see 请 as 言 + 青 in under a second'; 'no picture can be drawn over 醬 or 藏'; 'a dense simplified character such as 蔬 or 酱 packs 15–17 strokes'; '炒 爆 焗 煲 卤 涮 蒸 拌 炝 烩 (cooking methods on every menu)'.
problem: Four errors, three of which would ship as wrong content. (1) 请 = 讠 + 青 in SIMPLIFIED, not 言 + 青. 言 + 青 = 請, the TRADITIONAL form. Verified by stroke decomposition against hanzi-writer-data: 请 = 10 strokes, 請 = 15, 讠 = 2, 言 = 7. This is the brief's flagship pedagogical example for its highest-leverage recommendation (phonetic-series ordering), in a product the brief elsewhere targets at mainland simplified signage. (2) 醬 is traditional; the simplified form is 酱 — the brief mixes scripts inside an argument about simplified. (3) 酱 is 13 strokes, not 15–17 (traditional 醬 is 18; 蔬 = 15 ✓; 藏 = 17 ✓). (4) 焗 (jú, baked/oven-cooked) and 煲 (bāo, clay-pot) are Cantonese/Guangdong-HK cuisine terms, not 'on every menu' — and they are largely absent from the Chengdu menus the brief specifically proposes photographing, where the register is 麻辣, 水煮, 干煸, 回锅, 毛血旺. A register claim needs a region attached.
corrected_claim: Corrected: 请 decomposes as 讠 (semantic, speech) + 青 (phonetic, qīng) in simplified. 酱 is the simplified form (13 strokes); 醬 is traditional (18). For the typography argument use 蔬 (15) or 藏 (17), which do carry the stroke density claimed. Menu register is REGIONAL: 焗/煲 = Cantonese; 炝/烩 = northern; 麻辣/水煮/干煸/回锅 = Sichuan. If the corpus is photographed in Chengdu, the cooking-verb inventory is the Sichuan one, and the brief's example list is the wrong list for its own fieldwork plan. ADDITIONAL HAZARD THE BRIEF MISSED ENTIRELY: simplified→traditional is 1:many, and the brief lists Unihan kTraditionalVariant as a spine field with no warning. Verified mappings: 干→[乾, 幹], 发→[發, 髮], 只→[隻, 祗, 衹], 台→[臺, 檯, 颱], 历→[歷, 曆], 钟→[鐘, 鍾], 复→[復, 複], 尽→[盡, 儘], 系→[係, 繫], 表→錶, 板→闆, 松→鬆, 斗→鬥. 干 is on every Sichuan menu (干煸, 干锅, 豆干) and its correct traditional form is 乾; auto-picking 幹 instead yields a character that reads as an expletive in Taiwanese usage. Never auto-convert. Store both forms per string, or ship simplified only.

original_claim: VERIFIED: fetched a representative hanzi-writer-data character file. Structure is {strokes, medians, radStrokes} at roughly 2.5–3 KB per character for a 7-stroke character […] so a 3,000-character bank is ~8 MB raw / ~2–3 MB gzipped.
problem: The brief generalised from a single unrepresentative file. 你.json is 2,106 bytes — well BELOW the dataset mean. I measured the whole of hanzi-writer-data@2.0.1: 9,574 per-character JSON files, mean 3,368 B, median 3,273 B, range 217–8,621 B. So 3,000 characters is 9.64 MB raw, not ~8 MB. On compression I measured a real 1,200-character concatenation: 3.75 MB raw → 1.53 MB gzip -9 → 1.21 MB brotli q11 (41% / 32%). Scaling that, 3,000 characters is ≈3.9 MB gzip / ≈3.1 MB brotli, not '2–3 MB gzipped'. Both figures are ~25–30% low.
corrected_claim: Measured on hanzi-writer-data@2.0.1: 9,574 characters, mean 3,368 B / median 3,273 B per file. A 3,000-character bank is 9.64 MB raw, ≈3.9 MB gzipped, ≈3.1 MB brotli; a 1,200-character bank is 3.85 MB raw / 1.53 MB gzip / 1.21 MB brotli. original_claim: it generalises the pictographic principle to a script in which roughly 80–90% of characters are 形声 phono-semantic compounds […] The phono-semantic proportion (~80%+ of characters in the 說文解字 and higher in modern inventories) is a settled descriptive fact in Chinese linguistics, not a contested claim. […] IMPLICATION: order the item bank BY PHONETIC SERIES, teaching 青 → 请 清 情 晴 睛 as a block. This is the single highest-leverage structural decision available.
problem: I could reach no scholarly source this session (WebSearch budget exhausted at 200/200 before I started; scholar.google.com, semanticscholar.org, arxiv.org, aclanthology.org, journals.plos.org, doi.org, ncbi, osf.io, unicode.org, en.wikipedia.org all return 403 at the egress proxy — only github.com, raw.githubusercontent.com, api.github.com, registry.npmjs.org and pypi.org resolve). So this remains unverified after my review too. But two things are wrong with the framing even without a source. (a) DENOMINATOR. The ~82% figure is a TYPE count over the Shuowen Jiezi (c. 100 CE, ~9,353 entries) and the 90%+ figures are type counts over large modern inventories including rare characters. Neither denominator is a 1,200-character signage bank, where high-frequency characters skew toward simple non-compound forms. (b) PREDICTIVENESS ≠ PROPORTION. Being 形声 in origin does not mean the phonetic component predicts the modern Mandarin reading — millennia of sound change and the 1950s simplification have severed many series. DeFrancis's own emphasis, as I recall it, is a much lower figure (around two thirds) for characters whose phonetic gives a USABLE clue, and that is the number the product decision actually depends on. 青 → 请 清 情 晴 睛 is the textbook best case (five characters, one syllable, tone-varying only), not the typical one.
corrected_claim: Grade this as two separate claims. The type-count statistic (~80–90% 形声 by origin) is well established in the descriptive literature but is denominator-dependent and was NOT verifiable this session. The inference the brief draws from it — that phonetic-series ordering is 'the single highest-leverage structural decision available' — is a design bet, not a finding, and should be labelled as one. Before committing content-authoring weeks to a phonetic-series table, run the cheap empirical test on your own bank: for each character, check whether the phonetic component's own reading matches the character's reading exactly, in syllable-only (tone-differing), or not at all. Publish those three proportions for YOUR 1,200 characters. If the exact+tone-differing share is below roughly half, series ordering is not worth the authoring cost and the effort belongs in the semantic-component/radical column instead. The DeFrancis (1984) 'ideographic myth' anchor is real and appropriate; the specific percentage attributed to it needs checking against the book.

original_claim: Part 2 licensing is largely SOLID because the primary sources are files on GitHub that I read directly […] These do not need re-running. […] Proceed now on Part 2 licensing decisions — those are verified and are the ones that gate what can ship.
problem: The confidence allocation is inverted, and that is the single most consequential thing wrong with the brief. Part 2 is where I found the largest MEASURABLE errors: the Noto Sans SC size is ~4x high, the glyph count ~5x high, the Fontsource packaging description is simply wrong, the hanzi-writer-data sizes are ~30% low, the CC-CEDICT 'primary source' is a 53-line test fixture, and the Unihan-for-pinyin recommendation would ship wrong content on 12.9% of characters. Every one of those errors is in a finding graded 'strong' and explicitly excluded from re-verification. The pattern is consistent: where the brief READ a licence text it is reliable (I re-confirmed makemeahanzi COPYING, the full Arphic Public License, both OFL files including the 'Source' RFN, hanzi-writer-data's APL declaration, elkmovie/hsk30's MIT header and Pleco attribution, and every HSK count — all correct); where it INFERRED a quantity or described a package's behaviour it is not.
corrected_claim: Split Part 2 by evidence type, not by part number. LICENCE TEXTS READ VERBATIM — reliable, re-confirmed by me, no re-run needed: makemeahanzi COPYING (dictionary.txt LGPL-3.0-or-later from Unihan + CJKlib; graphics.txt Arphic PL from AR PL KaitiM GB / AR PL UKai) ✓; Arphic Public License full text ✓ including §1 verbatim-copy, the 'Freely Available … you can charge for this service' definition, §2(a) prominent-notice, §2(b) designated-place copyleft, §0 rename permission, §3 auto-termination — plus TWO clauses the brief missed: §2's explicit mere-aggregation carve-out (which is what actually protects your app code) and §5's no-further-restrictions bar; Source Han Sans LICENSE.txt OFL 1.1 with 'Copyright 2014-2025 Adobe … with Reserved Font Name Source' ✓; Noto CJK Sans/LICENSE OFL 1.1 with NO copyright line and NO RFN ✓ (so the brief's 'use Noto and rename the subset' is right); hanzi-writer-data license = APL ✓; elkmovie/hsk30 MIT © 2021 Pleco Inc. ✓; all HSK 3.0 counts ✓ exactly. QUANTITIES AND PACKAGE BEHAVIOUR — every one I could test was wrong; re-measure before use. One caveat the brief omitted while calling the HSK counts 'VERIFIED': the elkmovie/hsk30 files carry the header "OCR'ed but not extensively proofread (yet)", so treat individual entries as unproofread OCR even though the aggregate structure checks out perfectly.
