original_claim: PSTM r = .31 … 'This protects the ~30% of the variance-in-uptake that PSTM would otherwise silently impose as a difficulty tax.'
problem: Arithmetic error in the implication, which is where the architecture decision is made. r = .31 means r² ≈ .096 — PSTM accounts for roughly 9–10% of variance, not 30%. The brief inflates its own headline effect threefold in the sentence that spends engineering budget. Worse, the brief correctly scolds others for overstating r=.31 two sentences earlier ('the folk claim … overstates a r=.31') and then commits the same overstatement itself. The meta-analysis (Kurita 2026, ITL, 52 effect sizes / 18 studies, r=.31 [.21,.41], PSTM test type a significant moderator, scoped to AUDITORY vocabulary) verifies exactly as described — the finding is fine, the implication is not.
corrected_claim: PSTM explains roughly 9–10% of variance in auditory L2 vocabulary acquisition (r = .31), of unknown magnitude for orthographic learning in a logographic script. The design rule (audio optional, never gating, never scored) survives, but it is a cheap-insurance decision against a ~10% effect in an adjacent task, not protection of 30% of anything.
sources: Kurita, K. (2026). Revisiting the effects of phonological short-term memory on second language vocabulary acquisition: A meta-analysis. ITL – International Journal of Applied Linguistics. https://doi.org/10.1075/itl.25009.kur — verified: 52 effect sizes, 18 studies, r = .31, PSTM test type a significant moderator, learning context approaching significance, scoped to auditory L2 vocabulary.

original_claim: 'The self-reference effect is large in the lab (d ≈ 0.65 vs semantic encoding).'
problem: The 0.65 figure does not match what Symons & Johnson (1997) is reported to contain. Accessible summaries of the meta-analysis (129 studies) give a mean weighted effect around d ≈ .45–.50, and — structurally important — the SRE is SMALLER when self-reference is compared with other-reference than when compared with semantic encoding. The brief attaches the largest number it could find to the comparison that yields the smaller one. I could not read the full text (publisher and repository domains are egress-blocked), so I am flagging a discrepancy rather than asserting the replacement figure with certainty; either way 0.65 is unverifiable from any source I could reach.
corrected_claim: Symons & Johnson (1997) report a mean weighted d of approximately 0.50 for the self-reference effect, smaller for self-vs-other than self-vs-semantic comparisons, from 129 studies of trait-adjective lists with undergraduate samples at short retention intervals. Grade it moderate, not large. The brief's actual recommendation (frame items as second-person scenarios, build nothing) is proportionate and should stand — it just should not be sold on an inflated number.
sources: Symons, C. S., & Johnson, B. T. (1997). The self-reference effect in memory: A meta-analysis. Psychological Bulletin, 121(3), 371–394. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9136641/
Semantic Scholar record: https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/The-self-reference-effect-in-memory:-a-Symons-Johnson/1a59cefe5401fa58c0e65bdac7e9f9607f5fe51f

original_claim: 'Curiosity states enhance memory for BOTH the anticipated item and incidental material encountered during the anticipation window — a direct neural warrant for the bet-then-reveal structure.' Implication: hold a ~1.5–2 s anticipation beat; put the component breakdown in the high-curiosity window.
problem: This is the neuroscience-justifies-a-UI-decision failure mode, in its purest form, and it is the worst finding in the brief. Three independent faults. (1) 'Direct neural warrant' is category error: midbrain/NAcc BOLD does not measure dopamine, and no fMRI result constrains an interface. Strip the imaging and the behavioural claim carries the whole load — the neuroscience is decoration. (2) The behavioural leg the brief actually leans on is the INCIDENTAL-memory result, which is the weak half of Gruber et al. Later work reports the OPPOSITE: memory was poorer for scholastic facts presented after high- versus low-curiosity trivia questions (npj Science of Learning, 2024), and the literature describes curiosity effects on incidental information as weak, inconsistent, and underpowered. (3) Gruber's incidental material was UNRELATED FACES. The brief transfers this to task-RELEVANT instructional content (the component breakdown) — and the 2024 study, whose incidental material was scholastic facts, is the closer analogue and goes the wrong way. Separately, the '~1.5–2 s' beat is invented; no source in or out of the brief specifies a duration.
corrected_claim: Curiosity reliably improves memory for the answer you are curious ABOUT (that much replicates). Its effect on incidental material encountered during the anticipation window is small, inconsistent, tightly time-locked, and has been shown to REVERSE for scholastic content. Delete 'neural warrant' entirely. The bet-then-reveal structure is defensible as a prequestion/pretest (finding 23, which is well evidenced) — that is the same design, obtained honestly. Do NOT justify putting the component breakdown on the reveal by curiosity-driven incidental encoding; if anything the nearest evidence says curiosity about the answer may crowd out the surrounding instructional content. Drop the invented 1.5–2 s constant or label it as a product-feel decision.
sources: Gruber, M. J., Gelman, B. D., & Ranganath, C. (2014). States of curiosity modulate hippocampus-dependent learning via the dopaminergic circuit. Neuron, 84(2), 486–496. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0896627314008046
States of epistemic curiosity interfere with memory for incidental scholastic facts. npj Science of Learning (2024). https://www.nature.com/articles/s41539-024-00234-w
Temporal proximity to the elicitation of curiosity is key for enhancing memory for incidental information. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7812865/
Curiosity Killed the Cat but Not Memory: Enhanced Performance in High-Curiosity States. Brain Sciences (2022). https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9313209/

original_claim: 'Hard UI cap: the resolution screen shows at most FOUR new visual chunks at once … that is six-plus chunks and will exceed visual WM for a beginner.' Justified by Cowan (2001) ~4 and 'visual STM ~3'.
problem: Two errors stacked. First, a conceptual one: Cowan's limit is on chunks held in the focus of attention IN THE ABSENCE OF THE STIMULUS. A resolution screen whose elements all remain visible imposes essentially no storage demand — the display IS the memory, and the learner re-samples it by looking. Capacity limits govern what must be RETAINED across a gap, not how many things may be simultaneously on a persistent screen. The correct construct for a visible display is element interactivity / extraneous load — which the brief already invokes correctly in findings 20 and 26 and then abandons here. Second, an evidential one: the '~3 for visual' figure inherits the discrete-slot model of visual working memory, which is actively contested by continuous-resource accounts. Deriving a hard integer UI constant from a model whose integer is the disputed part is exactly the false precision this brief exists to prevent. Cowan-over-Miller is correct and well supported; its use here is not.
corrected_claim: Cowan's ~4-chunk limit is the better-supported capacity estimate (strong), but it does not license a count of on-screen elements. Re-derive the reveal-screen rule from cognitive load: limit the number of elements the learner must INTEGRATE to understand the item, and gate anything that is reference material rather than integration material behind a tap. That yields nearly the same screen the brief wants (kill the radical table and the etymology note) without pretending a psychology constant fixes a layout number. Drop 'at most four'; state the rule as 'one target, one decomposition, one contrast, nothing else on the integration path.'
sources: Cowan, N. (2001). The magical number 4 in short-term memory. Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 24(1), 87–114.

Ma, W. J., Husain, M., & Bays, P. M. (2014) and the slots-vs-resources debate; see 'Resources masquerading as slots: Flexible allocation of visual working memory', Cognitive Psychology (2016). https://www2.psy.unsw.edu.au/Users/CDonkin/publications/cp16b.pdf
Failure of self-consistency in the discrete resource model of visual working memory. Cognitive Psychology (2018). https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0010028518300239
Suchow, Fougnie, Brady & Alvarez (2014). Terms of the debate on the format and structure of visual memory. https://bradylab.ucsd.edu/pdfs/SuchowFougnieBradyAlvarez2014.pdf

original_claim: 'Never render a stroke-order animation on the resolution screen — strokes add elements without adding structure, which is the exact opposite of chunking.'
problem: Over-generalised from a single interference study (which manipulated radical markings AND stroke animations SIMULTANEOUSLY) into a blanket ban, and it contradicts the strongest Chinese-specific training evidence available — including the very paper the brief unknowingly quotes its chunking arithmetic from. Guan, Liu, Chan & Perfetti (2011, JEP 103(3), 509–522): 48 adult CFL learners, five consecutive days, character-handwriting-to-read vs pinyin-typing-to-read; the handwriting group was BETTER on form recognition and meaning, the typing group better on phonology. Cao et al. (2013, J. Neurolinguistics 26, 440–461) trained adult CFL learners by writing, visual chunking, or reading-only and found writing training increased visual attention to orthographic form (P100). Stroke-level motor engagement is not 'elements without structure'; it is the best-evidenced orthographic-encoding manipulation in CFL research.
corrected_claim: The defensible rule is the narrow one the interference study actually supports: do not present stroke-order animation CONCURRENTLY with radical markings on the same screen. Keep the separate and correct rule that the DECOMPOSITION unit must be components, never strokes. But do not ban stroke/writing content outright — a brief optional tracing or stroke-animation affordance on the reveal is, on current evidence, the highest-value Chinese-specific encoding manipulation the brief rules out, and it is the one intervention with a five-day training study and a three-month follow-up behind it.
sources: Guan, C. Q., Liu, Y., Chan, D. H. L., & Perfetti, C. A. (2011). Writing strengthens orthography and alphabetic-coding strengthens phonology in learning to read Chinese. Journal of Educational Psychology, 103(3), 509–522. https://sites.pitt.edu/~perfetti/PDF/Writing%20strengthens%20Guan%20JEP.pdf

Cao, F., Rickles, B., Vu, M., Zhu, Z., Chan, D. H. L., Harris, L. N., Stafura, J., Xu, Y., & Perfetti, C. A. (2013). Early stage visual-orthographic processes predict long-term retention of word form and meaning. Journal of Neurolinguistics, 26(4), 440–461. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0911604413000043
Comparison studies of typing and handwriting in Chinese language learning: A synthetic review. System (2021). https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0883035521000100

original_claim: Chunking arithmetic ('10.15 strokes, 98% of characters ≤5 chunks, 2.1 strokes/chunk, 5.2 strokes/radical') attributed to an unauthored ResearchGate item, 'Using Meaningful Interpretation and Chunking to Enhance Memory'.
problem: Misattribution, and an expensive one. Those exact figures come from Cao, Rickles, Vu, Zhu, Chan, Harris, Stafura, Xu & Perfetti (2013), Journal of Neurolinguistics 26(4), 440–461 — a controlled training study of adult CFL learners comparing writing, visual-chunking, and reading-only training, with measurement immediately after training AND AGAIN THREE MONTHS LATER. The brief cites the numbers and misses the study. This is the single best retention-interval-disciplined Chinese-specific source in the whole space and the brief lists 'no delayed retention measure' as a gap while holding a three-month study in its hand.
corrected_claim: Attribute the arithmetic to Cao et al. (2013), Journal of Neurolinguistics 26(4), 440–461, and read that paper in full before shipping the decomposition spec. Note the arithmetic is a CORPUS STATISTIC about the script, not an experimental result — 'material_type: both' is wrong for it; it is not a memory finding at all, it is an input to one. The experimental result in the same paper (visual-chunking training produced the largest N170 orthographic-tuning response; writing training increased P100 attention to form) is what should carry evidential weight, and I could not access its behavioural retention outcomes.
sources: Cao, F., et al. (2013). Early stage visual-orthographic processes predict long-term retention of word form and meaning: A visual encoding training study. Journal of Neurolinguistics, 26(4), 440–461. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0911604413000043
Author PDF (egress-blocked in this environment): https://www.lrdc.pitt.edu/perfettilab/pubpdfs/EarlyStageVisualOrthographic.pdf

original_claim: Systematic material_type mislabelling across at least six findings, most of them tagged 'lab-wordlist'.
problem: The brief sets itself a labelling discipline and then breaks it repeatedly, always in the direction that makes lab findings look more like classroom findings or vice versa. Verified instances: (a) Little et al. (2012) is tagged lab-wordlist but used TWO PROSE TEXT PASSAGES with a final cued-recall test after a filled retention interval — educational prose at short delay; the interval is not stated anywhere in the finding. (b) Bisra et al. (2018) is tagged lab-wordlist but self-explanation research uses expository text, worked examples, and maths/science problems in instructional settings across 20 coded moderators — it is squarely classroom/educational. (c) The prequestion meta-analysis is tagged lab-wordlist but prequestion studies use texts, lectures and videos. (d) Chen et al. (2018) is tagged lab-wordlist but the defining feature of that paper is HIGH-ELEMENT-INTERACTIVITY INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIAL, the opposite of word lists. (e) Gruber et al. (2014) is tagged lab-wordlist but used trivia questions and face images. (f) The Pelzl typeface study is tagged lab-wordlist but is lab LOGOGRAPHIC character learning — closer to the target task than the label admits, which understates rather than overstates, but is still wrong.
corrected_claim: Re-label: Little 2012 → lab-prose (final cued recall after a short filled delay); Bisra 2018 → classroom/instructional; prequestion meta-analysis → classroom/instructional; Chen 2018 → classroom/instructional (high element interactivity); Gruber 2014 → lab-trivia+faces; Pelzl 2025 → lab-logographic, single session. The brief's own diagnostic — 'nonsense syllables at ten minutes sold as guidance for months of Chinese' — applies most sharply to Tulving & Thomson (1973) and Morris/Bransford/Franks (1977), both correctly tagged lab-wordlist but both used to settle product-defining questions ('define the criterion task and design backwards from it', 'items must be photographed-from-life') on the strength of word-pair experiments at minutes-to-a-day delays.
sources: Little, J. L., Bjork, E. L., Bjork, R. A., & Angello, G. (2012). Psychological Science, 23(11), 1337–1344. https://bjorklab.psych.ucla.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/13/2016/07/Little_EBjork_RBjork_Angello_2012.pdf
