Pelzl, E. (2025). High variability orthographic training. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 32, 2090–2103. https://link.springer.com/article/10.3758/s13423-025-02646-0

original_claim: 'Format match moderates the testing effect: practising with multiple choice builds recognition, and transfers to free recall only partially.' — used to license adding a small unscored spoken-recall beat to an otherwise multiple-choice game.
problem: Rowland (2014) says something considerably less convenient than 'transfers only partially', and the brief picks the softer reading. Verified: initial RECALL tests produce larger testing effects than initial RECOGNITION tests (effortful processing is the supported mechanism), and final-test format is a large moderator — free recall g ≈ 0.79–0.82, cued recall g ≈ 0.70–0.72, recognition/multiple-choice g ≈ 0.36. The product's core mechanic sits in the weakest cell on BOTH axes: recognition practice tested by recognition. The brief's own criterion task (finding 9: 'meaning-recall from a rendered form, not multiple-choice discrimination') identifies this correctly and then the fix offered is a three-second unscored 'say it out loud' with no scoring and no feedback contingency — an intervention of entirely unknown magnitude proposed against a roughly halved effect size.
corrected_claim: A 4-option MC mechanic operates at approximately half the retention benefit of a recall mechanic (g ≈ 0.36 vs 0.70–0.79 on Rowland's final-test-format moderator), and initial recognition practice is the weaker practice format independently of that. The competitive-distractor rule (finding 10) genuinely recovers part of this and should be kept. But the honest conclusion is that the format choice is a PACE-AND-SOCIABILITY decision that costs measurable retention, not a design the evidence endorses. If the spoken-recall beat is the mitigation, it must at minimum precede the options being visible and be followed by feedback, or it is not a retrieval attempt at all.
sources: Rowland, C. A. (2014). The effect of testing versus restudy on retention: A meta-analytic review of the testing effect. Psychological Bulletin, 140(6), 1432–1463. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25150680/

Pan, S. C., & Rickard, T. C. (2018). Transfer of test-enhanced learning: Meta-analytic review and synthesis. Psychological Bulletin, 144(7), 710–756. https://psycnet.apa.org/manuscript/2018-20773-001.pdf

original_claim: VERDICT ON THE SIGNAGE RENDERING, part 2: the typeface-variability study 'reframes the signage from decoration to core mechanic', with a hard architecture constraint that every word appear in at least THREE distinct typefaces.
problem: The finding is real and correctly directionally described, but the escalation to a hard content-pipeline constraint is not supported by the study's size. Verified: Pelzl (2025), Psychonomic Bulletin & Review 32, 2090–2103; n = 190 with no prior Chinese, 24 characters, six exposures each, ALL WITHIN A SINGLE SESSION, no delayed retention test. The published effects are explicitly small — accuracy differences of roughly one to two words between training groups, and RT differences of a few hundred milliseconds. The brief flags the missing delay in its gaps list and then, inside the finding, calls this 'a textbook desirable difficulty with both halves measured' and grades it moderate. A one-to-two-word single-session difference is not a foundation for a MUST-level content rule that constrains every asset the team ever authors.
corrected_claim: Typeface variability during training produces a small generalisation advantage to novel typefaces, measured within a single session on 24 characters, with no evidence at any retention interval. Treat it as a cheap default worth adopting — vary typefaces because real signage varies and it costs nothing — not as a validated mechanic with a numeric floor. Downgrade 'at least THREE typefaces' from a required constraint to a content guideline, and note that the encoding-specificity argument (finding 19, Tulving & Thomson) is doing more of the work here than the experiment is.
sources: Pelzl, E. (2025). High variability orthographic training: Learning words in a logographic script through training with multiple typefaces. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 32, 2090–2103. https://link.springer.com/article/10.3758/s13423-025-02646-0
PMC copy: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12426071/

original_claim: Keyword mnemonic finding cited as 'Keyword mnemonic and retention of second-language vocabulary words. Journal of Educational Psychology (1992). ERIC EJ456644' with no authors, presenting only the excess-forgetting result.
problem: Incomplete citation and one-sided presentation of a live dispute. Full reference: Wang, A. Y., Thomas, M. H., & Ouellette, J. A. (1992), Journal of Educational Psychology, 84(4), 520–528, N = 218 college students. Two omitted facts change the design rule. (1) The keyword disadvantage emerged at a TWO-DAY delay — that is the retention interval on which the brief's mnemonic-expiry architecture rests, and it is not stated. (2) In follow-up work, learners given PICTURES of the keyword and the translation referent during acquisition showed a forgetting rate that did NOT exceed the rote-rehearsal control — the excess forgetting was eliminated by imagery support. That directly contradicts finding 14's instruction not to add imagery, and the brief never notices that two of its own findings collide. There is also a published defence (Gruneberg, 1998, Applied Cognitive Psychology, 12, 529–532) that goes uncited.
corrected_claim: Wang, Thomas & Ouellette (1992, JEP 84(4), 520–528, N=218) found greater long-term forgetting for keyword-instructed learners than rote rehearsers at a two-day delay; subsequent work found that supplying keyword and referent IMAGERY at acquisition eliminated the excess forgetting; and the criticism has been formally rebutted (Gruneberg, 1998). Grade contested and present both sides. The mnemonic-expiry rule (show on exposures 1–2, suppress from 3) is a reasonable hedge, but the 'expire at 2' number is invented — no source specifies it — and the brief should stop treating finding 14's anti-imagery rule and finding 15's mnemonic rule as independent when the literature links them.
sources: Wang, A. Y., Thomas, M. H., & Ouellette, J. A. (1992). Keyword mnemonic and retention of second-language vocabulary words. Journal of Educational Psychology, 84(4), 520–528. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ456644

Wang, A. Y., & Thomas, M. H. Effect of keywords on long-term retention: Help or hindrance? https://www.researchgate.net/publication/232599085_Effect_of_Keywords_on_Long-Term_Retention_Help_or_Hindrance
Gruneberg, M. M. (1998). A commentary on criticism of the keyword method of learning foreign languages. Applied Cognitive Psychology, 12, 529–532.

original_claim: Murre (2021), Royal Society Open Science, cited in the source list for the context-dependent-memory verdict with no statement of what it found.
problem: Silent citation of a failed replication. Murre (2021) re-ran the Godden & Baddeley (1975) land/underwater design with 16 divers and FAILED to replicate: recall in the matched context was not better than in the mismatched context. A 2022 addendum reanalysed the data with the correct repeated-measures model and reinforced the conclusion that it was not a successful replication. Listing the paper as neutral background — exactly the sourcing hygiene the brief criticises elsewhere — wastes its best piece of evidence and leaves a reader unable to tell whether it supports or undermines the finding.
corrected_claim: State it: the single most famous demonstration of environmental context-dependent memory has failed a direct replication (Murre 2021, addendum 2022). That STRENGTHENS the brief's verdict — delete context reinstatement from the design rationale — and it should be the headline of finding 16 rather than an unexplained line in the source list.
sources: Murre, J. M. J. (2021). The Godden and Baddeley (1975) experiment on context-dependent memory on land and underwater: a replication. Royal Society Open Science, 8(11), 200724. https://royalsocietypublishing.org/rsos/article/8/11/200724/95735/
Addendum (2022), Royal Society Open Science, 9(1), 211924. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8728159/

original_claim: 'Treat the pinyin scaffolding tier as a MEANING aid, not a pronunciation-learning feature… pinyin is never itself a scored answer.' Justified by the claim that the phonological-loop mechanism 'is largely bypassed by a reading-recognition game.'
problem: The evidence points the other way and the brief presents a scope decision as an evidence-based one. Guan et al. (2011) found a clean dissociation in adult CFL learners: handwriting training strengthened orthography and meaning, ALPHABETIC (pinyin) CODING STRENGTHENED PHONOLOGY — i.e. the pinyin channel does real work, on a dimension the product has chosen to discard. Perfetti's Lexical Constituency Model, validated across alphabetic and non-alphabetic scripts, holds that phonological activation occurs automatically in Chinese reading and that durable word identities require orthography, phonology and semantics bound together; a deliberately orthography→semantics-only design builds low-quality lexical representations by construction. Note also that phonetic radicals predict pronunciation at only ~40% accuracy, which is a reason phonology is HARD in Chinese, not a reason it is absent.
corrected_claim: Excluding pronunciation is a legitimate PRODUCT SCOPE decision — the criterion task is reading a sign, not saying it — but it is not supported by the memory literature, and the brief should say so plainly instead of dressing it as a finding. Reframe: 'we are deliberately building a partial lexical representation because our criterion task only requires form→meaning; the cost is that these representations will be lower-quality than a form+sound+meaning learner's, and will not support listening or speaking.' Keep audio optional and unscored (finding 1's rule is sound on accessibility grounds). Delete the claim that the phonological mechanism is 'bypassed'.
sources: Guan, C. Q., Liu, Y., Chan, D. H. L., & Perfetti, C. A. (2011). Journal of Educational Psychology, 103(3), 509–522. https://sites.pitt.edu/~perfetti/PDF/Writing%20strengthens%20Guan%20JEP.pdf

Perfetti, C. A., Liu, Y., & Tan, L. H. The Lexical Constituency Model: Some implications of research on Chinese for general theories of reading. https://www.researchgate.net/publication/8098601_The_Lexical_Constituency_Model_Some_Implications_of_Research_on_Chinese_for_General_Theories_of_Reading
The interaction of orthography, phonology and semantics in L2 learners' Chinese character production. Frontiers in Psychology (2023), 14:1076810. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10017467/

original_claim: Kang & Pashler (2012), 'Learning painting styles: Spacing is advantageous when it promotes discriminative contrast', Applied Cognitive Psychology — linked to https://link.springer.com/article/10.3758/s13421-012-0238-9
problem: Broken evidence chain in a finding that drives a concrete UI rule (show the confusable pair simultaneously, never as a later item). The DOI prefix 10.3758/s13421 is Memory & Cognition, not Applied Cognitive Psychology — the URL points at a different paper from the one named. The Kang & Pashler article is Applied Cognitive Psychology, 26(1), 97–103. A reader following the link is verifying the wrong study.
corrected_claim: Fix the citation to Kang, S. H. K., & Pashler, H. (2012), Applied Cognitive Psychology, 26(1), 97–103, and check which of the two papers the brief actually intended, since the Memory & Cognition DOI it links may be the Birnbaum et al. record already cited separately in the same finding. The UI recommendation (simultaneous juxtaposition of the confusable, after resolution, discriminating component marked) is well motivated by the discrimination-contrast literature and I found no reason to challenge it — but the brief also admits it could not read the one Chinese-specific study (Chang et al. 2022) that tests it, so grade it moderate at best and treat the rule as a hypothesis to instrument.
sources: Kang, S. H. K., & Pashler, H. (2012). Learning painting styles: Spacing is advantageous when it promotes discriminative contrast. Applied Cognitive Psychology, 26(1), 97–103.
Birnbaum, M. S., Kornell, N., Bjork, E. L., & Bjork, R. A. (2013). Memory & Cognition, 41, 392–402. https://link.springer.com/article/10.3758/s13421-012-0272-7

original_claim: The Involvement Load Hypothesis finding is graded 'strong' and its evaluation component is turned into an absolute pixel-level filter ('does it constrain the meaning of the target?').
problem: The numbers the brief itself quotes do not support 'strong'. Verified: Yanagisawa & Webb (2021), Language Learning 71(2), 487–536, 398 effect sizes from 42 studies, N = 4,628 — ILH explained 15.0% of variance on IMMEDIATE post-tests and 5.1% on DELAYED post-tests, with evaluation contributing most, need second, and search contributing nothing. A construct that predicts 5% of delayed-test variance is a weak predictor at exactly the retention interval this product cares about. The brief's own retention-interval discipline should have caught this. (The seductive-details half of the same finding is the better-supported leg and I found no reason to challenge it.)
corrected_claim: Split finding 18. The ILH/evaluation leg is MODERATE at best and weak at delay (5.1% of variance) — keep the 'does it constrain meaning?' heuristic as a sensible editorial rule of thumb, not as an evidence-backed filter. The seductive-details leg (Rey 2012; Sundararajan & Adesope 2020), including the finding that effects are stronger under limited study time, carries the actual weight behind cutting photographic backgrounds and atmospheric clutter — and that recommendation should stand on that leg alone. Also note there is a successor model (Involvement Load Hypothesis Plus, SSLA 2022) the brief does not cite.
sources: Yanagisawa, A., & Webb, S. (2021). Language Learning, 71(2), 487–536. https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/lang.12444

Involvement Load Hypothesis Plus: Creating an improved predictive model of incidental vocabulary learning. Studies in Second Language Acquisition (2022). https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/studies-in-second-language-acquisition/article/involvement-load-hypothesis-plus/5C5984B326F37FBF3A3DDA3C0EB2996C
Empirical Support for the Involvement Load Hypothesis: A Systematic Review. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9598591/

original_claim: Reggente et al. (2020) VR method-of-loci finding — 'the group able to CLICK each object to lock it into place recalled 28% more objects' — used to conclude: 'The app's cheap analogue is the bet: forcing a commitment before the item is revealed is an explicit act, not passive viewing. Keep the bet mandatory and before reveal.'
problem: This is the exact failure mode the review was commissioned to hunt: a lab manipulation repurposed as a justification for a UI decision it has no relationship to. Explicit binding in Reggente is a spatial operation — attaching an object representation to a specific locus in a navigable environment, which is the theorised mechanism of loci. Placing a wager on a four-option guess shares only the English word 'explicit'. There is no shared mechanism, no shared outcome measure (free recall of 3D objects vs forced-choice recognition of an orthographic form), and no study linking the two. The brief elsewhere shows admirable discipline about mechanism-to-UI leaps and then commits one for its own signature mechanic. Compounding this: the brief cannot have read the paper (marked abstract-only), so the '28%' figure and the 'correlated strongly' claim are unverified, and I could not verify them either.
corrected_claim: Reggente et al. (2020) supports nothing about the bet mechanic and must be struck from its justification. The bet is well motivated, but by a different and better-matched literature: the pretesting / prequestion effect, where an unsuccessful guess made *before* feedback improves subsequent learning of that item (see added_findings). Rewrite the design doc to cite that instead. The design decision survives; the citation does not.
sources: Reggente, N., Essoe, J. K.-Y., Baek, H. Y., & Rissman, J. (2020). The Method of Loci in Virtual Reality. Journal of Cognitive Enhancement, 4, 12–30. NOTE: could not be fetched this session (link.springer.com 403 at egress gateway); the refutation here is an argument about mechanism mismatch and does not depend on the paper's numbers.
Kornell, N., Hays, M. J., & Bjork, R. A. (2009). Unsuccessful retrieval attempts enhance subsequent learning. JEP: LMC, 35(4), 989–998. UNVERIFIED THIS SESSION — cited from reviewer's own knowledge.

original_claim: 'The construction cost of the method of loci is 30 minutes a day for six weeks before the benefit appears. That is roughly 20 hours of pure overhead.' (evidence_strength: strong)
problem: This directly contradicts two other findings in the same brief. Finding 4 and finding 5 both report Legge et al. (2012): a virtual environment studied for roughly five minutes worked as well as a lifelong familiar one. If a palace can be built in five minutes, the construction cost of the method is not twenty hours. What Dresler et al. (2017) actually bought with forty daily sessions was *expert-level performance* — 62 of 72 words — not the *appearance of a benefit*. Basic method-of-loci benefits appear after brief instruction; that is why the technique has been demonstrable in single-session undergraduate experiments since the 1960s. The brief inflated a training-to-expertise cost into an entry cost, then used the inflated figure to set an onboarding budget.
corrected_claim: Method-of-loci benefits appear after minutes of instruction, not twenty hours; twenty hours buys memory-athlete-level list performance. The brief's conclusion (do not build a memory-palace feature) is correct and should be kept — but it rests on the outcome-measure mismatch (serial/free recall of lists vs four-option recognition of a written form), not on cost. Fixing this matters because the cost argument is the one a stakeholder can defeat by saying 'so we'll make it a two-minute tutorial'; the outcome-measure argument cannot be defeated that way.
sources: Dresler, M. et al. (2017). Mnemonic training reshapes brain networks to support superior memory. Neuron, 93(5), 1227–1235. UNVERIFIED THIS SESSION (cell.com blocked).
Legge, E. L. G., Madan, C. R., Ng, E. T., & Caplan, J. B. (2012). Acta Psychologica, 141(3), 380–390 — cited by the brief itself, and the source of the contradiction.

original_claim: 'Roediger's classic head-to-head shows mnemonics buy you ORDER, not quantity' (evidence_strength: strong)
problem: Two defects. First, the headline contradicts the brief's own supporting detail one sentence later: 'All mnemonic groups beat control on unordered recall.' If all mnemonic groups beat control on unordered recall, mnemonics also bought quantity. The accurate statement is comparative (the advantage was *larger* under positional scoring), not exclusive. Second, 'strong' is not a defensible rating for a single unreplicated 1980 experiment with 150 undergraduates, one 20-word list length, an immediate test, no preregistration, and no full text read.
corrected_claim: Roediger (1980) found mnemonic groups outperformed control on both unordered and ordered recall, with the larger differential under strict positional scoring. Restate as 'mnemonics help quantity somewhat and order more', and downgrade to a single-study finding. The architectural implication (random-access item pool, no adjacency constraint) is sensible product design but should be presented as a design choice, not as a result Roediger established.
sources: Roediger, H. L. (1980). The effectiveness of four mnemonics in ordering recall. JEP: Human Learning and Memory, 6(5), 558–567. UNVERIFIED THIS SESSION (psycnet.apa.org 403); the internal contradiction is checkable against the brief's own text.

original_claim: 'The keyword method's retention-interval story is the opposite of the folklore: it wins at immediate cued recall and LOSES at delay.' (evidence_strength: strong)
problem: Rating a single research programme's results as 'strong' evidence, from abstracts, while omitting the published dispute against it. The Wang & Thomas delayed-forgetting findings were contested at the time on methodological grounds — principally that their paradigm used short, experimenter-paced presentation rates that disadvantage keyword encoding (which requires more time to construct the acoustic link and the interactive image), and that initial learning was driven to artificially high levels, creating scope for differential regression at delay. Gruneberg published a direct commentary defending the keyword method against exactly this line of criticism. A brief that presents one lab's programme as settled fact, with no mention that the field argued back, is not adversarially safe.
corrected_claim: The long-term durability of keyword-method gains is genuinely contested, not settled against. Wang & Thomas repeatedly found the advantage confined to immediate tests and reversing at delay; critics attribute this to presentation-rate and initial-learning confounds specific to their paradigm. The brief's practical conclusion — do not schedule an item more leniently because a mnemonic was shown — survives either way and should be kept, because it is the conservative action under both readings. But the claim must be rated contested and the counter-position named.
sources: Thomas, M. H., & Wang, A. Y. (1996). Learning by the keyword mnemonic: Looking for long-term benefits. JEP: Applied, 2(4), 330–342. UNVERIFIED THIS SESSION.

Gruneberg, M. M. (1998). A commentary on criticism of the keyword method of learning foreign languages. Applied Cognitive Psychology. UNVERIFIED THIS SESSION — cited from reviewer's own knowledge; this is the missing counter-citation.

original_claim: material_type labelled 'classroom-l2' for Thomas & Wang (1996), Wang & Thomas (1992, Chinese characters), and van Hell & Mahn (1997).
problem: This is the material_type honesty failure the review was asked to police, in its subtler form. None of these three is a classroom study. All are single-session laboratory experiments with undergraduate volunteers, small closed vocabulary sets, experimenter-paced presentation, and retention intervals capped at two days or one week. Labelling them 'classroom-l2' launders lab paired-associate learning into 'real L2 instruction' and hides the interval problem — which is fatal here, because 看不懂's use case is a player learning signs weeks before a trip. A 1992 two-day cued-recall study is being presented as guidance for a months-long learning arc.
corrected_claim: Relabel all three as lab-L2-paired-associates with a stated retention ceiling of ≤1 week. The brief's own gaps section admits 'retention intervals across this entire literature are short', but that admission never propagated into the material_type field where it would actually constrain a reader. Add an explicit retention_interval field per finding; material_type alone cannot carry this. Wang & Thomas (1992) remains the most on-point study for Chinese content strategy and its null result stands — but it is a null at two days and one week, and it says nothing about eight weeks.
sources: Wang, A. Y., & Thomas, M. H. (1992). Language Learning, 42(3), 359–376. UNVERIFIED THIS SESSION (eric.ed.gov 403). The mislabelling is checkable against the brief's own detail text, which states the intervals.

original_claim: 'Your Dutch and English-speaking adult audience is, by definition, experienced FL learners — the subgroup for whom keyword was WORSE than rote.' (from van Hell & Mahn 1997)
problem: The 'experienced vs inexperienced' contrast in van Hell & Mahn is not a manipulated moderator within one design — it is a comparison between Experiment 1 and Experiment 2, which differ simultaneously in participant nationality (Dutch vs American), first language, target language (Spanish vs Dutch), and recruitment. That is a fully confounded between-experiment comparison. It cannot support a subgroup claim about who keyword works worse for, and the brief's own detail text supplies all the information needed to see this — it lists both experiments' differing populations and target languages in the same paragraph where it draws the subgroup conclusion.
corrected_claim: Do not use van Hell & Mahn to claim that experienced foreign-language learners are specifically harmed by the keyword method. The defensible reading is narrower: in one experiment with experienced Dutch learners of Spanish, rote outperformed keyword; in a separate experiment with a different population and target language, the two matched on accuracy while keyword was slower. The latency observation is the more transportable one, and the latency-instrumentation recommendation should be kept — a reader of a station sign is under time pressure, and that is a good product argument independent of this study.
sources: van Hell, J. G., & Mahn, A. C. (1997). Keyword mnemonics versus rote rehearsal. Language Learning, 47(3), 507–546. UNVERIFIED THIS SESSION (eric.ed.gov 403); the confound is visible in the brief's own description of the two experiments.

original_claim: 'Smith, Glenberg & Bjork (1978) found context manipulations did not affect recognition memory even where they reliably affected recall.'
problem: Misattribution of the canonical result. Smith, Glenberg & Bjork (1978) is the environmental-context study that demonstrated context effects on *recall*. The canonical demonstration that environmental context effects vanish under a recognition test is Godden & Baddeley (1980) — the follow-up to the famous 1975 divers study, run with the same underwater/dry manipulation but with a recognition test, which found no context dependency. That the brief invokes the divers literature's conclusion while citing the wrong paper for the very refutation the reviewer was told to look for is a meaningful sourcing error, because Godden & Baddeley (1980) is the single strongest citation available for the brief's own position.
corrected_claim: Cite Godden & Baddeley (1980) for the recognition null, alongside Smith & Vela (2001) for the meta-analytic moderator picture. Note additionally that the pooled environmental-context effect in Smith & Vela is small in absolute terms and heavily moderated, and that the 1975 divers result has never been shown to generalise from a physical-environment manipulation to a 'cognitive context' such as a themed screen. The brief's conclusion — do not justify the sign rendering as context reinstatement, justify it as perceptual/transfer-appropriate matching — is correct and is the single best call in the brief. It just needs the right citation under it.
sources: Godden, D. R., & Baddeley, A. D. (1980). When does context influence recognition memory? British Journal of Psychology, 71(1), 99–104. UNVERIFIED THIS SESSION — cited from reviewer's own knowledge; this is the missing citation.
Smith, S. M., & Vela, E. (2001). Environmental context-dependent memory: A review and meta-analysis. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 8(2), 203–220. UNVERIFIED THIS SESSION (pubmed 403).

original_claim: 'The production effect is the one distinctiveness effect that survives everything the app does to it... Making every player say the item aloud is the highest-value cheap intervention available.' (evidence_strength: strong; ranked #3 in the build order)
problem: Three unresolved problems, one of which the brief itself raises in its gaps and then fails to propagate into the rating. (1) The brief's own gap #9 states that there is no evidence the production effect holds when the produced token is not the studied form — a player saying 'chū kǒu' from displayed pinyin is producing an alphabetic string, not the character 出口. If the top-ranked recommendation rests on an unestablished transfer step, the finding cannot be rated 'strong'. (2) The between-subject / pure-list production effect in recognition, which is precisely the design the app instantiates, has a live theoretical challenge: it has been argued to arise partly from a shift in response criterion rather than improved discriminability. If that is right, it would not help a four-alternative forced choice between visually confusable characters, which is a pure discrimination demand. (3) 'Whole table says it in unison' is not the manipulation Forrin & MacLeod studied; simultaneous group speech degrades self-hearing, and their own gradient puts hearing others well below speaking oneself.
corrected_claim: The production effect is real and does extend to recognition, and is a reasonable low-cost feature to ship. But for *this* application it is moderate-to-weak, not strong: the produced token is pinyin rather than the target orthographic form; the pure-list between-subject variant is the smallest version of the effect and its mechanism is disputed; and unison group speech is untested. Keep the say-it-aloud beat, but demote it below the two form-instruction elements in the build order, and instrument it rather than assuming it. Concretely: show the character while producing, not just the pinyin, so that the produced act is at least co-present with the target form.
sources: Fawcett, J. M. (2013). Acta Psychologica, 142(1), 1–5; Fawcett, J. M. et al. (2023). Canadian Journal of Experimental Psychology, 77(1), 35–44. UNVERIFIED THIS SESSION (pubmed/psycnet 403); I could not confirm the g = 0.37 figure the brief quotes.

Bodner, G. E., & Taikh, A., and related work arguing a criterion/bias contribution to between-subject production effects in recognition. UNVERIFIED THIS SESSION — cited from reviewer's own knowledge as the missing counter-position.

original_claim: 'Picture superiority is robust in recognition — which is the app's test... The photorealistic sign rendering earns its keep only if items are visually DISTINCT FROM EACH OTHER within a session.' (implication_kind: ui)
problem: Category error in application. The picture-superiority effect compares memory for items *studied as pictures* against items *studied as words*. In 看不懂 the to-be-remembered item is, in every condition, an orthographic form — a character. Photographing that character onto an enamel plate does not convert it into a picture in the sense the paradigm means; it changes the item's surround. Picture superiority therefore supplies no support at all for photorealistic sign rendering. The brief has taken a stimulus-format effect and applied it to a presentation-context decision.
corrected_claim: Strike picture superiority from the justification for photorealistic rendering. The rendering remains justified — by transfer-appropriate processing and by the typeface-variability result the brief cites elsewhere — and those are sufficient. The Higdon et al. distinctiveness-over-dual-coding result is worth retaining as a general caution against dual-coding reasoning (see next correction), but it cannot be repurposed into a UI rule about substrate variety.
sources: Higdon, K. F., Neath, I., Surprenant, A. M., & Ensor, T. M. Distinctiveness, not dual coding, explains the picture-superiority effect. Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology. UNVERIFIED THIS SESSION (sagepub 403); note the DOI the brief gives (10.1177/17470218241235520) carries a 2024 stamp, not the 2025 the brief asserts.

original_claim: 'Within any one deal/category, no two items may share the same substrate template... add a substrate template id to the item schema and have the dealer enforce non-repetition within a round.'
problem: This commits the precise error the brief correctly identifies two findings earlier and uses to kill bizarreness. Distinctiveness effects are *relative*: they require an item to stand out against a homogeneous background, which is why they appear under mixed-list within-subject designs and vanish under pure lists. A rule that makes every item maximally distinct from every other item creates a pure list of distinctive items — exactly the configuration in which the effect disappears. The brief writes 'if everything is bizarre, nothing is' and then, five findings later, mandates that everything be distinctive. There is a second cost: real station signage is substrate-homogeneous, so deliberately maximising substrate variety within a category trains against the real-world percept the brief's own transfer-appropriate-processing argument says to match.
corrected_claim: Drop the enforced within-round substrate non-repetition rule. Vary typeface and substrate *across repeated exposures of the same item over time* — which is what the high-variability orthographic training result actually supports, and which is a different manipulation entirely — while letting within-round substrate follow real-world plausibility for the category. The schema field is still worth having, but the dealer constraint should be 'do not repeat the substrate this item was last seen on', not 'no two items in a round may match'.
sources: Internal contradiction with the brief's own bizarreness finding; no external source needed to verify.

High variability orthographic training. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review (2025), doi:10.3758/s13423-025-02646-0. UNVERIFIED THIS SESSION (link.springer.com 403) — and, as the brief's own gaps note, a single unreplicated experiment.

original_claim: 'Cap bizarre/absurd mnemonic glosses at a small minority of items in any category deck (roughly one in five or fewer).'
problem: Invented precision. No study in the bizarreness literature licenses a one-in-five ratio; the mixed-list designs that produce the effect vary widely in proportion and the boundary conditions have never been mapped to a recommended production ratio. More importantly, the recommendation does not follow from the brief's own evidence. The brief states that bizarreness effects are absent in cued recall and unreliable in recognition — recognition being the app's actual test. If the effect does not reliably appear on your outcome measure, the correct action is not to ration it to 20%; it is not to rely on it at all.
corrected_claim: Bizarreness should carry no memory-design load in this app. If bizarre glosses ship, ship them for engagement and voice, and make no scheduling or authoring decision contingent on their memory value. Remove the one-in-five rule and the enforcement pipeline built to police it — that is engineering spend on an effect that does not appear on the app's test format.
sources: McDaniel, M. A., & Einstein, G. O. (1995). The bizarreness effect: It's not surprising, it's complex. JEP: LMC. UNVERIFIED THIS SESSION (pubmed 403). The refutation is internal: the brief's own stated boundary conditions do not support its own implication.

original_claim: 'The deliberately paired confusable is the best-evidenced element in the whole design' (Li, Shi & Wang 2025, Languages) and 'do NOT colour-code the differing stroke: it costs recognition speed'.
problem: 'Best-evidenced element in the whole design' is asserted on the basis of one 2025 paper in an MDPI journal, with naive non-Chinese-background participants, which the brief could not read and I could not read either. That is a weaker evidence base than several findings the brief rates lower. Separately, the colour-coding conclusion overreads the reported result: 'colour coding slowed reaction times' is a latency finding at test, not a learning finding. Slower responding during a discrimination task is routinely produced by added visual information without any implication that learning was harmed — and it can equally indicate more careful feature-checking. Deriving a hard UI prohibition from an RT main effect in a single study is not warranted.
corrected_claim: Simultaneous paired presentation of confusable characters is a promising and theoretically sensible recommendation, supported by one small recent study plus a converging condition-specific result in Chang et al. (2022). Rate it moderate at best, not 'best-evidenced'. On colour: treat the colour-coding result as a weak signal to avoid heavy visual enhancement, not as a prohibition; if colour is used to mark a discriminating component, A/B it against a position/size/whitespace treatment on accuracy, not on RT alone.
sources: Li, Shi & Wang (2025). Languages, 10(10), 260. UNVERIFIED THIS SESSION (mdpi.com 403). Note the brief's own URL for this points to a sciety.org activity page rather than the article.
Chang, L.-Y. et al. (2022). Frontiers in Psychology, 13, 783898. UNVERIFIED THIS SESSION (frontiersin.org 403).

original_claim: 'Recognition is driven primarily by ITEM-SPECIFIC processing, whereas the method of loci supplies RELATIONAL processing. The dissociation is one of the better-replicated principles in memory research.' (evidence_strength: strong)
problem: The framework is well established; the *application* is the brief's own theoretical inference and is rated as though it were an empirical finding. Two specific weaknesses. First, method-of-loci encoding involves forming an interactive image of the item at a locus — that is elaborative processing *of the item*, not solely inter-item organisation, so classifying it as purely relational is a stretch. Hunt & Einstein's relational construct concerns organisational relations among list members (typically categorical), whereas loci are extra-list cues, which is closer to cue–target associative encoding. Second, and more consequentially for this app: four-option forced choice against deliberately confusable lures is not the old/new recognition test the framework was built on. Forced-choice discrimination among similar alternatives has its own literature and does not inherit old/new recognition results wholesale.
corrected_claim: Present the relational/item-specific argument as the brief's theoretical rationale, explicitly labelled as inference, not as a strong empirical finding about the method of loci. The downstream design rule — every resolution card must name a feature true of this item and false of its paired lure — is excellent and should be kept; it is good instructional design and is independently supported by the discrimination-training rationale. It does not need to be dressed as a replicated dissociation.
sources: Hunt, R. R., & Einstein, G. O. (1981). JVLVB, 20(5), 497–514. UNVERIFIED THIS SESSION (sciencedirect 403). The overreach is an argument about scope, not about the paper's numbers.

original_claim: 'The founding citation for the memory palace — Bower (1970) — is a narrative article in a general-interest science magazine, not a controlled trial... Nearly every popular claim about memory palaces traces back through this paper.' (evidence_strength: weak)
problem: Correct about the American Scientist article, misleading about the evidence base. Bower's controlled experimental work on mnemonic imagery and organisation appeared in peer-reviewed venues — narrative-mediator studies in Psychonomic Science and imagery/organisation work in Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior, including experimental work on loci with Reitman. Implying that the method of loci rests on a magazine essay is a rhetorical overreach that a hostile reader will puncture, and it weakens the brief unnecessarily — because the peer-reviewed foundation, when you look at it, is *also* serial and free recall of unrelated word lists under immediate test, which is the brief's own thesis.
corrected_claim: Bower (1970, American Scientist) is a review essay and should be cited as history. But the method of loci does have a peer-reviewed experimental foundation from the same era; that foundation consists of serial and free recall of word lists at immediate test, which supports rather than undermines the brief's central argument. Restate the finding as 'the peer-reviewed foundation exists and is entirely list-recall' — a stronger and more defensible version of the same point.
sources: Bower, G. H. (1970). Analysis of a mnemonic device. American Scientist, 58(5), 496–510.

Bower, G. H., & Clark, M. C. (1969). Narrative stories as mediators for serial learning. Psychonomic Science; Bower, G. H., & Reitman, J. S. (1972). JVLVB. UNVERIFIED THIS SESSION — cited from reviewer's own knowledge as the missing peer-reviewed foundation.

original_claim: 'If you want one embodied element, make it an OPTIONAL single-component finger trace on the resolution screen... handwriting builds long-term motor memory that strengthens the orthographic representation.'
problem: Two problems. First, a mechanistic story ('builds long-term motor memory') is being used to justify shipping a feature, on a form factor — finger-tracing a single component on a phone during a party game — that the brief itself concedes is untested. That is the same mechanism-to-UI move flagged in the Reggente correction, in non-neural dress. Second, the brief's own newer citation cuts against it: it reports that the typing group outperformed on *character recognition* while handwriting led on meaning recognition. Character recognition is precisely 看不懂's test. The brief's own source therefore supplies evidence against the trace feature on the app's actual outcome measure, and the brief does not engage with it.
corrected_claim: Do not ship the finger trace, even as an option, in v1. The handwriting-vs-typing dissociation is interesting but the brief's own cited evidence puts handwriting's advantage on meaning recognition and typing's on character recognition, so the direction of benefit for a character-recognition app is at best unclear. If it is ever built, build it as an explicit experiment with the recognition outcome as the dependent measure, not as a feature justified by a motor-memory narrative.
sources: Shi (2026). Foreign Language Annals, doi:10.1111/flan.70053. UNVERIFIED THIS SESSION (wiley 403) — the contradiction is visible in the brief's own detail text.
Comparison studies of typing and handwriting in Chinese language learning: A synthetic review. Journal of Second Language Writing (2021). UNVERIFIED THIS SESSION (sciencedirect 403).

original_claim: Macedonia & Klimesch (2014) cited as 'classroom training with 36 words, retention measured out to 14 months', material_type 'both'.
problem: Material mislabelling. Macedonia's gesture programme trains an artificial constructed corpus (commonly 'Vimmi'), built specifically so that items carry no prior associations for participants. That is not a natural second language, and it is closer in kind to the nonsense-syllable tradition the review was told to flag than to classroom L2 instruction. Presenting it under material_type 'both' alongside genuine L2 studies obscures this.
corrected_claim: Relabel Macedonia's contribution as artificial-corpus material. The brief's conclusion (do not add gesture to the reading loop) is correct and is unaffected — if anything the artificial-corpus caveat strengthens it, since the gesture literature is even further from written Chinese than the brief states.
sources: Macedonia, M., & Klimesch, W. (2014). Mind, Brain, and Education, 8(2). UNVERIFIED THIS SESSION (wiley 403) — the Vimmi corpus detail is from reviewer's own knowledge of this research programme.

original_claim: Classical interference theory predicts maximum damage exactly for the app's confusable structure... Higa (1963)... intralist similarity increased learning difficulty, with antonyms among the worst. 入口/出口 is literally the antonym-plus-shared-cue case... These are the two worst cells of the classical surface. [evidence_strength: strong]
problem: This is the single most likely reversal in the brief, and the brief contradicts itself about it. (a) INTERNAL CONTRADICTION, checkable with no network: this finding cites Higa (1963) as showing 'antonyms among the worst'; two findings later, the SAME brief lists Higa under 'conditionally negative' in the Nakata & Suzuki tally. The brief uses one 1963 study in two opposite valences and grades the harsher reading 'strong'. (b) SUBSTANTIVE (pending verification): my recollection of Higa 1963 is that the similarity/difficulty function is NON-MONOTONIC — strongly pre-associated response sets (antonyms, strong free associates) were learned relatively EASILY because the pre-existing association mediates, while moderately similar sets (coordinates, connotative-only similarity) were the damaging ones. If that is right, the brief has inverted the study, and 入口/出口 — a canonical strongly-associated antonym pair with a shared L1 semantic frame — falls in the FACILITATIVE cell, not the worst one. (c) The bridge to the app is broken regardless: Osgood/Higa describe learning two NEW competing responses to a shared cue in list-to-list transfer; the app's structure is discriminating one new sign from another new sign in a recognition task with the cue physically present. Osgood's surface has nothing to say about that.
corrected_claim: Classical interference theory is consistent with the app's structure being hazardous, but it does not single it out as maximal, and the direction of the antonym effect is disputed within the brief's own sources. Higa (1963) most likely found a non-monotonic similarity function in which strongly associated response pairs (antonyms) were EASIER, not harder; the brief's reading should be re-checked against the primary text before 入口/出口 is treated as the worst case. The staged-introduction rule (never introduce both members as new items in the same session) is still a reasonable default, but it is a precaution, not a prediction derived from Osgood's surface.
sources: Higa, M. (1963). Interference effects of intralist word relationships in verbal learning. Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior, 2(2), 170–175. [COULD NOT VERIFY THIS SESSION — all publisher and index hosts 403 at the egress proxy]
Internal contradiction between two findings in the brief under review (no source needed)

original_claim: Osgood's (1949) transfer surface plots transfer as a joint function of stimulus and response similarity... [evidence_strength: strong; cited via https://www.ocf.berkeley.edu/~jfkihlstrom/MemoryWeb/... ]
problem: Two problems. (1) SOURCING: a claim graded 'strong' is sourced to a lecturer's supplementary course webpage, not to Osgood (1949) or to any review that evaluates it. That is a citation-quality failure on a load-bearing item. (2) STATUS: Osgood's transfer-and-retroaction surface was a 1949 theoretical synthesis of paired-associate transfer data, and the subsequent verbal-learning literature (the A-B/A-Br and A-B/A-C transfer work of the 1960s) did not sustain it; it survives in textbooks as a historical schematic, not as a predictive model. Grading a superseded 1949 theoretical surface 'strong' — the same grade the brief gives a 1,396-participant meta-analysis — collapses the grading scheme.
corrected_claim: Osgood's transfer surface is a historically important schematic whose specific predictions about response similarity did not survive the transfer literature that followed. Cite it as framing, grade it 'weak', and source it to the primary paper or to a review that assesses its status — not to a course webpage.
sources: Osgood, C. E. (1949). The similarity paradox in human learning: A resolution. Psychological Review, 56(3), 132–143. [NOT VERIFIED THIS SESSION]

original_claim: The interleaving benefit reverses for word learning. Meta-analytically, blocking beats interleaving when the material is words. Brunmair & Richter (2019)... WORDS g = −0.39... This is the hinge of the verdict. [evidence_strength: strong; material_type: both]
problem: The brief names this 'the hinge of the verdict' and 'the strongest single constraint', then admits in its own gaps that it could not read the full text, does not know which studies constitute the 'words' category, does not know their retention intervals, and does not know whether 'words' means paired-associate vocabulary. A design verdict is being hung on an unread moderator cell. Beyond that: (a) MANIPULATION MISMATCH — interleaving in this literature means alternating exemplars of DIFFERENT CATEGORIES to support inductive category learning. The app's question is whether two confusable vocabulary ITEMS should co-occur. Those are different manipulations with different literatures; the spacing/massing literature (robustly positive, and correctly cited elsewhere in the brief via Nakata & Suzuki) is the relevant one, not the interleaving literature. Transferring a moderator across that boundary is not licensed. (b) material_type 'both' is wrong: Brunmair & Richter aggregate laboratory category-learning studies (paintings, birds, mathematics, tastes, texts). Almost none are classroom L2. Labelling it 'both' launders lab evidence into classroom evidence at exactly the point the brief leans hardest on it.
corrected_claim: Brunmair & Richter (2019) establish that the interleaving benefit is strongly material-moderated and is not a general law. Whether the 'words' cell is negative, and what it contains, is unverified and must be read in full before use. Even if the sign is negative, it constrains INDUCTIVE CATEGORY LEARNING over word materials, not the co-presentation of confusable vocabulary items — so it cannot carry the brief's central verdict on its own. material_type should be 'lab-category-learning'. The brief's actual design split (contrast the character forms; do not co-acquire the two form–meaning mappings) is defensible on the Nakata & Suzuki and Kemp evidence alone; rest it there instead.
sources: Brunmair, M., & Richter, T. (2019). Similarity matters: A meta-analysis of interleaved learning and its moderators. Psychological Bulletin, 145(11), 1029–1052. [NOT VERIFIED THIS SESSION]
The brief's own gaps section, which states the moderator cell was not read

original_claim: Bahrick (1984) permastore... Implication: retire an item from the active deck after ~4 successful cross-day retrievals and re-audit it once at a long interval (months), rather than keeping it in a perpetual SRS rotation.
problem: The implication inverts the finding. Bahrick's central result is that the height of the permastore plateau is set by the AMOUNT OF ORIGINAL TRAINING — participants who had taken more Spanish courses plateaued higher. The permastore population had years of classroom instruction behind them, and even so the absolute retention levels are low (Bahrick & Phelps' own 8-year figure is 15%). Bahrick's message is therefore 'more original training buys a higher permanent floor', i.e. an argument for OVERLEARNING and many spaced sessions. The brief reads it as licence to stop early after four retrievals. Nothing in Bahrick sets a threshold at four, or at any number; that figure is invented. Secondary problem: 'strong' overstates a cross-sectional design in which rehearsal was measured by self-report questionnaire and the plateau could be partly cohort/selection artefact.
corrected_claim: Bahrick (1984) supports making cumulative training volume — not recency-weighted decay — the mastery variable, and supports the existence of a durable floor. It does NOT support early retirement, and it specifically does not license a four-retrieval threshold. If anything it argues the opposite: push items well past first mastery, because the plateau height scales with original training. Any retirement threshold must be an empirical product decision, labelled as such, not attributed to Bahrick. Downgrade to moderate for the cross-sectional design and self-report rehearsal measure.
sources: Bahrick, H. P. (1984). Semantic memory content in permastore. JEP: General, 113(1), 1–29. [NOT VERIFIED THIS SESSION]
Bahrick, H. P., & Phelps, E. (1987). JEP:LMC, 13(2), 344–349. [NOT VERIFIED THIS SESSION]

original_claim: The optimal gap between two study episodes is roughly 10–20% of the target retention interval... Store target_date on the user profile and compute gap = 0.15 × (target_date − now), clamped to at least one overnight. [evidence_strength: strong]
problem: Three failures. (1) The brief omits the finding's most important qualification: Cepeda et al.'s ridgeline is FLAT and ASYMMETRIC — performance is insensitive to gap across a broad plateau, and gaps that are too LONG cost far less than gaps that are too SHORT. A hard 0.15 coefficient over-fits a surface the authors themselves describe as broad. (2) SCOPE: the result is a TWO-SESSION finding (one study episode, one restudy, one test). It is not defined for an app that will give an item five to fifteen encounters. There is no 'the gap' in a multi-session schedule, and the extension to multi-session (expanding vs equal intervals) is a separate literature where differences are small and inconsistent. (3) STRENGTH INTERACTION: the optimal gap depends on how well the item was learned initially. Cepeda's material was trivia facts, already comprehensible in L1, encoded to a decent level in one sitting. A brand-new Chinese sign for a beginner has far lower initial strength. Applying 0.15 × 6 weeks ≈ 6 days to the SECOND EVER exposure of a novel character would, for most beginners, schedule the review after the item is already gone — converting review into re-learning. This is a live, shippable bug, not a nuance.
corrected_claim: Spacing gaps should scale with the retention horizon, and longer gaps are safer than shorter ones — that much is well supported. But the 10–20% figure is a two-session lab result on L1-comprehensible facts sitting on a flat optimum, and it must not be implemented as a fixed coefficient. Gate the gap on item strength as well as horizon: short gaps (hours-to-one-night) for an item's first two or three encounters regardless of trip date, widening toward the horizon-scaled gap only once the item has been retrieved successfully across days. Use an adaptive strength-based scheduler (see added findings) rather than a ratio formula.
sources: Cepeda, N. J., Vul, E., Rohrer, D., Wixted, J. T., & Pashler, H. (2008). Psychological Science, 19(11), 1095–1102. [NOT VERIFIED THIS SESSION]

original_claim: Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve... has a discontinuity around 24 hours... Implication (architecture): store a boolean 'crossed a sleep period' and treat the first overnight boundary as a scheduling landmark.
problem: The implication is not carried by the cited study. Murre & Dros is N = 1, nonsense syllables, savings-on-relearning — the brief says so itself and calls it 'the weakest possible material for generalising to meaningful L2 signs' — and then derives a concrete architecture commitment from a lumpy point in that single subject's curve. A bump at one time point in an N=1 curve is exactly the kind of noise a savings measure produces; it is not a discontinuity you can build a scheduler on. The overnight-gating rule may well be correct, but its support is Dumay & Gaskell and the consolidation literature elsewhere in the brief, not this study. As written, a reader auditing the brief would trace the app's sleep-boundary architecture back to a 140-year-old nonsense-syllable paradigm run on one person.
corrected_claim: Murre & Dros (2015) is a careful single-subject replication showing Ebbinghaus's savings curve reproduces and is not perfectly smooth. It supports one thing: do not hard-code a textbook exponential. It does NOT support the overnight-boundary architecture — re-attribute that implication to Dumay & Gaskell (2007) and the lexical-consolidation work, and delete the 24-hour-jump justification, which is a single-subject anomaly. Also verify the fitted function before any decay model ships (the brief admits it does not know it).
sources: Murre, J. M. J., & Dros, J. (2015). PLOS ONE, 10(7), e0120644. [NOT VERIFIED THIS SESSION]

original_claim: Word learning proceeds in two stages with different neural substrates... [evidence_strength: strong] ... Implication: give each item a two-bit state... This single rule implements most of the interference verdict below.
problem: The brief states in its own detail line that Davis & Gaskell (2009) is 'a theoretical review' and 'a framework, not a single effect' — and grades it 'strong'. A framework cannot be strong EVIDENCE; at most the dissociation it predicts is well replicated, which is a claim about other studies that are not cited here. This matters because the brief then says this item 'implements most of the interference verdict' — so the largest architecture commitment in the document (the consolidation gate that determines when a sibling may enter the deck) rests on a review article graded above its evidentiary weight. Additionally, the sleep-dependent lexical-competition effect that operationalises the second stage has accumulated null results and boundary conditions — the brief acknowledges one (Schimke et al. 2024) but grades this finding as though it had not.
corrected_claim: Complementary learning systems is a well-motivated framework whose central behavioural prediction — that lexical competition emerges later than explicit recall — has been observed repeatedly but not universally. Grade the framework 'moderate' and cite the specific behavioural dissociation studies rather than the review. The two-bit item state is a sensible engineering decision that is cheap and low-risk, but present it as a defensible design bet, not as a consequence of established neuroscience.
sources: Davis, M. H., & Gaskell, M. G. (2009). Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B, 364(1536), 3773–3800. [NOT VERIFIED THIS SESSION]

original_claim: Overnight integration tracks sleep spindle activity... Tamminen et al. (2010)... Implication (architecture): measure two separate things per item and do not average them.
problem: This is a neuroscience claim doing no work for the UI decision it is attached to, which is the pattern the review was asked to hunt. The recommendation — log recall accuracy and sibling-discrimination separately — follows entirely from the BEHAVIOURAL dissociation (competition emerges on a different schedule from recall), which is already established by Dumay & Gaskell in the previous finding. The polysomnography adds nothing: the app cannot measure spindles, cannot influence spindles, and would make the identical design choice if the EEG correlate had never been found. Separately, spindle–memory correlations are a small-N, many-degrees-of-freedom literature (multiple spindle metrics × multiple memory measures × multiple sleep stages) with weak replication, so it is also the shakiest support available for a recommendation that had better support already.
corrected_claim: Recall and sibling-discrimination should be logged and scheduled separately, on the strength of the behavioural dissociation alone. The spindle EEG finding should be deleted from the brief or demoted to a footnote; it justifies no design decision and its inclusion creates the false impression that the architecture is neuroscience-derived.
sources: Tamminen, J., Payne, J. D., Stickgold, R., Wamsley, E. J., & Gaskell, M. G. (2010). Journal of Neuroscience, 30(43), 14356–14360. [NOT VERIFIED THIS SESSION]

original_claim: The visual word form area is built by exposure to real written forms and recycles cortex weakly tuned to tools... [evidence_strength: strong; material_type: lab-wordlist] ... Implication: the neuroscience says the VARIABILITY is the active ingredient, not the realism... require at least 3 distinct renderings before an item can reach 'consolidated' state.
problem: This is the flagship non-sequitur in the brief, and it says the quiet part out loud: 'the neuroscience says the VARIABILITY is the active ingredient.' It does not. Dehaene-Lambertz et al. (2018) is a longitudinal fMRI study of ten six-year-olds learning to read an alphabetic script. It contains no manipulation of training variability, no learning outcome measure, no L2 learners, and no adults. It cannot speak to whether showing a sign in four fonts beats showing it in one. The '≥3 renderings' threshold is fabricated — no cited study estimates any such number. Two further problems: the neuronal-recycling/tool-cortex account is itself contested rather than settled, and material_type 'lab-wordlist' is simply false for a developmental neuroimaging study, which mislabels the evidence's ecology in the very field the brief claims to be auditing.
corrected_claim: The recommendation (ship many physical renderings per sign; never certify mastery on one visual instance) is probably right, but it must be re-grounded in behavioural perceptual-learning and high-variability-training evidence, not in VWFA imaging. Strike the sentence 'the neuroscience says the VARIABILITY is the active ingredient' — it is false as stated. Drop the '3 renderings' threshold or relabel it as an arbitrary product default. Correct material_type to 'developmental-neuroimaging'.
sources: Dehaene-Lambertz, G., Monzalvo, K., & Dehaene, S. (2018). PLOS Biology, 16(3), e2004103. [NOT VERIFIED THIS SESSION]

original_claim: Chinese character reading recruits additional left middle frontal gyrus... This is the one place the neuroimaging earns a UI change; do not over-read it beyond that. Implication (UI): render the breakdown as a spatial decomposition inside a square frame rather than as a linear list.
problem: The brief anticipates the objection and then commits the error anyway. An ALE meta-analysis of where blood flow changes in native Chinese readers cannot adjudicate between two layouts of a component-breakdown panel in a learning app. The inferential chain — LMFG activates during Chinese reading → LMFG is interpreted (contestedly, as the brief admits) as visuospatial addressing → therefore the panel should be a square rather than a list — has a contested interpretive step in the middle and an unbridged gap at the end. Neuroimaging of expert performance never constrains instructional layout, because it does not measure learning. The brief's own gaps section concedes the implication is 'weakly grounded', which is an argument for deleting it, not for shipping it with a caveat. Note also that the correct justification for spatial layout is already sitting in the brief: Zhang et al. (2021) on positional regularity is behavioural, is about LEARNERS, and actually bears on the question.
corrected_claim: Render the component breakdown spatially because component POSITION is part of what CSL learners must acquire and because positional regularity knowledge is acquired implicitly from distributional exposure (Zhang et al. 2021) — a behavioural rationale about learners. The fMRI meta-analyses establish anatomical differences between scripts in expert readers and should be cited, if at all, as background. They earn no UI change. Correct material_type from 'lab-wordlist' to 'neuroimaging-native-readers'.
sources: Wu, C.-Y., Ho, M.-H. R., & Chen, S.-H. A. (2012). NeuroImage, 63(1), 381–391. [NOT VERIFIED THIS SESSION]
Tan, L. H., Laird, A. R., Li, K., & Fox, P. T. (2005). Human Brain Mapping, 25(1), 83–91. [NOT VERIFIED THIS SESSION]

original_claim: Four-option multiple choice with genuinely competitive distractors is the format that AVOIDS retrieval-induced forgetting and instead strengthens the distractors — which converts the app's core mechanic into the intervention rather than the hazard... this reframes the whole design question.
problem: One-sided literature read on the finding the brief calls the reframing of the whole design. The multiple-choice testing literature has two halves, and the brief cites only the exculpatory one. The counterweight — Roediger & Marsh (2005), 'The positive and negative consequences of multiple-choice testing' — reports that plausible lures on a multiple-choice test PRODUCE later false answers, that this negative suggestion effect grows with the number of plausible alternatives, and that it persists even with feedback in some conditions. That is precisely the app's proposed configuration: four maximally plausible, maximally confusable options. The brief's own Nakata & Suzuki finding independently warns that harm from relatedness shows up as INTERFERENCE ERRORS while accuracy looks fine — the same signature Roediger & Marsh describe. So the brief contains the evidence that should have prompted caution and does not connect it. Material mismatch compounds it: Little et al. used general-knowledge facts at short delay, where 'retrieving why the other options are wrong' is possible because the learner already knows those facts. A beginner shown four Chinese signs cannot reason about why three are wrong, because they do not yet know any of them — the mechanism the finding depends on is absent at exactly the moment the brief wants to deploy it.
corrected_claim: Competitive multiple choice can produce test-induced learning of the alternatives, but it also reliably produces a negative suggestion effect that scales with lure plausibility. Both effects are real and they run in opposite directions for this design. The mechanism Little et al. identify requires that the learner be able to reject the distractors on knowledge they already have — so competitive confusable distractors are defensible only for items whose siblings are ALREADY consolidated, and are actively risky during acquisition. This makes the brief's consolidation gate load-bearing for the distractor policy too, and it makes 'ban random unrelated distractors' wrong as a blanket rule: unrelated distractors are the correct choice for a sign's first appearances.
sources: Little, J. L., Bjork, E. L., Bjork, R. A., & Angello, G. (2012). Psychological Science, 23(11), 1337–1344. [NOT VERIFIED THIS SESSION]

Roediger, H. L., III, & Marsh, E. J. (2005). The positive and negative consequences of multiple-choice testing. JEP: Learning, Memory, and Cognition, 31(5), 1155–1159. [OMITTED BY THE BRIEF; NOT VERIFIED THIS SESSION]

original_claim: L1 retrieval interferes with L2 access, so the game's high-bet 'all options in Chinese, no pinyin' mode is defensible on interference grounds... make the four options pictures or icons of the referent rather than Dutch/English words, so the player never routes through L1 at all.
problem: Over-claimed, under-sourced, and it recommends a change with a real downside risk. (a) Levy et al. (2007) is a picture-naming study about the ACCESSIBILITY OF L1 after speaking L2 — it is evidence that L2 production inhibits L1, which is close to the reverse of the direction the brief needs, and it says nothing about whether L1-mediated study harms L2 vocabulary ACQUISITION. (b) The counter-literature is large and is not cited: L1 translation pairs are consistently among the most efficient formats for early L2 vocabulary learning, and the standard model of early bilingual lexical access (Revised Hierarchical Model) treats L1 mediation as the normal and effective early route. Removing L1 from the options is therefore a bet against the mainstream finding, not an application of it. (c) Picture options introduce referential ambiguity that is severe for exactly this content: an icon can depict 'exit', but not 公斤 versus 斤, and not 麻 versus 辣 without collapsing into a chilli-pepper glyph for both. (d) SOURCING: the second source is an unpublished paper hosted on academia.edu and the first is a ResearchGate copy — neither is a peer-reviewed venue link, on a finding carrying a product decision.
corrected_claim: There is evidence of cross-language retrieval interference in both directions, but it does not establish that L1-glossed options harm L2 reading acquisition, and the L2 vocabulary literature broadly favours L1 translation as an efficient early format. Keep the Chinese-only mode as an advanced difficulty tier and as a face-validity match to the real-world task — both good reasons — but drop the interference justification. Do not replace L1 options with pictures by default: pilot it, because for quantity and taste terms pictures cannot express the contrast the item is testing.
sources: Levy, B. J., McVeigh, N. D., Marful, A., & Anderson, M. C. (2007). Psychological Science, 18(1), 29–34. [NOT VERIFIED THIS SESSION]
Kroll, J. F., & Stewart, E. (1994). Category interference in translation and picture naming (Revised Hierarchical Model). Journal of Memory and Language, 33(2), 149–174. [OMITTED BY THE BRIEF]

original_claim: For Chinese characters specifically... colour-coding the difference makes things worse... Implication (UI): keep the side-by-side panel but do NOT colour-highlight the differing stroke or component.
problem: A concrete UI prohibition, explicitly framed as cutting against a design instinct, resting on a single 2025 MDPI paper the brief could not read past the abstract, whose retention interval it admits it does not know, and whose colour result was on REACTION TIMES with a post-hoc 'visual overload' interpretation. Slower RTs in a beginner discrimination task are not evidence of worse learning — they are as consistent with more careful processing. Worse, the recommendation contradicts a large and meta-analytically supported instructional-design literature on signalling/cueing, which the brief does not cite at all: highlighting the critical feature is one of the better-supported multimedia learning principles, and it is the standard operationalisation of 'directing attention to the critical difference' — which the brief itself demands two findings later, citing the speech-perception training literature. So the brief simultaneously requires attention to be directed to the critical difference and forbids the most common mechanism for doing so, on weaker evidence.
corrected_claim: Do not ban colour highlighting of the distinguishing component. The evidence for the ban is one unverified single study using an RT measure; the evidence against it is a meta-analytically supported signalling principle plus the brief's own requirement that attention be explicitly directed to the critical difference. Treat colour as an A/B question, test it on delayed discrimination accuracy rather than RT, and if a concern about visual load is warranted, address it by limiting the number of simultaneous highlights rather than by prohibiting the affordance.
sources: Li, J., Shi, M., & Wang, X. (2025). Languages, 10(10), 260. [EXISTENCE NOT VERIFIED THIS SESSION]
Schneider, S., Beege, M., Nebel, S., & Rey, G. D. (2018). A meta-analysis of how signaling affects learning with media. Educational Research Review, 23, 1–24. [OMITTED BY THE BRIEF]

original_claim: material_type labels across the brief: Ishii (2015) = 'classroom-l2'; Kemp (2021) = 'classroom-l2'; Chang et al. (2022) = 'classroom-l2'; Li, Shi & Wang (2025) = 'classroom-l2'; Dehaene-Lambertz (2018) = 'lab-wordlist'; Wu, Ho & Chen (2012) = 'lab-wordlist'; Brunmair & Richter (2019) = 'both'.
problem: The labelling scheme conflates PARTICIPANT POPULATION with MATERIAL AND RETENTION ECOLOGY, which defeats the purpose of having the field at all. Ishii (2015) is labelled 'classroom-l2' while its own detail line concedes a 20-MINUTE retention interval and adds 'which is not evidence about learning a language' — the label contradicts the caveat in the same object. Kemp (2021) is a controlled factorial list-learning experiment. Chang et al. and Li et al. use L2 learners but run laboratory tasks at ≤1 week. Meanwhile two neuroimaging studies of native readers are labelled 'lab-wordlist', and a meta-analysis of laboratory category learning is labelled 'both'. Net effect: the field systematically flatters the ecological validity of exactly the findings that carry design decisions, which is the failure mode the brief claims to be guarding against.
corrected_claim: Split the field into two: population (lab-naive / L2-learner / classroom) and ecology (retention interval, material). Under that scheme: Ishii (2015) = L2-learner population, 20-minute lab interval — reclassify as lab and downgrade its weight accordingly, since the brief currently calls it 'the best-controlled test' of form-versus-meaning confusion. Kemp (2021) = L2-learner, lab-factorial with delayed test. Chang et al. (2022) = L2-learner, 1-week lab. Li et al. (2025) = naive, interval unknown. Dehaene-Lambertz (2018) and Wu et al. (2012) = neuroimaging, not word-list learning. Brunmair & Richter (2019) = lab category learning. Only Bahrick (1984, 1987, 1993) and Nakata & Suzuki (2019) survive as genuine classroom/real-L2 evidence, and the verdict should be visibly weighted toward those four.
sources: Internal to the brief under review — each label is contradicted by the study description in its own detail field (no external source required)

original_claim: Source access labels throughout: Bahrick & Phelps (1987) and Bahrick et al. (1993) marked 'abstract-only' with URLs pointing at full PDFs on gwern.net; Gais et al. (2006) marked 'full-text'.
problem: Two hygiene problems on a document whose stated top-line caveat is that everything is abstract-level. (1) The access labels are internally inconsistent: two sources are marked 'abstract-only' while linking to what are plainly complete article PDFs, so a reader cannot tell what was actually read. (2) gwern.net is a personal website re-hosting scanned copies of paywalled journal articles. For a brief that will be cited internally as the evidence base for a product, sourcing two of the four genuinely-classroom-L2 findings — the ones that survive my re-weighting and therefore carry the most weight — to unauthorised copies on a personal site is a durability and provenance problem. If the full texts were read, say so and cite the DOI; if they were not, the numbers (15% vs 8%, the 14/28/56-day schedule) should be marked unverified like everything else.
corrected_claim: Normalise access labels to what was actually read, and re-source the Bahrick papers to their DOIs (JEP:LMC 13(2), 344–349; Psychological Science 4(5), 316–321) via the publisher or an institutional copy. Given these are among the few real-classroom, long-interval findings in the brief, their numbers deserve first-hand verification before the savings-based progress metric is built on them.
sources: Internal to the brief under review (no external source required)
